file: 1994/1994-09-18_pyramid scam_marketing breakthrough_new recruit_amazingly wealthy_being your own boss_one thousand dollars_the world pays_money_scam.gif
title: Pyramid Scam Pitched as Breakthrough

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember, it's not a pyramid scam, it's a marketing breakthrough.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The beauty of it is a new recruit is born every minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we guaranteed to become amazingly wealthy?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: While being our own boss?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, unless you're lazy or ethical.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Each person you recruit pays you one thousand dollars. The recruits get their own recruits and charge them two thousand, and so on.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eventually, every person on earth will be giving you money. And that adds up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't argue with the math.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel like we're a big family.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The best part is that every person on earth will get rich!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Actually, the last recruit kinda gets it in the shorts.

setting: Presentation room with an easel and a couch
situation: Dogbert gives a slideshow-style pitch to Dilbert and Wally for a get-rich-quick scheme he insists is not a pyramid scam. The two eagerly buy in, convinced of guaranteed wealth and enthusiastic about the math. Dogbert finally admits that whoever recruits last loses out.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally believe everyone on earth can get rich from a pyramid scheme, and Dogbert casually admits the last recruit gets ruined, which exposes the scam's inevitable flaw.
summary: A scheming dog sells two gullible coworkers on a money-making plan whose mathematics quietly guarantees a loser at the bottom.

file: 1994/1994-12-16_ratbert as intern_high traffic cube_look busy_ratbert looks busy_at computer.gif
title: Ratbert the Busy-Looking Intern

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Since you won't go away, I'll make you an intern.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Great! What's an intern?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You'll spend your day in a high-traffic cube trying to look busy. Your main function is to make the rest of us glad we're not you.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How did people ever look busy before computers?

situation: Dilbert gives Ratbert, who keeps hanging around, the job of intern and explains that it means sitting in a high-traffic cubicle pretending to be busy. Ratbert is then shown at a computer, clicking the mouse and pondering how people appeared busy before computers existed.
punchline: The intern's real job is to look busy and make everyone else feel better about their own jobs, and Ratbert finds computers the perfect tool for faking productivity.
summary: Dilbert hands the persistent Ratbert a made-up internship whose only duty is to look occupied, and the little rat happily discovers that a computer makes that easy.

file: 1994/1994-11-20_share accomplishments_created dcoument_desktop publishing_two day class_digitized photos_color highlights_multi column_clip art_icons_visual mosaic_add topic_some content_enjoy work.gif
title: Fancy Document With No Content

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's go around the table and share our accomplishments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created a document this week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But this is no ordinary document!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I bought a $500 desktop publishing program and took a two-day class to learn it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I incorporated digitized photos and color highlights in a multi-column page layout!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Clip-art icons are sprinkled liberally around the page to form a visual mosaic!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Next week - God willing - I'll add a topic and some content.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you remember when I said you should enjoy your work? I didn't mean it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At the boss's request, the team shares accomplishments, and Dilbert proudly describes a document he created using a newly purchased desktop publishing program and a two-day class. He lists all the flashy formatting features but admits the document still has no topic or content. The boss, irritated, says he didn't really mean it when he told Dilbert to enjoy his work.
punchline: Dilbert spent his time and money on fancy formatting and clip art while producing a document with nothing in it, and the boss's retraction of his advice to enjoy work shows his exasperation.
summary: An employee brags about a visually elaborate but completely empty document, leaving his boss regretting having encouraged him to have fun at work.

file: 1994/1994-03-03_meeting_preliminary recommendation_radically reengineered_business process_coughed skull_business.gif
title: Reengineering Recommendation Causes Skull Cough

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's our preliminary recommendation for radically reengineering our business processes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Aaagh! Cough spoit!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bonk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He coughed up his skull.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll bet that smarts.

situation: Dilbert hands a report with his team's preliminary recommendation for radically reengineering the company's business processes across the desk to a boss who is mostly off-panel. The boss lets out a horrible cough and a skull bounces onto the desk. Afterward Dilbert tells Dogbert that the boss coughed up his skull, and Dogbert dryly comments on it.
punchline: Dogbert deadpans that coughing up one's skull must hurt, a casual reaction to an absurd and gruesome result of simply receiving a reengineering report.
summary: A manager receives a proposal to overhaul company operations and responds by hacking up his own skull, leaving a dog to quip about the pain.

file: 1994/1994-10-04_coffeee iv_exercise_given up sleep_nutrition_intravenous_caffeine_main line java_health.gif
title: Coffee Drip Coworker Holds Aorta

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's the job going, Anne?

transcript.speaker: Anne
transcript.text: Much better, now that I've given up sleep, exercise and nutrition in favor of coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Any adverse effects?

transcript.speaker: Anne
transcript.text: This is the aorta of the last person who asked me that.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker named Anne how her job is going. She is wired up to a coffee pot dripping directly into her arm like an IV, and she says she has given up sleep, exercise and healthy eating in favor of coffee. When Dilbert asks about side effects, she holds up a human aorta, implying she has become violent toward people who ask.
punchline: The caffeine-addicted coworker has become so unhinged that she has apparently ripped the aorta out of the last person who asked about adverse effects.
summary: A coworker hooked up to an intravenous coffee drip admits her lifestyle has collapsed, then reveals a grisly souvenir from the last person to question her.

file: 1994/1994-03-08_budget analyst_budget cuts_intelligent choices_understand enginering_strategy.gif
title: Budget Analyst Told to Cut

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Susan, I want you to make some budget cuts throughout my department.

transcript.speaker: Susan
transcript.text: But I'm only the budget analyst.

transcript.speaker: Susan
transcript.text: I couldn't possibly understand all the engineering projects enough to make intelligent choices.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? Great! I thought it was just me!

transcript.speaker: Susan
transcript.text: Shall I whomp up a strategy while I'm at it?

situation: The Boss orders Susan, the budget analyst, to make budget cuts across his engineering department. She objects that she doesn't understand the engineering projects well enough to choose wisely. The Boss cheerfully welcomes this, as it shows he isn't the only one who doesn't understand, and she offers to come up with a strategy too.
punchline: The Boss is delighted to learn that someone else is also clueless about the engineering projects, so ignorance becomes a qualification for making the cuts and even for setting strategy.
summary: A manager gleefully hands budget slashing to an analyst who admits she knows nothing about the projects, taking her ignorance as a welcome sign of kinship.

file: 1994/1994-01-09_personal life_engineering project_mission_find girlfreind_feasible alternatives_calculate attractiveness_buying power_attractive baboon_face transplant.gif
title: Engineering Approach to Finding Girlfriend

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should approach my personal life as if it were an engineering project.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What is the mission of this project?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Find a girlfriend!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good. Now consider the feasible alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Define "feasible."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Never mind. Let's move on.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now let's calculate your attractiveness ratio so we can narrow the field of girlfriend options.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's see... Your buying power narrows the choices to a woman who just got a face transplant from a baboon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it was an attractive baboon. I should call her.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Somewhere between desire and engineering lies stupidity.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dilbert and Dogbert talking across a desk
situation: Dilbert decides to treat his love life like an engineering project, and Dogbert plays along as project consultant, defining the mission and the feasible alternatives. After calculating Dilbert's attractiveness ratio and buying power, Dogbert concludes his only option is a woman with a baboon face transplant. Dilbert hopefully suggests the baboon might have been attractive.
punchline: Dilbert's rigorous engineering method leads only to a dismal dating pool, and his desperate optimism about an 'attractive baboon' shows that desire overrides his engineering logic, which Dogbert labels stupidity.
summary: A lovelorn engineer applies project-management methods to dating, only to be told his realistic prospects are a woman with a baboon's face.

file: 1994/1994-06-04_inflation eating_no real opportunity_other compnaies_downsizing_miss the 80s_get away with anything.gif
title: Boss Exploits Downsizing Era Leverage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You've got inflation eating you from the bottom... and no real opportunity for a promotion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And as long as all the other companies are downsizing too, you have no leverage. I can get away with anything!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I miss the eighties.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does this hurt?

situation: The Boss gleefully explains to Dilbert that inflation is eroding his pay, promotions are unlikely, and widespread downsizing means Dilbert has no bargaining power. In the last panel, Dilbert wistfully says he misses the eighties while the Boss, standing behind him, is doing something painful to him, asking if it hurts.
punchline: Because employees have no leverage in a downsizing job market, the Boss can literally abuse Dilbert physically and get away with it, making the eighties' better job market look appealing.
summary: Armed with the knowledge that workers can't afford to quit in a shrinking job market, a manager smugly demonstrates his freedom to mistreat an employee.

file: 1994/1994-04-03_bun_eat a bug_evalution_motivation_performance evaluation.gif
title: Eat a Bug for Excellent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your performance this year was "fair."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I'll raise your appraisal to "excellent" if you'll eat a bug.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Say what?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Eat a bug.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't have much luck with the other management techniques so I'm kinda winging it now.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do I get to pick the bug?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's way more motivational if I pick the bug.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How did your evaluation go?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: MXLNT

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do I get a bun?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You guys are never happy.

setting: The Boss's office during performance reviews
situation: The Boss tells Wally his performance was merely fair, then offers to upgrade his appraisal to excellent if he eats a bug. The Boss admits he is improvising because his other management techniques failed. Wally eats the bug and gets his rating, then Dilbert steps in for his own review and asks if he gets a bun with his bug.
punchline: The Boss's absurd bug-eating demand is met with compliance, and Dilbert's request for a bun shows employees will haggle over the terms of their own humiliation, prompting the Boss to complain they are never happy.
summary: A manager with no real motivational tools bribes his staff with better ratings in exchange for swallowing insects.

file: 1994/1994-02-25_eliminated budget_getting dumber_brain shrivel_hair different.gif
title: Training Cut Shrivels Dilbert's Brain

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've completely eliminated the budget for technical training!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting dumber every minute. My brain is starting to shrivel like a raisin!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get out of my office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Even my hair feels different.

situation: Dilbert storms into the Boss's office holding a paper and complains that the technical training budget has been completely eliminated. He dramatically claims he is getting dumber by the minute and that his brain is shrivelling. The Boss simply tells him to leave, and Dilbert walks out remarking that even his hair feels different.
punchline: Dilbert's exaggerated, deadpan claim that losing training is physically shrinking his brain (even changing his hair) mocks management's indifference to employee development, which the Boss answers only by dismissing him.
summary: After training funds are axed, an indignant engineer insists his intellect is withering while his uninterested manager just shoos him away.

file: 1994/1994-01-23_company cellular_dropped in john_fish it out_pager fell_array of tools_glasses_toilet_all needs.gif
title: Dilbert Drops Phone in Toilet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a replacement for my company cellular phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I dropped mine in the... john.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Again?? Why don't you reach in and fish it out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried, but then my pager fell in too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reach in and get them both.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried of course, but when my vast array of writing tools fell in they kind of wedged...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try it again!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Where are your glasses?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a replacement company cellular phone, admitting he dropped his in the toilet. The boss keeps telling him to reach in and retrieve the items, while Dilbert explains that his pager and then his pens also fell in. The boss finally notices Dilbert is not wearing his glasses.
punchline: The boss's insistence that Dilbert keep reaching into the toilet leads to the implication that Dilbert's glasses fell in as well, which he irritably refuses to discuss.
summary: A man asking for a new work phone after a bathroom mishap gets increasingly absurd orders from his boss to dig out each item he has lost.

file: 1994/1994-12-19_quality award_killed by sea turtle_went snorkeling.gif
title: Quality Award Named After Turtle Victim

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company has decided to compete for the "Millard Bullrush Quality Award."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bullrush? Isn't he the politician who went snorkeling and got killed by a sea turtle?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're faster than they look.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think we can win this.

situation: The Boss announces the company will compete for the Millard Bullrush Quality Award. Wally recalls that Bullrush was a politician killed by a sea turtle while snorkeling. The Boss remarks that turtles are faster than they look, and Wally concludes the company can win the award.
punchline: Wally and the Boss treat the award's namesake dying to a sea turtle as a sign the competition is weak, so winning the quality award seems easy.
summary: A manager's announcement of a quality contest turns into a discussion of the namesake's absurd death and the staff's confidence that it will be an easy win.

file: 1994/1994-05-27_rattus not rat_genus_larger community_squeak_forgot to laugh_so funny.gif
title: Rattus Demands Respect From Bob

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: From now on, Bob please refer to me as a "Rattus," not by the diminutive term "Rat."

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Frankly, I've never thought of folks like you in terms of your genus. I see you as part of a larger community.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Yeah - the community of things that go "squeak" when I step on them.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: That's so funny I forgot to laugh.

setting: A living room with a blue couch
situation: Ratbert, perched on the arm of a couch, asks Bob the green dinosaur to call him by the scientific name "Rattus" instead of "Rat." Bob replies that he thinks of Ratbert as part of a larger community rather than by genus, then reveals it is the community of things that squeak when he steps on them. Ratbert deadpans that he is not amused.
punchline: Bob turns a polite-sounding remark about 'community' into a threat, implying he steps on small creatures like Ratbert, and Ratbert sarcastically says it is too funny to laugh at.
summary: A small pet's bid for a more dignified name is met with a cheerfully menacing quip about squashing him underfoot.

file: 1994/1994-03-13_body language_politely tell_remove watch_smash watch_daily planner_feel good_act bored_self heimlich manuever_kerokian dodge_instructions.gif
title: Dogbert's Guide to Silencing Babblers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's body language update

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you hampered by the limits of conventional body language?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can help.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How can you politely tell somebody he's babbling?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Babble babble

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Remove the offender's watch while he babbles.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Babble

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Smash the watch with your daily planner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Babble

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whack!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: This won't stop the babble, but it will feel real good for a minute.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Babble

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Mmm

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Use this position to signal your surrender to the babble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Babble

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Next week: the Self-Heimlich Maneuver and the Kervorkian Dodge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Babble

situation: Dogbert presents a body language lesson on how to politely tell someone they are babbling. A coworker demonstrates by taking Dilbert's watch while he talks, smashing it with her daily planner, and finally slumping back in her chair in surrender while Dilbert keeps babbling regardless.
punchline: None of the increasingly violent 'polite' body language techniques stops the babbler, so the only real result is the brief satisfaction of smashing his watch and eventual resigned surrender.
summary: A mock instructional lesson shows ever more desperate ways to hint to a chatterbox that he should stop, none of which work.

file: 1994/1994-02-20_45 inch screen_communications staellite_cure disease_fish appear on screen_great products_marketing_new product_room freshener_telepathic user_whiten teeth_time travel_business.gif
title: Marketing's Impossible Product Wishlist

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How great products are designed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go talk to marketing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Groan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dave, tell me what marketing wants the new product to do.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: It has to have a 45-inch screen and still fit in a purse or a wallet.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: It needs to act as a communications satellite as well as a room freshener.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh...

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: It must cure deadly diseases and whiten your teeth while you sleep!

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Ha ha!! And it has to be capable of time travel!! And have a telepathic user interface!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Slap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could write a program that makes fish appear on the computer screen.

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Yeah... a lot of people want that.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and an office desk
situation: The Boss sends Dilbert to ask marketing what the new product should do. A marketing guy named Dave gleefully lists absurd, impossible features, escalating until Dilbert slaps him. Dilbert then offers a modest fish-on-screen program, and the chastened marketing man says that's what people want.
punchline: After being buried in impossible requirements, the marketing guy accepts a trivial fish-on-screen program as the winning product, implying customers will buy any gimmick and that marketing demands are detached from reality.
summary: A marketing rep rattles off wildly impossible product demands until Dilbert slaps him, then happily endorses a silly aquarium program instead.

file: 1994/1994-11-03_interdisciplinary task force_source of problem_xray skull_decision making process.gif
title: Bad Process Fixing Bad Process

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm starting an interdisciplinary task force to study our decision-making process.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, you're using a bad decision-making process to decide how to fix our bad decision-making process?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know how else we could find the source of our problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: X-ray your skull?

situation: The Boss announces he is forming an interdisciplinary task force to study the company's decision-making process. Dilbert points out the circular logic of using a flawed process to fix a flawed process. The Boss claims there is no other way to find the source of the problem, and Dilbert suggests he x-ray his own skull.
punchline: Dilbert implies that the real source of the company's bad decisions is the Boss's own head, which he suggests should be x-rayed to find the problem.
summary: A manager launches a committee to repair the company's faulty choices, and his employee sarcastically points to the manager himself as the obvious culprit.

file: 1994/1994-09-14_not welcome_against rules_eat ratbert_work not done_natural enemy_keyboard_mouse_computer_technology.gif
title: Cat Hunts Mouse on Keyboard

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're not welcome here, cat. It's against house rules to eat Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Cat
transcript.text: My work here is not done until I have pounced on my natural enemy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who are you, and what are you doing on my keyboard?

situation: Dogbert, standing with Ratbert, warns an unfamiliar cat that eating Ratbert is against house rules. The cat announces that its work is not done until it pounces on its natural enemy. In the last panel Dilbert finds the cat sprawled across his computer keyboard and asks who it is and what it is doing.
punchline: The cat's 'natural enemy' is the computer mouse, so it pounces on the keyboard hunting it instead of going after Ratbert, leaving Dilbert baffled by a stranger on his desk.
summary: A stray cat is warned off Ratbert, but its real prey turns out to be the computer mouse, which sends it face-first into Dilbert's keyboard.

file: 1994/1994-03-22_lunch date_rejction_says she's dead_seeing an illusion.gif
title: Faking Death to Avoid Lunch

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lunch? With you? I'd love to but... uh...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm clinically dead. What you see are merely the last involuntary spasms before I stiffen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a hand truck.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: This was a very bad idea.

situation: Dilbert invites a coworker to lunch, and she scrambles for an excuse, claiming she is clinically dead and merely twitching in her final spasms. Dilbert calmly answers that he has a hand truck, offering to wheel her along anyway. She regrets having made up such an absurd excuse.
punchline: Her ridiculous excuse backfires when Dilbert takes it literally and offers to haul her corpse to lunch on a hand truck, so the lie only makes the date harder to escape.
summary: A woman invents a grisly excuse to dodge a lunch invitation, only for her suitor to treat it as a logistical problem he can solve.

file: 1994/1994-04-16_makeup_real bother_a lot of work_admit_remove old makeup_bowling alley.gif
title: Makeup Removal and the Bowling Alley

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I've never minded putting makeup on, but it's a real bother to take it off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That seems like a lot of work, I must admit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I still think it's better to remove the old stuff.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It's only a problem at the bowling alley.

setting: Unspecified teal-background space, likely a date or casual conversation
situation: Dilbert chats with a curly-haired woman who complains that taking makeup off is a hassle. Dilbert politely says it sounds like a lot of work, then insists it is still better to remove the old makeup. The woman then reveals that the problem only comes up at the bowling alley, hinting at how she actually handles makeup.
punchline: Dilbert assumes she removes makeup, but her reply implies she just layers new makeup on top of the old and it only shows up when she gets hot or sweaty bowling, making his earnest advice both obvious and slightly rude.
summary: A woman admits she dislikes cleaning off cosmetics, and Dilbert's well-meaning advice is met with a deadpan hint that she mostly just keeps applying more.

file: 1994/1994-12-07_iso 9000 project_hand picked_manger_project.gif
title: Hand-Picked Team? Never Mind Why

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you for coming to the "ISO 9000" project kick-off meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Each of you was hand-picked by your manager for this project because...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... never mind why.

situation: Dilbert opens the kick-off meeting for an ISO 9000 project and tells the attendees they were each hand-picked by their managers. He starts to explain the reason, then looks at the unimpressive group seated around the table and trails off.
punchline: Dilbert realizes the real reason managers chose these people is that they were the least valuable or most expendable employees, so he cuts the explanation short.
summary: A project leader begins to flatter his team for being specially chosen, then thinks better of it once he sees who actually showed up.

file: 1994/1994-11-08_donate blood_good for society_too comepetetive_thirsty.gif
title: Competitive Blood Donation Drive Leaves Dilbert Thirsty

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't mind donating blood... it's good for society...

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But I'm worried that our company is getting too competitive about how much we give compared to other companies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Man, I'm thirsty!!

setting: Office hallway outside a company blood drive
situation: Two coworkers stand in line for a company blood donation, and one says he supports giving blood but worries the company is turning it into a competition against other firms. In the last panel, Dilbert wanders by looking drained, with a tube coming out of his arm, and complains that he is thirsty.
punchline: The company's competitive urge to out-donate rival firms has apparently led to Dilbert giving far too much blood, leaving him drained and thirsty.
summary: A charity blood drive turns into a corporate rivalry, and the cost is borne by a visibly depleted employee.

file: 1994/1994-11-15_first draft_sugesstions_nit picking_break up of marriage_wally_over does_critical.gif
title: Nit-Picking Reviewer Mocks Marriage Breakup

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I made a few thousand suggestions on your first draft.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Of all the pleasures of life, I think I like nit-picking the best!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That could explain the break-up of your marriage.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You wouldn't believe what SHE thought was fun.

situation: Wally hands Dilbert back his first draft covered with a few thousand suggestions and cheerfully declares that nit-picking is his favorite pleasure in life. Dilbert remarks that this habit might explain why Wally's marriage ended. Wally answers that his ex-wife's idea of fun was even stranger.
punchline: Wally's nit-picking is so extreme that it likely wrecked his marriage, yet he casually implies his ex-wife's idea of fun was the truly bizarre one.
summary: A coworker buries a colleague's draft in thousands of edits, gleefully admits he loves nitpicking, and brushes off a jab about his failed marriage.

file: 1994/1994-03-31_darwinian saga_evolution_invet computers_ironic twist_monkey_own species_tail_animals.gif
title: Monkey Gloats About Evolutionary Takeover

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: Your big mistake, evolution-wise, was inventing computers that are easier to use if you have a tail.

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: It's an ironic twist in the Darwinian saga. You've guaranteed the extinction of your own species.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop working while I'm talking to you, Zimbu!!

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: I can hear the evolutionary clock... tick-tick-tick-tick

situation: A monkey named Zimbu sits at a computer and lectures Dilbert about how humans made a fatal evolutionary error by building computers that favor tails. Dilbert, annoyed, tells the monkey to stop working while he is being spoken to. Zimbu keeps typing and taunts him with the sound of the evolutionary clock ticking.
punchline: The monkey smugly claims computers will make humans extinct, and Dilbert's only response is to scold it for working while he talks, missing the threat entirely.
summary: A tail-equipped monkey at a keyboard predicts that humanity has engineered its own obsolescence while its human coworker merely demands its attention.

file: 1994/1994-10-26_planning to focus_products killing people_steal office supplies_studies are flawed_urban areas_advertising.gif
title: Stealing Pens After Corporate Atrocities

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Ethics Advisor

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We know our products are killing people, but we're claiming the studies are flawed.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We're planning to focus our advertising on the youth market in poor urban areas.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: So, given all that, is it okay for me to steal office supplies?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd have to say yes.

situation: A worried employee consults Dogbert, the ethics advisor, and confesses that the company knows its products kill people, is denying the evidence, and plans to market them to poor urban youth. After this litany of corporate wrongdoing, he asks whether it is acceptable for him to steal office supplies. Dogbert approves.
punchline: After hearing about the company's monstrous behavior, the employee's only ethical worry is petty office-supply theft, and Dogbert cynically agrees that this minor crime is justified by comparison.
summary: A conscience-stricken worker lays out his employer's deadly and predatory practices, then asks his ethics advisor for permission to pocket some stationery.

file: 1994/1994-06-06_choke on donut_psychic powers_bob in office.gif
title: Psychic Coworker Reveals Bob's Hatred

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is Bob in his office?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Since Bob's office is all of twenty feet away, I'll have to use my psychic powers to determine the answer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could go look.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Bob hates you. He secretly wishes you'd choke on a donut.

situation: Dilbert asks a seated coworker whether Bob is in his office. She sarcastically claims she must use psychic powers because the office is twenty feet away, and when Dilbert suggests simply looking, she announces that Bob secretly hates him and wishes he would choke on a donut.
punchline: The coworker's lazy, sarcastic 'psychic' act turns into an unprompted and cheerfully cruel revelation that Bob secretly wants Dilbert dead.
summary: A lazy coworker mocks a simple question with fake clairvoyance, then casually drops a nasty secret about what a colleague thinks of Dilbert.

file: 1994/1994-05-14_huge time saver_final consulting_company_deadweight_employees.fired_company directory_business.gif
title: Consultant's Report Is the Directory

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my final consulting report on your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've listed all the deadweight employees who should be fired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is the company directory.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Finding that was a huge time-saver.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, hands The Boss his final report and says it lists all the deadweight employees who should be fired. The Boss looks at it and realizes it is simply the company directory. Dogbert replies that finding it saved him a lot of time.
punchline: The consultant's list of employees to fire is the entire company directory, implying everyone is deadweight and that consultants deliver lazy, low-effort work for high fees.
summary: A consultant presents a termination list that turns out to be nothing more than a staff phone book, which he proudly calls efficient.

file: 1994/1994-01-25_bad timing_corporate offcie_declared war_french embassy_satellite program_slingshot.gif
title: Elbonian Slingshot Satellite Launch Disaster

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The corporate office sent me to head up the Elbonian satellite launching program.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Ooh... bad timing. The French delivered their satellite early. We already tried to launch it with the town slingshot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It doesn't get much worse than this.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: It flattened the French embassy. They declared war an hour ago.

situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia, sent by the corporate office to lead the local satellite launching program. The Elbonians explain that they already launched the French satellite with the town slingshot, and it landed on the French embassy. France has responded by declaring war.
punchline: Dilbert's job turns out to be cleaning up a catastrophe that has already happened, since the primitive slingshot launch destroyed an embassy and started a war before he even arrived.
summary: A newly arrived engineer learns that the locals have already fired a foreign satellite from a slingshot, with diplomatic consequences.

file: 1994/1994-01-04_organization chart_management_bottom_most important employees_payed least_upside down chart.gif
title: Upside-Down Org Chart Pay Question

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've redesigned the organization chart to show management at the bottom supporting our most important employees!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Why do the most important employees get payed the least?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because they would never think of ideas like this upside-down chart concept.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss proudly presents a redesigned organization chart that places management at the bottom, supposedly supporting the most important employees. Dilbert raises his hand and asks why those important employees are paid the least. The Boss answers that they are paid less because they would never come up with an idea like this one.
punchline: The Boss's answer is self-congratulating nonsense that dodges the pay question, claiming employees earn less because they lack the brilliant ideas management has, such as a purely cosmetic chart flip.
summary: A manager unveils a flipped org chart as a gesture of respect, then dodges a pointed pay question by boasting about his own creativity.

file: 1994/1994-01-18_cubicle gestapo_plastic plant_rebel_evil_anti perspirant_breaking down_take a stand.gif
title: Dilbert's Sweaty Plastic Plant Rebellion

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to defy the cubicle gestapo and keep this plastic plant on my desk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a rebel... I'm evil. My anti-perspirant is breaking down!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes a man has to take a stand.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Could he stand someplace else?

situation: Dilbert sneaks a small plastic plant into his cubicle in defiance of office rules and becomes extremely nervous, sweating through his shirt at his own act of rebellion. He announces to Dogbert that sometimes a man has to take a stand, and Dogbert asks him to take it somewhere else.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of heroic rebellion is keeping a tiny plastic plant on his desk, and he is so anxious about it that he sweats profusely, which Dogbert answers with a dry request that he stand elsewhere (away from the smell).
summary: A timid cubicle worker nervously smuggles in a fake plant, sweating through his shirt, and his dog wants him and his stand to go away.

file: 1994/1994-05-21_change project_actual knowledge_changes_voicemail.gif
title: Uninvited to Your Own Project's Meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We just had a meeting and decided to change your project substantially.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We didn't invite you to the meeting because things go smoother when nobody has any actual knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, what are the changes?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I remember I'll leave you a voice mail.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that a meeting was held without him and that his project has been substantially changed. He explains that Dilbert was left out on purpose because things go smoother when nobody has real knowledge. When Dilbert asks what the changes are, the Boss casually says he may leave a voice mail if he remembers.
punchline: The Boss openly admits that excluding the person who actually knows the project is deliberate, then shows he can't even be bothered to communicate the changes reliably.
summary: A manager reveals he rewrote an engineer's project behind his back, excluded him on purpose, and may or may not mention the details later.

file: 1994/1994-11-01_product development process_buy in_managers_happy if dead_executive oversight_issues_blind_looked at bulb.gif
title: Executive Oversight Groups and Projector Blindness

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: Problem: Our product development process requires buy-in from managers who'd be happier if we all died.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: My solution is to create executive oversight groups who don't understand the issues and don't have time to meet.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I'm... I'm blind!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You looked directly at the bulb again.

setting: Conference room during a slide presentation
situation: A manager gives an overhead-projector presentation about a product development process that depends on hostile managers. His proposed fix is to add executive oversight groups that don't understand the issues and can't find time to meet. He then stares into the projector bulb and goes blind, while Dilbert and a coworker watch, unsurprised.
punchline: The presenter's solution adds useless bureaucracy to fix a bureaucratic problem, and his careless blinding from staring into the projector bulb mirrors his poor judgment.
summary: A presenter proposes clueless, unavailable oversight committees as the cure for a dysfunctional approval process, then blinds himself by staring into the projector lamp once more.

file: 1994/1994-01-16_stealth business suit_sound dampers_sticky note_special polymers_phone_pager_happiest man_sunday.gif
title: Stealth Suit Against Assignments, On Sunday

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a "stealth business suit" to avoid assignments at work today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you think, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (blank speech bubble)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha ha! My sound dampers have cancelled you out!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now watch what happens if somebody tries to attach a little yellow sticky note to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: See! Nothing sticks to the special polymers!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (blank speech bubble)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And my wireless phone and pager are encased in lead so they can't detect incoming calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, I'm off to "work." Ha ha ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There goes the happiest man who ever forgot it was Sunday.

situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert a bulky, padded suit he built to avoid work assignments. It supposedly dampens sound, repels sticky notes, and shields his phone and pager from incoming calls. He heads off to work delighted with himself, while Dogbert observes that it is actually Sunday.
punchline: Dilbert went to elaborate lengths to dodge work assignments on a day when nobody would have given him any, because he forgot it was Sunday.
summary: An inventor of an elaborate anti-assignment costume marches off to the office, unaware that it's the weekend.

file: 1994/1994-12-26_design interface_got out_hired professional_international terrorist_last week_went to yale_new employee_talks with dilbert.gif
title: Hiring a Terrorist for Interface Design

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a professional to help us design our product interface.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His last job was as an international terrorist. It's not a perfect fit but he went to Yale.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, I hear you went to Yale, Sven.

transcript.speaker: Sven
transcript.text: I yust got out last week.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has hired a professional to help design the product interface, then reveals the man was most recently an international terrorist but attended Yale. Dilbert makes small talk with the new hire, Sven, about Yale, and Sven's reply suggests he has just been released from prison.
punchline: Sven's answer implies that the 'Yale' he attended was a prison, not the university, and he was freed only last week, so the Boss's hiring choice is both unqualified and alarming.
summary: A boss brags about his unusual new design consultant, whose dubious background is made clear when he answers a question about his schooling with a reference to his recent release.

file: 1994/1994-07-03_comic book_adventure of boron_most boring man_ego_boron_slays marketing dept_engineers_respect in society_transfer mode technology.gif
title: The Adventures of Boron, Most Boring Man

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you drawing, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm creating a comic book called "The Adventures of Boron."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "The most boring man in the entire universe."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Boron looks like me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Geez, what an ego you have.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In chapter one, Boron slays the entire marketing department by explaining asynchronous protocols.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it's high time we engineers got a little respect in this society!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Furthermore, there are many advantages to asynchronous transfer mode switch technology!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: First, there's bandwidth...

situation: Dogbert is drawing a comic book called 'The Adventures of Boron' about the most boring man in the universe, and Dilbert notices the hero looks just like him. After Dogbert explains that Boron defeats the marketing department by lecturing on asynchronous protocols, Dilbert gets indignant about engineers' lack of respect. He then launches into a lecture on ATM switch technology, proving himself to be exactly like Boron while Dogbert has fallen over in boredom.
punchline: Dilbert protests that engineers deserve respect, then immediately starts boring Dogbert senseless with a technical lecture on networking, proving the comic's portrayal accurate.
summary: A cartoon dog sketches a hero who bores enemies to death, and the engineer who resembles him proves the point by droning on about network switching.

file: 1994/1994-06-11_smart like you_rat_garbageman_special gift_creativity_talent_ability to love.gif
title: Garbage Man Offers Consolation, Rat Burps

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I wish I were smart like you. Then I'd get some respect.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: We're all smart in different ways. Your special gift may be creativity, a talent, or even the ability to love.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I can burp my cheeks full... URP.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I'd go with that if I were you.

setting: Outdoors next to a garbage can
situation: Ratbert, sitting on a garbage can, tells a garbage man he wishes he were smart so he would get respect. The garbage man kindly says everyone is smart in different ways, suggesting creativity, talent or the ability to love. Ratbert offers his own special gift, burping his cheeks full, and the garbage man advises him to stick with that.
punchline: After a heartfelt speech about hidden talents, Ratbert's only gift is burping, and even the garbage man suggests he should go with it, implying he has no other talent.
summary: A sympathetic refuse collector tries to boost a lowly rodent's confidence, but the creature's proudest skill turns out to be gross and unimpressive.

file: 1994/1994-09-26_saint dogbert_priority matrix_agenda.gif
title: Saint Dogbert Enforces Meeting Agenda

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invited Saint Dogbert to bludgeon anybody who strays from the agenda into something stupid.

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: That reminds me of the productization of our Tiger Team's priority matrix.

transcript.speaker: Woman in meeting
transcript.text: Actually, that was on the agenda.

transcript.speaker: Man in meeting
transcript.text: Oops. Carry on.

situation: Dilbert announces he has invited Saint Dogbert, who wears a yellow mitre and holds a bone, to bludgeon anyone who wanders off the agenda into something stupid. A colleague then brings up the productization of the Tiger Team's priority matrix, and Dogbert strikes him down. A coworker points out that topic was actually on the agenda, and the injured man lies on the floor apologizing.
punchline: Business jargon sounds so meaningless that Dogbert assumed it was off-agenda nonsense, and clubbed a man for speaking something that was actually on the agenda.
summary: A meeting enforcer armed with a bone clubs a coworker for speaking gibberish that turns out to be an official agenda item.

file: 1994/1994-05-29_promotion_director_engineering group_assignment_fire them all_eliminate_passing off_dirty work_promotion for nothing.gif
title: Promoted to Fire Everyone Else

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, I'm promoting you to Director of the Engineering Quality Group!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wait a minute. I thought you were going to eliminate that group.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your assignment is to fire them all.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aaagh! That will be hideous!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And when I'm done you won't need a director. Then you'll fire me!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have my word that I will not fire you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, guys.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That would be a job for Executive Director Dilbert.

situation: The Boss promotes Wally to director of the Engineering Quality Group, and Wally celebrates until he realizes his assignment is to fire everyone in the group. He points out that once they are gone the director role is pointless and he will be fired too. The Boss promises not to fire him, then thinks of promoting Dilbert to handle that job.
punchline: The Boss keeps his word by technically not firing Wally himself, instead creating another promoted fall guy, Dilbert, to do it.
summary: A manager hands out a flashy promotion whose only duty is to dismiss the whole team, then simply recruits the next person to carry out the final cut.

file: 1994/1994-07-15_carpal tunnel_surgery_carpool_room in carpool_permanent damges_wear braces_medical.gif
title: Carpool Versus Carpal Tunnel Mix-Up

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hear you need a carpool urgently.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I need "carpal tunnel surgery."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The repetitive motion of typing has caused permanent damage. I have to wear braces until the surgery.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's no room in my carpool.

situation: Wally has heard a rumor that Dilbert urgently needs a carpool. Dilbert corrects him, explaining that he actually needs carpal tunnel surgery after typing-related damage and must wear wrist braces until then. Wally ignores the explanation and just says his carpool is full.
punchline: Wally has misheard 'carpal tunnel' as 'carpool' and, even after Dilbert explains his injury, he callously dismisses him without a hint of sympathy.
summary: A coworker mistakes a colleague's wrist injury for a transportation problem and brushes him off when the truth comes out.

file: 1994/1994-01-19_synthesize pheremones_attraction_few splashes_liked it.gif
title: Dilbert Becomes Attracted To Himself

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I synthesized the pheremones that make men and women attracted to each other.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A few splashes of this and I'll be irresistible.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you feel any different?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm starting to re-e-e-ally like me.

situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a flask of pheromones he has synthesized and splashes some on himself, expecting to become irresistible to others. Dogbert asks if he feels different, and Dilbert, flushed and steaming, reports that he is starting to really like himself.
punchline: The pheromone potion only makes Dilbert attracted to himself, since he is the only one affected, which is a self-absorbed and ironic failure of his plan to be irresistible to others.
summary: A homemade attraction potion works on the wrong person when its inventor ends up smitten with himself.

file: 1994/1994-08-26_dignity  enhancement_help employees_less money_hire someone_co workers.gif
title: Dignity Program Paid By Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sue was hired to run our new "dignity enhancement" program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Her charter is to help the employees feel good about themselves while they work harder for less money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can we afford to hire somebody new?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you remember those co-workers you used to have?

situation: The Boss introduces Sue, a newly hired manager of a 'dignity enhancement' program meant to make employees feel good while they work harder for less pay. Dilbert asks how the company can afford a new hire. The Boss cheerfully replies by pointing to the co-workers who are no longer there.
punchline: The company paid for the feel-good morale program by laying off Dilbert's co-workers, so the 'dignity' initiative is funded by the very cuts that destroy employee dignity.
summary: A manager unveils a morale-boosting hire whose salary comes straight from the jobs of departed colleagues.

file: 1994/1994-09-22_beat it out_changing mind_engineering_goons_project requirements_thoughts_won't share_meditation.gif
title: Requirements Forming in Boss's Mind

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: The project requirements are forming in my mind.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Now they're changing... Changing... Changing... Changing... Okay. No, wait... Changing... Changing... Done.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Naturally, I won't be sharing any of these thoughts with engineering.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I budgeted for some goons to beat it out of you.

situation: A manager sits across from Dilbert and narrates the project requirements as they form and keep shifting in his head. He then announces he won't share them with engineering. Dilbert, typing on his laptop, calmly replies that he has budgeted for goons to beat the information out of him.
punchline: Dilbert deadpans that he planned ahead for hired thugs to physically extract the requirements, since the manager's secretive, constantly changing requirements are otherwise impossible to get.
summary: A manager keeps his shifting project specs to himself, so an engineer has already funded some muscle to extract them by force.

file: 1994/1994-04-01_evolution favors monkeys_cages_as pets_humans treated.gif
title: Humans Already Live in Cages

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: Evolution favors monkeys. Eventually, humans will be kept in cages as pets

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bah!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Impossible! We humans will never allow ourselves to be treated like that!

transcript.speaker: Monkey
transcript.text: Now get out of my cubicle!

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, with a view of a row of cubicles
situation: A small monkey tells Dilbert that evolution favors monkeys and that humans will eventually be kept in cages as pets. Dilbert scoffs and insists humans would never allow themselves to be treated that way. The final panel shows the monkey on the far side of a row of cubicles, which look like cages, telling him to get out of its cubicle.
punchline: Office workers already live and work in cage-like cubicles, so Dilbert's claim that humans would never accept being caged is ironic.
summary: A monkey predicts humans will end up caged as pets, and Dilbert's confident denial falls apart when the cubicle farm looks exactly like a row of cages.

file: 1994/1994-10-18_board room_fire employees_no employees_task force_competitors_white rumps.gif
title: Firing Everyone, Then Forming Task Force

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our competitors are kicking our pasty white rumps.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm bringing in Dogbert to fire employees until we're stronger than the competition.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: How will the work get done with no employees?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd better form a task force to study that.

situation: At a board meeting, the Boss complains that competitors are beating the company and announces he will hire Dogbert to fire employees until the company is stronger. An executive asks how work will get done once there are no employees left, and the Boss decides to form a task force to study the question.
punchline: The Boss believes cutting staff makes a company stronger, and when confronted with the obvious flaw he reaches for a task force instead of reconsidering his plan.
summary: A boss plans to win against rivals by having a consultant dismiss staff, then responds to the glaring flaw by commissioning a study.

file: 1994/1994-06-22_job pays_headhunter_move_cold place_drivers license_look up gender_phone call_man_inquiring about job.gif
title: Headhunter Warns of Freezing Job

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Headhunter

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The job pays a hundred thousand.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But you'll have to move to a place that's so cold that mercury freezes.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I'll take it. How bad could it be?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Keep your drivers license on you so you can look up your gender if you forget.

setting: Dogbert's headhunting office and the candidate's desk, connected by a phone call
situation: Dogbert, working as a headhunter, phones a job candidate to offer a position paying a hundred thousand dollars. He then mentions the job requires relocating to a place so cold that mercury freezes. The candidate cheerfully accepts, and Dogbert adds a grim warning about how extreme the cold is.
punchline: The place is so cold that people lose all sensation and will need to check their driver's license to remember whether they are male or female.
summary: A headhunting dog lures a candidate into a high-paying job in a frozen wasteland and offers a darkly absurd survival tip.

file: 1994/1994-03-23_date_lisa_coffee at work_wash hair_saturday night_dinner date_rejected_clean hair.gif
title: Dilbert Rejects Lisa's Hair Excuse

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lisa, I was wondering if you'd like to go out to dinner Saturday night.

transcript.speaker: Lisa
transcript.text: Uh... I have to wash my hair Saturday. How about having coffee here at work instead?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll pass. I was hoping for someone with clean hair.

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker named Lisa out to dinner on Saturday night. She offers the classic excuse that she has to wash her hair and suggests coffee at work instead. Dilbert turns the excuse around, declining her counteroffer because he wanted a date with someone whose hair is clean.
punchline: Dilbert pretends to take her stock brush-off excuse literally, turning the rejection back on her with a sarcastic insult about her hair.
summary: A coworker's polite dodge of a date invitation gets tossed back at her by the man she turned down.

file: 1994/1994-07-17_internet_al gore_information superhighway_share ideas_blonde jokes_flirt college women_chat area_technology.gif
title: Internet Access Doesn't Mean Sharing Ideas

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can we cut this short? I'd like to get back to the information superhighway.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. I'm glad we connected you all to the Internet so you can share ideas with colleagues.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yeah, that's right. I want to go share ideas with my colleagues.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do people really share ideas with colleagues?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If I get an idea, I'm not sharing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I'll channel over to the Internet chat area and flirt with college women.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm still reading through five megs of blonde jokes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if Al Gore has any idea...

transcript.speaker: Al Gore
transcript.text: Hey, Tipper, here's another good one! Hee hee!

setting: Conference room, then office cubicles and Al Gore's office
situation: In a meeting, the Boss says he connected everyone to the Internet so they can share ideas with colleagues. The employees all want to leave the meeting to use the Internet, but Wally says he'd never share an idea, and the real uses are flirting in chat rooms and reading blonde jokes. Dilbert wonders whether Al Gore has any ideas, and the final panel shows Al Gore reading blonde jokes and calling to his wife Tipper.
punchline: Even the champion of the information superhighway uses it just to read blonde jokes, showing that the Internet is used for trivial entertainment instead of the idea-sharing it was promised for.
summary: Management touts the new Internet connection as a tool for collaboration, but everyone, including the Vice President, uses it for flirting and cheap jokes.

file: 1994/1994-01-27_all get out_french bombing_hardy breed_run_scare us.gif
title: Elbonians Stoically Ignore French Bombs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The French are bombing us!! Run!!

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We Elbonians are a hardy breed. Bombs don't scare us.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sploit

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sploit

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: 'Course I'd be lying if I told you this didn't sting like all get out.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: "Nupe" it.

setting: Muddy Elbonian landscape during a bombing
situation: Dilbert warns a group of mud-stuck Elbonians that the French are bombing them and urges them to run. An Elbonian calmly declares that his people are hardy and unafraid of bombs, while bombs thud into the mud around them. In the last panel one Elbonian has a bomb stuck in his back and admits it really hurts, while another says the bomb should be 'nuped'.
punchline: The Elbonian boasts about being unafraid of bombs while a bomb is lodged in him, then admits it hurts, undercutting his stoic pride.
summary: A proud, stoic local brags about toughness against air raids right up until an unexploded bomb lands on him and the pain gives him away.

file: 1994/1994-06-03_imagine_being a woman_men in training_people acknowledge_can't find keys_blouse falls off_distorted view_misogyny.gif
title: Sensitivity Training Goes Badly Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this sensitivity exercise, close your eyes and imagine how it feels to be a woman.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: People acknowledge my existence. They smile for no reason and hold the door open. I'm... I'm popular.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't find my keys.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm never going back. I can't. I won't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My blouse falls to the floor...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Break! Break!

situation: Dogbert leads a sensitivity training session and tells the attendees to close their eyes and imagine being a woman. Wally imagines that people are suddenly nice to him and hold doors open, while Dilbert fantasizes about his blouse falling off. Dogbert abruptly ends the exercise.
punchline: The men's fantasies about being a woman are shallow and self-serving (being popular, undressing), completely missing the point of sensitivity training, so Dogbert has to shut it down.
summary: A dog running a diversity workshop watches two men turn an empathy exercise into a shallow fantasy and hastily calls it off.

file: 1994/1994-11-14_project_assigned_maintain status quo_everybody likes project_not enough funding.gif
title: The Project That Wouldn't Die

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm assigning you to "The project that wouldn't die."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everybody likes this project too much to cancel it, but not enough to fund it properly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaarg!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now go out there and maintain the status quo!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You really shouldn't mix honesty with your motivational speeches.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to a zombie project that nobody will cancel but nobody will fund. Dilbert holds his head in despair as the Boss candidly explains why. The Boss then tries to wrap up with a rallying cry, and Dilbert criticizes his habit of blending honesty into pep talks.
punchline: The Boss's motivational speech is demoralizing because he accidentally tells the truth, that the project is doomed to limbo, and Dilbert points out that honesty and motivation don't mix.
summary: A manager hands over an underfunded, uncancellable project with a brutally frank pep talk that leaves his employee crushed.

file: 1994/1994-04-04_quality training_promoted_management_lobotomy_footsteps.gif
title: Promotion Requires a Lobotomy, Or Training

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only way to get ahead in this company is by getting promoted to management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm willing to do whatever it takes to get promoted. I want to follow in your footsteps.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'm wondering if a lobotomy is actually necessary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, we'll just run you through "quality" training.

situation: Dilbert stands in front of The Boss's desk and says he wants to get promoted into management and follow in the boss's footsteps. He wonders aloud whether a lobotomy is required to become a manager. The Boss reassures him that it isn't and that quality training will do the job instead.
punchline: The Boss's reassurance implies that managers are made mindless anyway, and that corporate "quality" training is an adequate substitute for a lobotomy.
summary: An ambitious employee asks whether brain surgery is a prerequisite for management and learns that a corporate training course accomplishes the same thing.

file: 1994/1994-08-08_after marriage_get phsyical_husband be mad_look sad_oddly appealing_dating a while_liz.gif
title: Dating a Married Woman's Rules

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've been dating for a while and I find you oddly appealing...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I don't believe in getting physical until after I'm married.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wouldn't your husband get mad?

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Sometimes it's okay just to look sad and shut up.

setting: Undefined blue background, likely a date
situation: Dilbert holds hands with his date, Liz, and tells her he finds her oddly appealing but won't get physical until he is married. He then asks whether her husband would get mad. Liz, who is apparently already married, replies that sometimes it's okay just to look sad and shut up.
punchline: Dilbert's principled stance on waiting for marriage is undercut by the fact that his date already has a husband, whom she says should simply be ignored, implying she expects him to tolerate being cheated on.
summary: A man's old-fashioned vow of abstinence collides with the revelation that his girlfriend is already married and unbothered by it.

file: 1994/1994-08-25_assist me_cartoonists disclaimer_cucumber mutants_disclaimer_not funny_quite a pickle_world domination.gif
title: Cartoonist Abandons Giant Cucumber Storyline

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I created you cucumber mutants to assist me in my bid for world domination!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bulletin

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: I interrupt this strip because the whole giant cucumber theme isn't as funny as I thought it would be. Let's go directly to the big finish.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Scott

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then Waldo grabbed the "Salad Shooter." There were peels everywhere!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sounds like quite a pickle.

setting: A room with giant cucumber mutants, then Dilbert's armchair
situation: Dogbert, standing on a desk, tells giant cucumber mutants he created them to help him dominate the world. In the second panel the cartoonist interrupts the strip to admit the cucumber theme isn't funny and jumps to the ending. In the last panel Dogbert recounts a story about a Salad Shooter and peels, and Dilbert replies with a pickle pun.
punchline: The cartoonist abruptly abandons his own failing joke premise and rushes to a deliberately groan-worthy pickle pun as the 'big finish'.
summary: Midway through a bizarre mutant vegetable plot, the author admits the gag isn't working and hurriedly wraps up with a corny pun.

file: 1994/1994-12-13_annoying rodent_cutest briefcase_following to work_ratbert_work to engineer_career in marketing.gif
title: Ratbert Follows Dilbert Into Marketing

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm following you to work.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll start out as an annoying rodent. But with hard work and training I'll work my way up to engineer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: May I suggest a career in marketing?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Is this the cutest little briefcase or what?!

setting: A sidewalk on the way to work
situation: Ratbert trails Dilbert on his commute and announces that he plans to start as an annoying rodent and work his way up to engineer. When Ratbert then shows off his own tiny briefcase and fishes for compliments, Dilbert suggests he go into marketing instead.
punchline: Ratbert's relentless cutesiness and shameless self-promotion make him a natural for marketing, and Dilbert implies that marketing values charm over engineering skill.
summary: A tiny rodent tags along behind an engineer and dreams of an engineering career, but his gushing self-promotion convinces the engineer he belongs in marketing.

file: 1994/1994-02-08_actual fashion_fridays_garanimals_new dress code_scrutinized_sears.gif
title: Casual Friday Fashion Panic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The new dress code allows casual clothing on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Gulp.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll have to make actual fashion decisions that will be scrutinized by hundreds of your co-workers!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm thinking "Garanimals" from "Sears".

situation: The Boss announces that the new dress code allows casual clothing on Fridays. Wally and Dilbert gulp nervously and clutch each other as the Boss points out they'll now have to make fashion choices that hundreds of co-workers will judge. Wally responds by planning to wear Garanimals, a children's mix-and-match clothing line from Sears.
punchline: Wally is so lacking in fashion sense that his solution to casual Friday is to dress in children's clothing designed so kids can't mismatch outfits.
summary: Faced with having to choose his own casual outfit, a fashion-challenged employee decides to rely on clothing made for little kids.

file: 1994/1994-03-14_projects floundering_bold strategy_reorganize_department_last month_bold.gif
title: Bold Strategy: Another Random Reorganization

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of our projects are floundering. I decided on a bold new strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me guess. You're going to randomly reorganize the department...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just like last month.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to admit that's bold.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that all projects are floundering and that he has chosen a bold new strategy. Dilbert correctly guesses it is another random reorganization of the department, just like the previous month. The Boss defensively insists that it is at least bold.
punchline: The Boss's supposedly bold strategy is just the same random reorganization he does every month, and he tries to excuse it by calling repetition boldness.
summary: A manager facing failing projects reaches for his usual fix of shuffling the department, and when called out he simply praises his own daring.

file: 1994/1994-04-09_bad luck_lottery tickets_fabulous wealth_delight_hedonistic_yesterdays date_old_expired_scam_scammer_cheater_rat_dog_animals.gif
title: Dogbert Sells Expired Lottery Tickets

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Value Priced Lottery Tickets

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I am drawn by the allure of fabulous wealth and a life of hedonistic delight... one please.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: This is dated yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ooh, bad luck. Try again?

situation: Dogbert sits behind a desk under a sign advertising value-priced lottery tickets. Ratbert eagerly buys one, dreaming of wealth, then discovers the ticket is dated yesterday. Dogbert shrugs off the problem and offers him another sale.
punchline: Dogbert's cheap lottery tickets are stale, so the buyer never had a chance of winning, and Dogbert glibly treats the scam as mere bad luck and invites him to buy again.
summary: A hopeful rat buys a bargain lottery ticket from a dog and learns it was already out of date when sold.

file: 1994/1994-08-23_genetic research_clone_obedient slaves_conquer_world dominion_living things_work on giant cucumbers_arms and legs.gif
title: Dogbert Orders Slave Army From Cucumber Scientist

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Genetic research

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like you to clone an army of obedient slaves for me. I plan to conquer the world and have dominion over all living things.

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: I mostly work on giant cucumbers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Mix in some arms and legs and give me two packages of seeds.

setting: Hallway and office of a genetic research department
situation: Dogbert strolls toward the genetic research lab and asks a scientist to clone an army of obedient slaves so he can conquer the world. The scientist admits his work is mostly on giant cucumbers. Dogbert is undeterred and tells him to add arms and legs to the cucumbers and hand over two packets of seeds.
punchline: Dogbert casually accepts a ridiculous plant-based army, treating world conquest as a simple gardening order, complete with a request for seed packets.
summary: A scheming dog seeking a clone army settles happily for a scientist's oversized vegetables fitted with limbs.

file: 1994/1994-10-25_ethics questions_co worker_pentium pc_run over foot_car accident_parking lot_dilbert.gif
title: Ethics Office: Running Over Pentium Owner

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I have a question for the ethics office.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If my co-worker has a "Pentium" PC and I have a 386, is it okay to run over his foot in the parking lot?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It seemed like a long-shot when I asked.

setting: Office cubicle and company parking lot
situation: Wally phones the company ethics office from his cubicle and asks whether it is acceptable to run over a co-worker's foot because that co-worker has a newer Pentium PC while Wally is stuck with a 386. In the last panel Wally sits in a red car in the parking lot, thinking about his question, while Dilbert stands next to another car in the foreground.
punchline: Wally treats computer envy as a legitimate justification for physical harm, and the thought bubble hints he went ahead with it anyway after asking the ethics office, with Dilbert as the likely victim.
summary: A jealous employee with an outdated computer checks with the ethics hotline before taking revenge on a better-equipped colleague with his car.

file: 1994/1994-08-30_classes_get mba_big name school_knowledge_not prestige_tonys_house_mbas_babe ratio.gif
title: Choosing a Dubious MBA School

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to take classes at night and get an MBA.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't need a big-name school. I'm in this for knowledge, not prestige.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about "Tony's House of MBAs"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The babe ratio is better at "MBA-O-Rama."

setting: Dilbert's home desk, covered in MBA brochures
situation: Dilbert announces he will study for an MBA at night and says he cares about knowledge rather than a prestigious school name. Dogbert, sitting across the desk, suggests a ridiculous-sounding school called Tony's House of MBAs. Dilbert then weighs in on a rival school based on its ratio of attractive women.
punchline: Dilbert's claim to be seeking pure knowledge collapses when he picks a school based on the babe ratio.
summary: A man who insists he wants learning over status ends up shopping for a degree factory on the strength of its dating prospects.

file: 1994/1994-09-12_animal eating rat_feel lucky_hat on head_optimist.gif
title: Ratbert Mistakes Pouncing Cat for Hat

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Optimist

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
