transcript.text: I feel lucky today.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Lucky, lucky, lucky.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I think a hat just blew onto my head!!

setting: A grassy outdoor path with bushes
situation: Ratbert strolls down a path feeling lucky and humming happily while a cat lurks in the bushes at the edge of the panel. The cat leaps through the air to pounce on him, and Ratbert lands under the cat without noticing. He cheerfully concludes that a hat has blown onto his head.
punchline: Ratbert's relentless optimism leads him to interpret a predator attacking him as a stroke of good fortune, a hat blowing onto his head.
summary: A cheerful little rat remains blissfully unaware that the predator on his head is not a piece of headwear.

file: 1994/1994-10-02_mathematical proof god_smartest garbageman_transposed varaiables_proves existence of dog_you exist_error_hear something.gif
title: Garbage Man Disproves Dilbert's Existence

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! Come here! I've done it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created a mathematical proof of the existence of God!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give it to me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is a job for the world's smartest garbage man.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: What can I do for you, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Check this math.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Clever... but he transposed some variables. This proves the existence of his dog.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Now we know you exist. And I must exist because "I think, therefor I am."

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: But since Dilbert wasn't thinking when he made this error, there's no proof that he exists.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Did you just hear something, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's no way to be sure.

setting: Dilbert's office, then an outdoor sidewalk with a garbage can
situation: Dilbert excitedly hands Dogbert what he believes is a mathematical proof of God's existence. Dogbert takes it to the world's smartest garbage man, who finds an error that instead proves the existence of Dogbert and himself, but not of Dilbert. When Dilbert objects, they pretend not to hear him.
punchline: The garbage man's logic concludes that Dilbert, having made a thoughtless error, cannot be proven to exist, so he and Dogbert smugly ignore Dilbert's protest.
summary: A flawed proof meant to demonstrate divinity ends up philosophically erasing its own author, courtesy of a brilliant trash collector.

file: 1994/1994-09-15_ctrl-alt -delete_keyboard_cat_dogbert called_animals.gif
title: Cat Sits on Keyboard, Reboots

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Get off of my keyboard, cat, or else!

transcript.speaker: Cat
transcript.text: Watch me act like I don't even hear you.

transcript.speaker: Cat
transcript.text: Ctrl-Alt-Del

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert!

setting: Dilbert's home desk with a desktop computer
situation: Dilbert threatens a cat that is lying on his keyboard. The cat calmly ignores him, then stretches its paws across the keys and presses Ctrl-Alt-Del, restarting the computer. Dilbert, alarmed, shouts the name Dogbert, suggesting the cat is really Dogbert in disguise.
punchline: The 'cat' deliberately hits Ctrl-Alt-Del to spite Dilbert, revealing it is really Dogbert, who is just as calculating and contemptuous as ever.
summary: A defiant cat on a computer keyboard makes good on its mockery by rebooting the machine, prompting a horrified accusation.

file: 1994/1994-08-10_profits down_bring own pencils_sell them_sidewalk_beg for money_money down.gif
title: Bring Your Own Pencils, Sell Them

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Profits are down again this quarter.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Starting tomorrow, you'll have to bring your own pencils to the office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you'll have to sell them out on the sidewalk.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's bad.

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert and a coworker that profits are down again. He then imposes escalating cost-cutting measures: employees must supply their own pencils, and then must sell pencils on the sidewalk. Dilbert only thinks 'That's bad' each time, his reaction growing flatter and more resigned.
punchline: The measures escalate from stingy to absurd, ending with employees effectively becoming street beggars, while Dilbert's repeated understated thought 'That's bad' shows the inadequacy of any reaction to management's nonsense.
summary: A manager responds to falling profits with ever more ridiculous demands on his staff while they silently note how bad it all is.

file: 1994/1994-12-24_strange smell_aroma technology_scent of lemon_employees more alert_lemon.gif
title: Aroma Technology Keeps Employees Docile

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a strange smell in the cubes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're using aroma technology!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, research shows that the scent of lemon makes employees more alert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not lemon.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My job's easier when you guys aren't too alert.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss there is a strange smell in the cubicles. The Boss explains it is part of a new aroma technology program and cites research that lemon scent makes employees more alert. When Dilbert points out the smell isn't lemon, the Boss admits he prefers employees to be less alert.
punchline: The company is deliberately pumping in a scent that dulls employees' alertness, because the Boss finds managing a less-alert workforce easier.
summary: A manager sells a mysterious office odor as a productivity boost, then cheerfully admits it is meant to keep his staff dull.

file: 1994/1994-11-02_employee survey_no startegy_quality team_root cause_employees are ninnies_more stock options.gif
title: Executives Blame Employees for Strategy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The employee survey showed that 95% of the company believes we have no consistent strategy.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: So the executives formed a "quality team" to determine the root cause of the problem.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: We've narrowed it down to either "employees are ninnies" or "we deserve more stock options."

setting: Conference room during a management presentation
situation: An executive reports to a meeting that an employee survey found nearly everyone thinks the company lacks a consistent strategy. The executives formed a quality team to find the root cause. The team's conclusions are that the employees are foolish or that the executives deserve more stock options.
punchline: The executives' investigation of their own strategy failure ignores any fault of their own and lands on blaming employees or rewarding themselves with more stock options.
summary: Management responds to damning survey feedback about their lack of direction by forming a team whose only theories flatter themselves.

file: 1994/1994-09-02_classes at night_eleven cheerios_gaining knowledge_knowledge_work all day.gif
title: Cheerios Up the Nose Knowledge

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't know how you do it. You work all day and now you take classes at night.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's hard, but you're gaining knowledge that couldn't be obtained any other way.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whump

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! I can hold eleven "Cheerios" in my nose!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And it's knowledge you can apply.

situation: Dogbert praises an exhausted Dilbert for working all day and taking night classes. Dilbert falls asleep face-first into his cereal bowl, then wakes up proudly announcing he can hold eleven Cheerios in his nose. Dogbert dryly notes that this is at least applicable knowledge.
punchline: After all his exhausting study, the only thing Dilbert has actually learned is a useless party trick, which Dogbert sarcastically calls knowledge he can apply.
summary: A sleep-deprived night student faceplants into his breakfast and discovers a pointless nasal talent, much to his dog's sarcastic approval.

file: 1994/1994-01-03_transferred_marketing_slaps employee_groggy_disoriented_fit in better_business.gif
title: Slap Employee Into Marketing Mindset

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sorry Dave, but you're being transferred to marketing and there's no budget to train you as a marketer.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: SLAP!

transcript.speaker: Dave
transcript.text: Where am I? I need a drink.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a temporary fix... but you'll fit in now.

situation: The Boss tells an employee named Dave that he is being transferred to marketing but there is no money to train him for the job. Instead of training, the Boss slaps him across the face, leaving him dazed and disoriented. The Boss says the slap is a temporary fix that will make Dave fit in with marketing.
punchline: Marketing people are implied to be dazed, clueless drinkers, so a slap that knocks Dave senseless is a free, cheap substitute for training him as a marketer.
summary: With no money for training, a manager knocks a transferred employee senseless so he will blend in with his new department.

file: 1994/1994-05-12_all assignments_big binder_same building_president_good word_two good words.gif
title: Ratbert's Binder Of Good Words

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: It looks like you've all done your assignments for me.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Your input is so important that I'll have it put in a big binder and stored in the same building that your president works!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And I'll put in a good word for you when I meet with your boss later today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about two good words?

situation: Ratbert, acting as a consultant, sits at a conference table where Dilbert and a coworker have handed in the assignments he gave them. He claims their input is so valuable it will be filed in a binder in the president's building, and offers to put in a good word with their boss. Dilbert, having done all the work, asks for two good words.
punchline: Ratbert's grand promises amount to filing the work away and a single good word, and Dilbert sarcastically haggles for more reward in exchange for doing a consultant's homework.
summary: A tiny consultant praises his staff's homework with hollow promises, and one of them wryly bargains for a bigger reward.

file: 1994/1994-01-06_boss brain_profitable_cut costs_selling products.gif
title: Profit Without Selling Anything

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Boss's Brain

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Humm

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Theoretically, if I cut costs enough we'll be profitable without selling any products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How do they get the ink in these things?

setting: The Boss's office, seated at his desk
situation: A caption introduces a peek inside The Boss's brain, shown as thought bubbles while he sits in his chair. He first muses that extreme cost cutting could make the company profitable even if it sells nothing. He then picks up a pen and wonders how the ink gets inside it.
punchline: The Boss's grand business insight is absurd, and his next thought shows his mind is equally occupied by trivial curiosities, implying his strategic thinking is no deeper than wondering about pens.
summary: A glimpse into the boss's head reveals a ridiculous plan to earn money by spending less than nothing, followed by idle puzzlement over a pen.

file: 1994/1994-08-19_dogbert outplacement agebcy_doa_freelance consulatants_cubicles_earn no money_equipped_phone_refurbished ego.gif
title: Dogbert's Outplacement Agency: Unemployed Consultants

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to the Dogbert Outplacement Agency, or "DOA" as I call it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here, nobody is "unemployed." You're freelance consultants who sit in cubicles and earn no money!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Every cubicle is equipped with a phone and a refurbished ego.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I will NOT work with that thing.

setting: Dogbert's outplacement agency, a room of cubicles
situation: Dogbert welcomes a newly laid-off Boss to his outplacement agency and walks him past the cubicles. He explains that the clients are relabeled as freelance consultants who sit at desks and earn nothing. In the last panel, the cubicle's phone and a tattered, refurbished ego are pointed out, and a small figure refuses to work with the ego.
punchline: Dogbert rebrands unemployment as freelance consulting, giving jobless people a cubicle and phone but no income, and the supposed morale boost is a battered, secondhand ego.
summary: A canine career counselor cheerfully redefines joblessness as self-employment while offering his clients nothing but an office nook and a used self-image.

file: 1994/1994-09-10_work harder_box_cucbicle_totally unmanageable.gif
title: Threatened With The Box

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Work harder or I'll have you put in the "box."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? I thought I was already in the box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is the box bigger than my cubicle?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These people are totally unmanageable.

situation: The Boss threatens Dilbert that he'll be put in 'the box' if he doesn't work harder. Dilbert calmly replies that he thought he was already in the box and asks whether the box is bigger than his cubicle. The Boss, now off to the side, thinks to himself that his employees are unmanageable.
punchline: Dilbert's cubicle is already so confining that the Boss's threat of a punishment box has no force, leaving the Boss frustrated that his intimidation fails.
summary: A manager's threat of confinement falls flat because the employee already works in what feels like a box.

file: 1994/1994-10-11_future trends_guess_more valid_published_share vision_people are dumb.gif
title: Publishing Guesses as Future Trends

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing a book of my guesses about future trends.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If it gets published then my guesses will seem more valid than other people's. I'll charge huge fees to share my "vision" with audiences.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why would people pay huge fees for guesses?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Trend number one is that people aren't getting any smarter.

setting: Living room couch at Dilbert's home
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch typing on a laptop and explains that he is writing a book of his guesses about future trends. He plans to use publication to make the guesses look credible and then charge large speaking fees. When Dilbert asks why anyone would pay for guesses, Dogbert replies that people are not getting smarter.
punchline: Dogbert's first predicted trend is that people remain gullible, which is exactly why his scheme of selling guesses as expert vision will work.
summary: A scheming dog plans to cash in on mere speculation by dressing it up as a published book of visionary forecasts.

file: 1994/1994-06-29_dogbert the publisher_book_minor changes_purple dinosaur_detective_eliminate the murder_murder mystery.gif
title: Purple Dinosaur Murder Mystery Rewrite

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Publisher

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like to publish your book. All it needs are a few minor changes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Make the main character a purple dinosaur instead of a detective. Add some upbeat songs and eliminate the murder.

transcript.speaker: Author
transcript.text: It's a murder mystery!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, that's original.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a book publisher, tells an author he wants to publish the manuscript with just a few minor changes. The changes turn out to be replacing the detective with a purple dinosaur, adding upbeat songs and removing the murder. The flustered author protests that it is a murder mystery, and Dogbert sarcastically replies that it is original.
punchline: The 'minor changes' would destroy the book entirely, and Dogbert's sarcastic 'that's original' dismisses a murder mystery as unoriginal while the purple dinosaur he wants is a blatant knockoff of an existing children's character.
summary: A publisher offers to print a manuscript but demands edits that would turn a gritty whodunit into a kids' show knockoff.

file: 1994/1994-07-02_felt like kissing_first date 85%_kiss good night_third date_wearing sweat pants.gif
title: First Date Only Counted 85%

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This was our third date, Liz. Tradition demands that you kiss me or give me the "let's be friends" talk.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: No, our first date only counted as 85% of a date because we were wearing our sweat pants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm 15% short?!!

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: It's too bad, because I really felt like kissing.

setting: Outside Liz's front steps at the end of a date
situation: Dilbert stands at the foot of a staircase with Liz and declares that, as it's their third date, she must either kiss him or give him the 'let's be friends' talk. Liz cheerfully replies that their first date only counted as 85% of a date because they were wearing sweat pants. Dilbert is dismayed to find he is 15% short, and she adds that she really did feel like kissing.
punchline: Liz uses absurdly precise date arithmetic to dodge the third-date expectation, politely rejecting Dilbert while pretending the decision is a technicality.
summary: A hopeful engineer is turned down at the end of a date by a woman who invents a percentage penalty for casual clothing.

file: 1994/1994-07-18_great solutions_bicycle seats_dorky pants_bicycle pants.gif
title: Dorky Pants Fix Bicycle Seats

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Great solutions in engineering

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Problem: Bicycle seats are hard. They hurt.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Analysis: There must be something wrong with your pants.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Solution: Dorky pants.

setting: A presentation area with a flip chart, in a light blue room
situation: In a recurring 'Great Solutions in Engineering' segment, Dogbert points at a flip chart showing a bicycle seat and states the problem that bicycle seats are hard and painful. He then blames the user's pants instead of the seat, while Dilbert stands with his back to the viewer, wearing shorts. Dogbert proposes 'dorky pants' as the solution.
punchline: Instead of redesigning the uncomfortable bicycle seat, the 'engineering' solution blames the user's clothing and prescribes padded, dorky-looking cycling shorts.
summary: A mock engineering case study dismisses a painful bike seat as the rider's wardrobe problem and recommends padded cycling shorts.

file: 1994/1994-05-22_project plan_every resource_task_dependency_road map_two weeks_tasks_two weeks late_dependencies are wrong_estimates_to be determined_ransom numbers_redo whole plan.gif
title: Perfect Project Plan, Random Numbers

transcript.speaker: Project manager
transcript.text: Let's spend the next four hours reviewing the project plan.

transcript.speaker: Project manager
transcript.text: I've detailed every resource, task and dependency into an exquisitely accurate road map.

transcript.speaker: Project manager
transcript.text: It took me two weeks, but it's the only way to make sure we're not wasting time.

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink jacket
transcript.text: My tasks are two weeks late because I was waiting for your input.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you left off one task, so all the dependencies are wrong.

transcript.speaker: Balding man with glasses
transcript.text: I'm changing all of my estimates to "to be determined."

transcript.speaker: Woman in pink jacket
transcript.text: Can we do that?! I've been using random numbers.

transcript.speaker: Project manager
transcript.text: I'll have to redo the whole plan.

transcript.speaker: Balding man with glasses
transcript.text: Don't worry. We won't do anything until we hear from you.

setting: Conference room during a project plan review meeting
situation: A project manager calls a four-hour meeting to review a painstakingly detailed project plan that took him two weeks to prepare. His colleagues respond that their own tasks are late because they were waiting on his input, that he omitted a task so every dependency is wrong, and that their estimates were random numbers anyway. He is left to redo the whole plan while the team promises to do nothing until he finishes.
punchline: The plan was so elaborate that it blocked all actual work, and the team will cheerfully keep idling until the planner finishes redoing it.
summary: An obsessive planner spends weeks perfecting a schedule while his team stalls waiting for it, then learns it is flawed and built on made-up estimates.

file: 1994/1994-07-30_exaggerating accomplishments_failing_monkey_more humiliating_stupid monkey_typical_zimbu_animals.gif
title: Sucking Up to a Monkey

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO cancelled his visit. He's sending his top aid, Zimbu the monkey, in his place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that typical? I spent a week exaggerating my accomplishments for this. Now he sends a stupid monkey!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What could be more humiliating than trying to suck-up to a monkey?

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: Failing at it?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the CEO has cancelled his visit and is sending his top aide, a monkey named Zimbu, instead. Dilbert complains that he spent a week exaggerating his accomplishments for the visit. When he declares that sucking up to a monkey is the most humiliating thing possible, the monkey replies that failing at it would be worse.
punchline: The monkey talks back with a cutting retort, suggesting that Dilbert's attempts to impress him are failing and that this failure is even more humiliating.
summary: A visiting executive's stand-in turns out to be a monkey, and it coolly mocks the employee who prepared to flatter it.

file: 1994/1994-05-05_product_what it does_who would duse it_rest later_plan to sell_psychic.gif
title: Requirements Gathering With No Requirements

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: We don't know what the product should do or who would use it.

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: But if you could tell us what it costs to build it, we'll figure out the rest later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What year do you plan to sell it?

transcript.speaker: Client
transcript.text: What am I — psychic or something??

setting: Conference room meeting at a table
situation: Dilbert, taking notes, meets with a client who wants a cost estimate for a product. The client admits he has no idea what the product should do or who would use it. When Dilbert asks a basic planning question about when it will be sold, the client reacts with indignation.
punchline: The client expects a precise cost estimate for an undefined product, yet gets offended when asked for even the simplest detail, showing the absurdity of demanding answers while providing no requirements.
summary: A client with zero product definition demands a price tag anyway, then bristles at the first clarifying question.

file: 1994/1994-10-17_client server_project_reasoning_six minutes_time line_world wide operations_understand.gif
title: If I Don't Understand It, It's Easy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I put together a time line for your project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I started by reasoning that anything I don't understand is easy to do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Phase one: Design a client-server architecture for our world-wide operations. Time: six minutes.

situation: The Boss shows Dilbert a project timeline he has drawn up. He explains that his method was to assume anything he doesn't understand must be easy. He then reads out the first phase: designing a client-server architecture for worldwide operations in six minutes.
punchline: The Boss estimates schedules by assuming that whatever he doesn't understand is simple, resulting in an absurd six-minute timeline for a huge technical task.
summary: A clueless manager builds a project schedule on the premise that ignorance equals simplicity, giving an enormous engineering job a laughably tiny time estimate.

file: 1994/1994-12-20_total quality method_bullrush award_honesty award.gif
title: The Honesty Award Doesn't Exist

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Describe how you used "Total Quality" methods on your last project. We're applying for the Millard Bullrush Quality Award.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know I didn't use "Total Quality." I'd have to lie.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sadly, Millard passed away before he could invent the Millard Bullrush "Honesty" award.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to describe how he applied Total Quality methods on his last project so the company can apply for a quality award. Dilbert bluntly says he never used them and would have to lie. The Boss cheerfully replies that no award for honesty exists.
punchline: The Boss implicitly admits that winning the quality award requires lying, since there is no honesty award to reward truthful answers.
summary: A manager wants a fabricated success story to win an award, and shrugs off Dilbert's honesty by noting that truthfulness earns no prize.

file: 1994/1994-08-29_prepare reports_outsourced jobs_write report_outsourcing_illogical.gif
title: Writing Your Own Outsourcing Defense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want all of you to prepare reports explaining why your jobs shouldn't be outsourced to consultants.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "It is my job to write this report. But if I were a consultant it would make no sense to compare me to myself. Outsourcing is illogical."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For some reason, I'm not taking as much pride in my work lately.

situation: The Boss tells his employees at a meeting to write reports justifying why their jobs should not be outsourced to consultants. Dilbert goes back to his desk and types an argument that is circular, since he is being asked to evaluate himself against a replacement. In the last panel he reflects that his pride in his work is fading.
punchline: Employees are forced to defend their own jobs in a self-evaluating, rigged process, and the threat of outsourcing is quietly destroying their motivation.
summary: Told to argue against being replaced by consultants, Dilbert finds the exercise so absurd that his enthusiasm for the job drains away.

file: 1994/1994-06-24_nineties woman_man pay dinner_slap a man_threatening.gif
title: Nineties Woman Threatens Dilbert Over Dinner

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: I'm a nineties kind of woman. I demand equality but the man must pay for dinner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: And recent surveys show that many women my age think it's okay to slap a man.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Really? Did they name the man?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Date
transcript.text: Don't make me come over there.

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits across from his date, who is reading a menu. She declares that she wants equality but expects the man to pay for dinner, then cheerfully cites surveys saying women think it's okay to slap a man. Dilbert nervously asks if the surveys named the man, and she threatens to come over and hit him.
punchline: Dilbert's timid question about whether the man was named gets answered with a direct threat of violence, showing her 'equality' is really a set of one-sided rules.
summary: A date who wants all the benefits of equality while keeping traditional privileges turns menacing when her companion hints at a worry.

file: 1994/1994-01-07_leaving compnay_opportunites_key pharses_we regret_years of service_footnote.gif
title: Reading Between the Lines of Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Tim will be leaving the company to pursue other opportunities."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Note the absence of key phrases such as "we regret" or "years of dedicated service." And notice that his new opportunity is not called "exciting."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think you're reading a little too much into that announcement.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No, I'm reading the footnote.

situation: The Boss reads aloud an announcement that Tim is leaving the company to pursue other opportunities. A cynical coworker dissects the wording, pointing out the missing expressions of regret and the lack of any 'exciting' description. The Boss says they're reading too much into it, but the coworker replies they are reading the footnote on the paper.
punchline: The coworker isn't over-interpreting the euphemistic announcement; the footnote itself apparently reveals that Tim was really fired or laid off.
summary: A staffer picks apart a bland departure memo for hidden meaning, and when told they're overanalyzing, reveals the fine print confirms their suspicions.

file: 1994/1994-03-12_rate of inflation_promotion_net worth_shopping cart_aluminum cans_all good carts.gif
title: Retirement Plan: Shopping Cart of Cans

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At the current rate of inflation, with no raises or promotions . . .

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Our net worth at retirement will be . . . a shopping cart full of aluminum cans.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'd better do something.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm going shopping before all the good carts are gone.

situation: Wally stands behind Dilbert at his computer and calculates that, with inflation and no raises or promotions, their retirement net worth will amount to a shopping cart of aluminum cans. Dilbert suggests they should do something about it. Wally's idea of action is to go shopping for a good cart before they run out.
punchline: Instead of trying to improve their finances, Wally resigns himself to poverty and rushes to secure the best shopping cart for his future life as a can collector.
summary: Two coworkers face a bleak financial future and one responds by planning for it rather than fighting it.

file: 1994/1994-03-29_commercially viable_hard drive_installed software_tail_zimbu_monkey_animals.gif
title: Secure But Unproductive Versus Monkey Genius

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Coworker
transcript.text: Well, well, it looks like Zimbu has designed another commercially viable product using only his tail.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could have done that... if I hadn't erased my hard drive when I installed my security software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't produce much, but it's very secure.

transcript.speaker: Zimbu
transcript.text: Here's another one.

situation: A coworker with pointed hair remarks that Zimbu the monkey has designed yet another marketable product using only his tail. Dilbert, arms crossed and defensive, claims he could have done the same if he hadn't wiped his hard drive while installing security software. He concedes he produces little but insists it is very secure, while the monkey keeps cranking out more.
punchline: Dilbert's heavy-handed security measures have destroyed his productivity, leaving him outperformed by a monkey typing with its tail.
summary: A tail-typing monkey keeps outproducing Dilbert, who blames his over-zealous security software for wiping out his work.

file: 1994/1994-05-18_arch nemesis_ttp_ttp project_join.gif
title: TTP Stands for The TTP Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, would you like to be on my "TTP" project?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What does "TTP" stand for?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's short for the TTP Project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I named it myself... So, do you want to join?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'd rather be your arch nemesis.

setting: Office, in front of plain purple background
situation: Dilbert asks Wally to join his project, called "TTP". When Wally asks what the acronym means, Dilbert explains it stands for "the TTP Project", a recursive and meaningless definition he proudly invented himself. Wally declines and says he would rather be Dilbert's arch nemesis.
punchline: Dilbert's self-referential acronym explains nothing, and the project sounds so pointless that Wally would rather be his enemy than join it.
summary: A circular acronym for a vague project makes a coworker refuse to participate and choose enmity instead.

file: 1994/1994-10-05_benefits_define reality_half the cost_keep objectives_rewrite business case_cut funding.gif
title: Half the Funding, Same Objectives

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to cut your project funding in half but keep the objectives the same.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a brilliant plan. We get all the benefits at half the costs!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why is it that the nuttiest people define reality?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And why couldn't I rewrite the business case to increase revenue?

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that his project's funding will be cut in half while the objectives stay exactly the same, calling it a brilliant plan. Dilbert quietly wonders why the nuttiest people get to define reality. The Boss, apparently misreading or ignoring this, adds that he could also rewrite the business case to increase revenue.
punchline: The Boss's solution to every problem is to redefine reality on paper, so he cheerfully proposes magically getting the same results for half the money and then inventing extra revenue the same way.
summary: A manager slashes a project's budget without touching its goals and then suggests simply rewriting the business case to conjure up more revenue.

file: 1994/1994-01-02_brain overload_experiences perceived_garbageman_illusions_inability to percieve_paths_physics_possibility_rat can't conceive_rats_time and motion.gif
title: Garbage Man Explains Reality to Ratbert

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What is reality, Mister Garbage Man?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Are you sure you're ready for that, Ratbert?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My mind is a blank slate!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Okay... Time and motion are just illusions created by your inability to perceive everything at once.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Everything that is possible exists as a path. You simply choose the path you wish to perceive.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: The only things you can't change are the experiences you've already perceived.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My head hurts.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: The contents of a garbage can are determined by what path I choose to perceive, not by what somebody else chose to discard.

transcript.speaker: Unknown
transcript.text: Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Brain overload!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Hey! There's a new VCR in here!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: C'mon, I'm expecting some great videos in the O'Briens' can.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy lawn beside a garbage can
situation: Ratbert sits on a garbage can and asks the garbage man to explain reality. The garbage man delivers a mind-bending lecture about time, motion and choosing paths to perceive, until Ratbert's brain overloads and he flails in pain. The garbage man then applies his philosophy to find a new VCR in the trash.
punchline: The garbage man's grand metaphysical theory of reality turns out to be a self-serving excuse for believing that he can will valuable discarded items, like a VCR, into the garbage cans he picks up.
summary: A trash collector's cosmic lecture on perception fries a small rat's brain before revealing it was all about scoring free electronics from the bins.

file: 1994/1994-09-19_big tech show_curly haired guys_salmon_spawning opportunites_vast sea_indistinct products_trade show_facial hair.gif
title: Trade Show Salmon Without Spawning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to the big technology show.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What do you do there?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will wade through a vast sea of mostly curly-haired guys with facial hair and glasses. And I will look at thousands of indistinct products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's like salmon returning to its birthplace.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But without the spawning opportunities.

setting: Dilbert's home, packing a suitcase beside a couch
situation: Dilbert packs his suitcase for a big technology trade show. When Dogbert asks what he does there, Dilbert describes wading through crowds of similar-looking bearded, bespectacled men and countless indistinguishable products. He compares it to salmon returning home, and Dogbert adds that there is no chance of romance.
punchline: A tech trade show is a crowd of nerdy men and bland products, like salmon swimming upstream, but with none of the mating payoff, which pokes fun at the lack of romantic prospects.
summary: Preparing for a tech expo, Dilbert likens the trip to a salmon run, and his dog quips that the comparison lacks the romantic payoff.

file: 1994/1994-04-25_making copies_spits out_commands in_copier paper_photocopy_paper flys_crinkle.gif
title: Copier Spits Out Crumpled Paper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Quantity... two sided... reduced to 98%... collated... with staple... portrait... two colors... darken... legal size paper...

transcript.speaker: Copier
transcript.text: Thip! Crinkle! Spoit!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If you want a photocopy set "thip crinkle and spoit" to no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It makes copies too??

situation: Dilbert programs a complicated list of options into a photocopier, including duplex, reduction, collating, stapling and legal paper. The machine merely crumples the paper and spits it out. A coworker explains that a 'thip crinkle and spoit' setting must be turned off if he wants an ordinary copy, and Dilbert is astonished to learn the machine also makes copies.
punchline: The copier is so overloaded with obscure features that making an actual photocopy is an afterthought Dilbert never knew about.
summary: A man wrestles with an overcomplicated copier that mangles his paper, only to discover that ordinary copying is just another buried option.

file: 1994/1994-06-15_city soccer league_never played_natural instinct_ball trajectory_team play_ruin concentration.gif
title: Dilbert's Engineering Soccer Instincts

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I joined the city soccer league.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never played, but as an engineer I have a natural instinct for ball trajectory and passing angles.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Where does the team play?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Coach doesn't want to ruin my concentration by telling me.

setting: Dilbert's home and a soccer field
situation: Dilbert announces he has joined the city soccer league despite never having played, claiming that being an engineer gives him a natural feel for ball physics. Dogbert asks where the team plays, and Dilbert admits the coach hasn't told him, saying it would ruin his concentration.
punchline: Dilbert's supposed engineering expertise is so overstated that he doesn't even know where his team plays, and he rationalizes the coach's neglect as a favor to his focus.
summary: A confident engineer who has never played the sport signs up for a soccer team, yet cannot say where the team even plays.

file: 1994/1994-03-10_no raises_no promotions_mathematical certainty_inflation_pooer_uncertainty_leader_not just manager.gif
title: Boss Announces Guaranteed Inflation Poverty

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company has announced there will be no raises or promotions this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now, there's a mathematical certainty that no matter how hard you work, inflation will make you poorer.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hated the old way, with all the uncertainty.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not just a manager, I'm a leader!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that the company is freezing all raises and promotions. He then cheerfully explains that inflation will inevitably make them poorer no matter how hard they work. He presents this as an improvement because it removes the uncertainty of the old system, and proudly calls himself a leader.
punchline: The Boss frames the guaranteed erosion of his employees' real income as a benefit and thinks delivering this bad news makes him a leader rather than just a manager.
summary: A manager spins a pay freeze as a positive by pointing out that rising prices will reliably leave his staff worse off.

file: 1994/1994-04-20_out bidding_control_dsn_creative investoment_money_consultants_spending_fast.gif
title: Bidding War Against Equally Clueless Rivals

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Bad news sir -- our arch rivals are out-bidding us for control of DSN.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Apparently they have even less creative investment ideas than we do.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Quick! Give more money to our consultants!!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: They're spending as fast as they can, sir!!

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, reports that a rival company is outbidding them for control of DSN. She adds that the rival's investment ideas are even less creative than theirs. The Boss panics and orders more money given to the consultants, and Carol replies that they are already spending as fast as they can.
punchline: The Boss's response to a bidding war is to throw more money at consultants, who are already burning cash as fast as possible, implying both sides are wasting money on uncreative, wasteful spending.
summary: A boss hears that a rival is winning a takeover contest and reacts by ordering a bigger payout to consultants who are already draining the budget.

file: 1994/1994-08-27_barbarian_binder family_loyal subjects_mister computer_spilled coffee_stapler_thwarted moat_king of cubicle.gif
title: King of the Cubicle Realm

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I am the king of my cubicle, the absolute ruler of this tiny realm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And these are my loyal subjects: Mister Computer, Mister Stapler, and the Binder Family.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Who spilled coffee?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The barbarian is thwarted at the moat.

situation: Dilbert sits in his cubicle daydreaming that he is a king ruling over his tiny domain, with his computer, stapler and binders as his loyal subjects. A coworker in a green tie stands outside the cubicle wall and asks who spilled coffee. Dilbert imagines the intruder as a barbarian stopped at the moat.
punchline: Dilbert's grandiose fantasy of ruling a cubicle kingdom turns a coworker's mundane complaint about spilled coffee into a barbarian invasion, highlighting how small and powerless his domain really is.
summary: A lonely office worker imagines his cubicle as a kingdom populated by office supplies, and casts a coworker asking about a coffee spill as a defeated invader.

file: 1994/1994-09-13_cat_not optimist_phrased better_rakberts head_stomp on it_yank off_bob the dinosaur_rat_dog_animals.gif
title: Poorly Phrased Cat-Yanking Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, I'll yank the cat off of Ratbert's head and you stomp on it!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: YANK

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: STOMP

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I could have phrased that better.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm not an optimist anymore.

setting: Outdoors against a plain blue sky
situation: Catbert is clinging to Ratbert's head, so Dogbert tells Bob the dinosaur that he will yank the cat off and Bob should stomp on it. Dogbert yanks, but Bob stomps at the same moment, and Ratbert is flattened instead of the cat. Dogbert then admits his instructions were poorly worded and says he is no longer an optimist.
punchline: Dogbert's vague instructions caused Bob to stomp on Ratbert rather than the cat, and Dogbert's dry remark about no longer being an optimist underplays the blunder.
summary: A badly worded plan to dislodge a cat from a rat's head ends with the dinosaur squashing the wrong animal.

file: 1994/1994-10-01_fired_hired back_other people are smarter_wally is dumb_boss is dumb_more money.gif
title: Fired Wally Returns as Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally? I thought you got fired.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I did.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But people outside the company appear smarter. So they hired me back as a consultant for way more money.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did you understand that? Don't feel embarrassed to ask for help on the hard stuff.

situation: Dilbert is surprised to find Wally at his desk after hearing he was fired. Wally explains that he was rehired as a consultant at a much higher rate, because outsiders are assumed to be smarter. He then condescendingly offers Dilbert help with anything he finds hard to understand.
punchline: Wally has gained a bigger paycheck and a sense of superiority simply by changing his status from employee to consultant, even though he is the same person who was fired.
summary: After being let go, a lazy coworker returns on a lucrative contract and now treats his former peer as someone needing his guidance.

file: 1994/1994-06-08_computer program_spelled wrong_colons_collen_ass.gif
title: Boss Mocks Code, Colons Insult

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saw the code for your computer program yesterday.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looked easy. It's just a bunch of typing. And half of the words were spelled wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't get me started about your over-use of colons.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They remind me of you, sir.

situation: The Boss lounges behind his desk and belittles the program Dilbert wrote, calling the code just a bunch of typing with misspelled words. He then complains about Dilbert's overuse of colons. Dilbert replies that the colons remind him of the Boss.
punchline: Dilbert subtly insults his boss by comparing him to colons, a pun on the colon as a body part (an ass), implying the Boss is one.
summary: A clueless manager dismisses a programmer's work as simple typing full of typos, and the programmer retaliates with a veiled anatomical insult.

file: 1994/1994-12-05_japanese model_copy best practices_long term investing_boss sings shaft.gif
title: Copying Japanese Best Practices: Karaoke

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've studied the Japanese model and decided to copy their best practices.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Long term investing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Karaoke!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shaft! Can you dig it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank God we don't have lifetime employment.

situation: The Boss announces that the company has studied the Japanese business model and will copy its best practices. Dilbert guesses long term investing, but the Boss means karaoke and stands on the table to belt out the theme from Shaft. Dilbert is left grateful that the company doesn't offer lifetime employment.
punchline: Management cherry-picks the silliest part of the Japanese model instead of the meaningful practices, and Dilbert is relieved he won't be stuck with this boss for life.
summary: A manager adopts only the fun, trivial piece of a famous management philosophy while the employee quietly dreads being stuck with him forever.

file: 1994/1994-08-13_impression_dog in space_physical humor_lost art.gif
title: Dogbert's Dog-in-Space Impression Flops

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And now I will give you my impression of a dog in space.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Physical humor is a lost art.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let me know if you find it.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, at his desk with a computer
situation: Dogbert announces he will perform an impression of a dog in space while Dilbert sits at his computer. In the second panel Dogbert is upside down in mid-air, apparently floating, while Dilbert keeps working. Dogbert remarks that physical humor is a lost art, and Dilbert deadpans that he should tell him if he finds it.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic reply implies that Dogbert's floating stunt wasn't funny at all, so physical humor is not so much lost as absent from his act.
summary: Dogbert attempts a zero-gravity pantomime for an unimpressed Dilbert, who responds with a dry jab at the performance.

file: 1994/1994-05-23_steering committee_calla meeting_department heads_override_moot point_leaders only.gif
title: Overriding Steering Committee With Unschedulable Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you remember what the steering committee decided about my project?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'd better call a meeting with all the department heads. Their orders will override the steering committee and make it a moot point.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It will take months to get on all of their calendars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And don't invite yourself. It's for leaders only.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss whether he remembered the steering committee's decision on Dilbert's project, and the Boss admits he didn't. The Boss then tells Dilbert to call a meeting of all department heads so their orders can override the committee. When Dilbert points out that scheduling it will take months, the Boss adds that Dilbert isn't allowed to attend.
punchline: The Boss's solution to forgetting a decision is to create an impossible-to-schedule meeting that excludes the very person who needs the answer, ensuring the project stays stuck.
summary: A manager who forgot a committee's ruling sidesteps the issue by ordering an unschedulable leaders-only meeting that the project owner can't even attend.

file: 1994/1994-06-23_called to brag_dogbert headhunting service_no skill_pays 100k_dogbert job.gif
title: Boss Brags About Skill-Free Job

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is Dogbert's headhunting service.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got a job that pays a hundred thousand per year and requires no skill whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I didn't say it's available. I called to brag about my own job.

setting: Dogbert's headhunting office and the Boss's office, on the telephone
situation: Dogbert answers the phone at his headhunting service. The Boss calls and describes a job paying a hundred thousand a year that needs no skill, which sounds like an opening. He then clarifies that the job isn't available and he only called to brag about his own position.
punchline: The Boss's own job pays handsomely and requires no skill, and he is so oblivious that he openly brags about it as an insult to the skill-based pay system.
summary: A manager phones a recruiter to boast about his own cushy, well-paid, talent-free position rather than to fill any vacancy.

file: 1994/1994-10-12_key boards replaced_motion sensing_computer screen_3d image_technical professionals_engineer_moron_engineering.gif
title: Futuristic Gadgets Make Engineers Look Foolish

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Futurist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Someday, keyboards will be replaced by motion-sensing rings on your fingers...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The computer screen will be projected in your glasses as a 3-D image.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: These developments will not enhance the image of technical professionals.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Are you an engineer?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a moron. Common mistake.

setting: Dogbert's desk and a hallway or office where people are using futuristic computer gear
situation: Dogbert, billed as a futurist, predicts that keyboards will be replaced by motion-sensing finger rings and that screens will be projected onto eyeglasses in 3-D. A caption warns this won't help the image of technical professionals. In the last panel, Dilbert and another man flail their hands in the air while wearing the gear, and a bystander asks whether they are engineers.
punchline: People wildly waving their hands at invisible screens look so ridiculous that an engineer has to say he's a moron, and the other person responds that it's a common mistake, implying engineers and morons are easily confused.
summary: A pet prophet foresees wearable computing, and the resulting hand-waving makes tech workers look like fools.

file: 1994/1994-01-14_dogbert_reincarnation fund_rich already_customer_needs help_van.gif
title: Reincarnation Fund Meets Broke Hippie

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Invest your money in my reincarnation fund and you'll be rich in a future life.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: But I am rich in this life, for I have love in my heart and music in my soul.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So, can you help me push my van home?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like you'll also have sharp pain in your muscles.

situation: Dogbert pitches a reincarnation fund to a customer in a headband and sunglasses, promising riches in a future life. The customer says he is already rich in love and music, then asks Dogbert to help push his broken-down van home. Dogbert declines by pointing out the physical pain the customer will have.
punchline: Dogbert mocks the customer's claim of spiritual wealth by noting that his actual prospects are poverty and sore muscles from pushing his van.
summary: A scam-peddling dog is told by a free-spirited prospect that he needs no money, until the man's request for help with his dead van reveals how poor he really is.

file: 1994/1994-02-02_exorcise demons_stupidity_posess_stupidity gone_boss_empty suit.gif
title: Exorcising Stupidity Leaves Empty Suit

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hold still while I exorcise the demons of stupidity that possess you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Out! Out! I command you demons of stupidity to be gone!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The suit is now safe.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thanks!

setting: Office, with Dogbert standing on a desk wearing a yellow pointed hat and holding a wand
situation: Dogbert, dressed in a ceremonial yellow hat and holding a wand, performs an exorcism on the Boss to drive out the demons of stupidity that possess him. After Dogbert commands the demons to leave, the Boss's body vanishes, leaving only his empty suit and tie. Dogbert declares the suit safe, and a voice from the empty suit thanks him.
punchline: When all the stupidity is removed from the Boss, nothing is left of him but an empty suit, implying that stupidity is all there is to him.
summary: A costumed Dogbert casts out the foolishness from his boss and discovers that nothing remains once it's gone.

file: 1994/1994-07-10_share accomplishements_meeting_share_tiger team_lock up session_meeting cancelled_nothing tangible_busy work_business.gif
title: Padding Accomplishments With Buzzwords

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's each share our accomplishments for the month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To the untrained observer it might seem like I didn't accomplish anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: However, I did strategically "position" my project by socializing it within the company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then Wally and I held a "tiger team" lock-up session.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I prepared the executive briefing package for the big meeting that got canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Since then I've spent most of my time looking for the best project management software to use.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I did it all within ten percent of my budget goal!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Looking good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. All I did was that tiger thing.

setting: Conference room during a monthly status meeting
situation: The boss asks everyone to share their monthly accomplishments. Dilbert admits he seemingly did nothing, then dresses up trivial activities in management jargon: socializing his project, a tiger team session, a briefing for a canceled meeting, and shopping for software. He caps it by claiming he stayed within budget, and the boss approves.
punchline: Dilbert makes essentially zero real output sound impressive with buzzwords and a budget claim, leaving Wally impressed and feeling his own tiny effort was the real accomplishment.
summary: A worker with no real results spins idle busywork into an impressive-sounding progress report that wins the boss's approval.

file: 1994/1994-09-17_executive style decison_cucbicle_illegible question scrawled_loose original_excuses.gif
title: Executive-Style Decision: Lose the Original

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This item will require your usual executive-style decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know: Keep it on your desk for three weeks, then sneak it back to my cubicle with an illegible question scrawled in the margin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or, for your convenience, I have made no copies; so you can lose the original and claim you gave it back to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm.

situation: Dilbert brings a document to The Boss that needs a decision. He sarcastically describes the boss's usual routine of sitting on paperwork for weeks and then returning it with a useless illegible note. He then helpfully offers to make it easier by providing no copies, so the boss can simply lose the original and blame Dilbert, and the boss seems to consider the suggestion.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic description of the boss's decision-avoiding habits is taken by the boss as a helpful tip, as he ponders the offer to lose the only copy.
summary: A sarcastic employee spells out his boss's habit of stalling on paperwork, only to have the boss weigh the idea of simply losing the document and blaming him.

file: 1994/1994-01-08_shot from cannon_building_crash window_lands on desk_dilbert_travel budget cuts_primitive_begs for busfare.gif
title: Shot From Cannon Into Meeting

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Boom!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crash!

transcript.speaker: Man at table
transcript.text: I hear your company is trimming travel budgets.

transcript.speaker: Traveler
transcript.text: Can anyone lend me bus fare to get home?

setting: Office building exterior and a conference room
situation: A cannon on the side of an office building fires a businessman with a briefcase through the air. He crashes through a window and lands face-first on a conference table where other employees are meeting. One attendee remarks on the company's travel budget cuts, and the dazed traveler asks for bus fare home.
punchline: The company's travel budget cuts are so extreme that business travelers are literally launched from cannons to reach their destinations, leaving them stranded with no money for the trip back.
summary: A salesman blasted by cannon into a conference room meeting wryly asks to borrow bus fare after hearing about slashed travel funds.

file: 1994/1994-05-28_genus_derogatory word_rat_rattus_define its own name_dog_smarter than stupid rattus_animals.gif
title: Rat Demands Respectful Name, Dog Retaliates

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: From now on, I prefer that you not refer to my genus by the derogatory word "rat."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The correct word is "rattus." It is the right of any group to define its own name. You must respect that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't call me a dog any more. From now on my correct name is "smarter-than-a-stupid-rattus."

setting: Dogbert's home, with a TV on a purple cushion
situation: Ratbert stands before Dogbert, who is lounging on a cushion beside a small TV. Ratbert insists on being called "rattus" instead of "rat" and says every group has a right to define its own name. Dogbert turns the same argument around by declaring his own insulting new name.
punchline: Dogbert exploits Ratbert's own principle of self-defined names to give himself a title that insults Ratbert, showing the 'right to define your name' argument can be used as a weapon.
summary: A rat demands a more dignified label for his species, so a dog invokes the same right to rename himself with a name that mocks the rat.

file: 1994/1994-11-18_old computers_spare wrokstaion_screen saver.gif
title: Boss Hogs the Fancy Workstation

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is just great... We engineers have old IBM 286 PCs and you have a SPARC workstation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but the only thing you know how to do is stare at the screen saver.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How does that ball keep bouncing?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If anybody needs me I'll be scrolling some text.

situation: Wally complains that the engineers are stuck with obsolete IBM 286 PCs while the Boss has a powerful SPARC workstation. He points out that the Boss only uses it to watch the screen saver. The Boss, transfixed, wonders how the ball keeps bouncing, and Wally sarcastically announces he'll go scroll some text.
punchline: The Boss has the best computer in the department yet uses it only to watch a screen saver, while Wally mocks that he himself is doing equally pointless busywork.
summary: An engineer grumbles about a manager's expensive workstation being wasted on staring at a bouncing-ball display.

file: 1994/1994-09-06_phone poll_dogbert_voting twice_each call costs_money making_opinions.gif
title: Dogbert's Pay-Per-Opinion Phone Poll

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on TV)
transcript.text: People are so stupid they should pay me to listen to their opinions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on TV)
transcript.text: If you disagree, you can call my phone poll at 555-DOG-BERT. Each call costs two dollars.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm voting twice.

situation: Ratbert watches Dogbert on a TV broadcast declaring that people are so stupid they should pay him to hear their opinions. Dogbert then invites anyone who disagrees to call his phone poll at two dollars per call. Ratbert, having taken the bait, picks up the phone and announces he will vote twice.
punchline: Dogbert insults his audience and then charges them to disagree, and Ratbert proves him right by eagerly paying twice to object.
summary: A television Dogbert tricks viewers into paying to dispute his claim that they are foolish, and a viewer cheerfully proves the point by phoning in twice.

file: 1994/1994-12-06_9000 crtification_great on brochures_certificates_consistent process_lie on brochures.gif
title: ISO 9000 Certification Brochure Lies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of getting our "ISO 9000" certification.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We don't know what it is, but it looks great on brochures.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it certifies that we follow a consistent process.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's us; we always lie on our brochures.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to obtain ISO 9000 certification, admitting he has no idea what it is but that it will look good in marketing brochures. Dilbert explains it certifies a consistent process, and the Boss misreads this as describing the company's habit of lying in its brochures.
punchline: The Boss thinks 'consistent process' describes the company's consistent dishonesty in its marketing, revealing that the certification is purely for show.
summary: A clueless manager pursues a quality certification solely for its marketing appeal and then cheerfully mistakes its meaning for his company's habitual dishonesty.

file: 1994/1994-02-22_buzzword bingo_buzzword_very attentive_proactive leadership_bingo.gif
title: Buzzword Bingo Wins at Meeting

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Here's your "Buzzword Bingo" card for the meeting.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: If the boss uses a buzzword on your card, you check it off. The objective is to fill a row.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're all very attentive today. My proactive leadership must be working!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bingo, sir.

situation: Wally hands Dilbert a buzzword bingo card and explains the rules: check off each buzzword the boss says and try to complete a row. In the meeting, the boss praises everyone for being so attentive. Wally replies 'Bingo, sir,' having just completed his row.
punchline: The boss mistakes the staff's close attention for the effect of his leadership, when they are really listening for his buzzwords, and his phrase 'proactive leadership' is what completes Wally's bingo.
summary: A game that turns corporate jargon into a competition leaves a clueless manager crediting himself for his employees' rapt attention.

file: 1994/1994-04-24_voice controlled computer_envious_mouse driven_color printer denied_delete a file_curses.gif
title: Voice-Controlled Computer Envy Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Expand... window

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, look who got a voice-controlled computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Insert... column

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: If I were a lesser engineer I might be envious.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Add... row

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I don't mind using my prehistoric mouse-driven computer.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And I'm not bitter about my request for a color printer being denied!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: At least I won't work all day then accidentally...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Delete... a file!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: [symbols of cursing]

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please... not in front of the computer.

situation: Dilbert tests his new voice-controlled computer by speaking commands aloud while a jealous coworker stands behind him complaining about his own outdated mouse-driven machine and denied color printer request. The coworker's bitter rant leads him to shout 'delete a file' as a pointed remark, which the voice-controlled computer picks up. Dilbert then has to ask him not to swear in front of the computer.
punchline: The envious coworker's angry outburst and cursing gets interpreted as voice commands by the computer, so Dilbert must ask him to stop swearing near it.
summary: A resentful colleague grumbles at a voice-operated computer user and ends up shouting commands the machine might obey.

file: 1994/1994-06-28_book publishing_reject authors_untalented dolts_publish something_conventional wisdom.gif
title: Dogbert's Publishing House Rejects Everyone

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's the book publishing business coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I get to reject dozens of authors every day! I call them untalented dolts and they thank me for it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Eventually, you have to actually publish something.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, well, that's the conventional wisdom.

setting: Dogbert's office or home, with Dogbert behind a book
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert how his new book publishing business is going. Dogbert happily explains that his favorite part is rejecting dozens of authors daily and insulting them. Dilbert points out that a publisher must eventually publish something, and Dogbert dismisses this as mere conventional wisdom.
punchline: Dogbert has built a publishing business around the fun of rejecting and insulting authors, and brushes off the core purpose of publishing as just conventional wisdom.
summary: A gleeful dog turns the power to reject aspiring writers into his whole business model and shrugs off the idea that a publisher should print books.

file: 1994/1994-04-12_weasel_mink_boss_dilbert.gif
title: Boss Corrects Weasel to Mink

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired a weasel to help us write our business case.

transcript.speaker: Weasel
transcript.text: Whisper whisper.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I say weasel? I meant mink.

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert that he has hired a weasel, an actual weasel in a shirt and tie, to help write the company's business case. The weasel whispers in the Boss's ear, and the Boss immediately corrects himself to say he hired a mink instead. Dilbert stands by silently as the Boss swaps the word.
punchline: The weasel is sensitive about being called a weasel, so the Boss swaps in the more upscale 'mink', mocking how business writing relies on shady, deceitful people and euphemisms.
summary: A manager brags about bringing in a weasel to craft a business case, then hastily rebrands the creature as a mink after it whispers a complaint.

file: 1994/1994-10-09_ask dilbert_attractive_bad hair_engineers can't lie_hairdo_insults woman_make ship date_technical questions_truth_bugs are features.gif
title: Engineers Can't Lie About Bugs

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I brought Dilbert, in case you have any technical questions about our product.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Heh-heh... Engineers don't know how to lie. The truth will be mine.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Uh-oh

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Ted said your product is bug-free. Is that true, Dilbert?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... yes, that's true.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean... basically true. Technically true. Sort of...

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Phew.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No-o-o!! It's a lie! All the bugs were reclassified as security features just to make the ship date!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And we both think you could be attractive if you'd just do something with your hair.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Why did I bring you along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The evidence suggests that you're stupid.

situation: Ted brings Dilbert to a meeting with a female customer, believing an engineer can vouch for the product. The customer says engineers can't lie, and Dilbert first confirms the product is bug-free, then cracks and admits the bugs were relabeled as security features to hit the ship date. He then blurts out an insult about her hair, and Ted wonders why he brought him.
punchline: Ted's plan to use an honest engineer backfires completely, as Dilbert's inability to lie leads him to expose the product's bugs and insult the customer, then he coolly tells Ted he was stupid to bring him.
summary: A salesman's attempt to use a truthful engineer as proof of product quality collapses when the engineer confesses the secret and offends the customer.

file: 1994/1994-01-15_ratio_liquidity to stupidity_reincarnation fund_985 water_cheap suit_amazing brain.gif
title: Dogbert's Reincarnation Fund Flattery Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good news — your ratio of liquidity to stupidity is very low. You qualify to invest in my reincarnation fund!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If my ratio is low, that means I'm ... uh...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Made of liquid!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd say you're 98% water, 2% cheap suit, and what's left is your amazing brain.

setting: Dogbert's office, with the Boss seated across the desk
situation: Dogbert, acting as a financial salesman, tells the Boss he qualifies for a reincarnation fund because his ratio of liquidity to stupidity is very low. The Boss misreads the ratio and concludes he must be made of liquid. Dogbert plays along with a flattering breakdown of the Boss's composition.
punchline: Dogbert's flattery about the Boss's 'amazing brain' is mathematically absurd, since 98% water plus 2% suit leaves nothing for a brain, quietly insulting him while he takes it as a compliment.
summary: A scheming Dogbert pitches an afterlife investment and hides an insult inside praise for his gullible, easily flattered customer.

file: 1994/1994-10-13_dogbert_speech_have and have nots_dumb ones_cavemans_unevolved.gif
title: Technology Have-Nots Run the Boardroom

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the futurist

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Society will become divided into technology "haves" and "have nots."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eventually the two groups will take different evolutionary paths.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then, as now, the "have nots" will be the policy makers.

transcript.speaker: Caveman
transcript.text: Oog make mission statement.

setting: A lecture hall where Dogbert is giving a speech, then a prehistoric-style conference room
situation: Dogbert, billed as a futurist, lectures an audience that society will split into technology haves and have nots who evolve along different paths. The strip then shows the have-nots as primitive cavemen seated around a conference table, where one announces he is writing a mission statement.
punchline: Dogbert predicts that the technologically backward cavemen will still be in charge of policy, which satirically implies that the people running organizations are clueless and primitive, and that they still busy themselves with corporate rituals like mission statements.
summary: A pontificating dog forecasts a tech-driven human split, then reveals that the primitive branch will still hold all the power and draft corporate mission statements.

file: 1994/1994-04-19_static_copyright_fifty billion_film library_blow deal_copyrighted everything.gif
title: Dogbert Copyrights Blank TV Static

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't copyright the static on blank TV channels!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I already did.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't let my company pay fifty billion dollars to buy your so-called film library.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I already am.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I may have to blow the whistle on this little deal.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It'll have to be a nose whistle -- I copyrighted everything else.

situation: Dilbert confronts Dogbert, who has copyrighted the static on blank TV channels and is selling it as a 'film library' to Dilbert's company for fifty billion dollars. When Dilbert threatens to blow the whistle on the deal, Dogbert reveals he has already copyrighted every other kind of whistle.
punchline: Dogbert has copyrighted so many things that Dilbert's only remaining option for whistleblowing is a nose whistle, showing there is no escape from his scheme.
summary: A scheming dog sells a gullible company worthless TV static as a priceless library and pre-empts the whistleblower's every option.

file: 1994/1994-01-28_another war_elbonia_france_french embassy_french stopped bomb_goading_nothing worth destroying_scarp metal.gif
title: Elbonia Profits From French Bombing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...The French stopped bombing Elbonia when they realized there was nothing worth destroying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ironically, the GNP of Elbonia tripled by selling the bomb fragments for scrap. When I left they were trying to goad France into another war.

transcript.speaker: French Embassy Staff
transcript.text: You call this swill champagne?? If we drank this we'd have to eat snails to get the taste out of our mouths too!!

setting: Dilbert's living room, then outside the French Embassy
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair with Dogbert and recounts his trip to Elbonia, explaining that the French stopped bombing the country because nothing was left worth destroying. He adds that Elbonia's economy tripled by selling the bomb fragments as scrap, and that they now want France to attack again. In the last panel, two figures outside the French Embassy complain bitterly about the poor quality of their champagne.
punchline: Elbonia is so impoverished that being bombed is its best economic opportunity, and the strip then mocks French snobbery with embassy staff insulting the champagne they are served.
summary: A returning traveler describes a country so poor that wartime wreckage became its main export, while diplomats elsewhere sneer at bad bubbly.

file: 1994/1994-03-28_commercial prodcuts_secret_evoultion_zimbu the monkey.gif
title: Monkey Outperforms Engineers Using Tail

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Zimbu the monkey designed three commercial products this week! We'd better find out his secret.

transcript.speaker: Wally
