transcript.text: He's using his tail! He has a natural advantage!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I feel the jaws of evolution on my throat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good gravy! Did you see him cut and paste?!

situation: Wally and Dilbert are alarmed that a monkey named Zimbu designed three commercial products in a single week and decide to investigate his secret. They peek over a cubicle wall and watch the monkey working at a computer, using his tail. Wally feels threatened by evolution, and Dilbert is stunned by how easily the monkey cuts and pastes.
punchline: The engineers feel so threatened by a monkey out-producing them that they treat his tail as an evolutionary advantage, while cut and paste is revealed as the unremarkable skill behind his supposed brilliance.
summary: Two coworkers spy on a prolific monkey colleague and panic that nature itself has made them obsolete.

file: 1994/1994-03-30_use tail_operate mouse_engineers_no tail_rocky_new programmer.gif
title: Monkey Programmer Uses Tail

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Zimbu, you're not supposed to use your tail to operate the mouse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If tails were a natural advantage for engineers then evolution would provide us all with tails!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I don't believe you've met Rocky, our new C programmer.

situation: Dilbert scolds Zimbu, a monkey coworker at a computer, for using his tail to operate the mouse, and argues that tails would not be an engineering advantage or evolution would have given everyone one. The Boss then introduces Rocky, the new C programmer, who is another tailed monkey-like coworker standing beside him.
punchline: Dilbert's smug evolutionary argument against tails is immediately undercut when the boss introduces yet another tailed hire, showing the company keeps hiring monkeys regardless of his logic.
summary: After Dilbert lectures a monkey colleague about evolution and tails, his boss arrives with another tailed new hire to meet him.

file: 1994/1994-11-11_buy put options_engineers order_management approval_stock_dogcart the consultant.gif
title: Consultant Advice Tanks Company Stock

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend letting the engineers order their own supplies without management approval.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Yes!!! I'm rich!! Ha ha ha ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I recommend buying "put" options in your stock.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Whoo! Whoo! Whoo!

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises a manager to let engineers order their own supplies without management approval. The manager laughs gleefully, believing he will get rich, and Dogbert follows up by recommending he buy put options in his own company's stock. The manager celebrates, apparently pleased that the plan will wreck the company's share price.
punchline: Dogbert's advice is so ruinous that the only way to profit is to bet against the company's stock, implying that letting engineers buy supplies freely will bankrupt the business.
summary: A consultant suggests a spending policy so disastrous that the gleeful executive is told to bet against his own company's shares.

file: 1994/1994-08-21_proposal_alternatives_lobby government_tax breaks_idiot run businesses_quit job_new career_handing out towels_cow chips_bull shit.gif
title: Boss Demands Alternatives, Gets Insults

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your proposal doesn't address the alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There aren't any reasonable alternatives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There are always alternatives! Give me alternatives!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No wonder nothing gets done around here — not enough alternatives.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "We could lobby the government to give tax breaks to all idiot-run businesses."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "I could quit this stupid job and start a new career handing out towels at the gym."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Or we could use cow chips instead of microchips and save millions."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's a cow chip?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This job would be an example.

setting: The Boss's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Boss rejects Dilbert's proposal because it doesn't list alternatives, even after Dilbert says there are no reasonable ones. Dilbert goes back to his computer and writes a set of alternatives that insult the company and the Boss. When the Boss asks what a cow chip is, Dilbert answers that the job is an example.
punchline: Dilbert dresses up insults as 'alternatives' and ends by calling the Boss's job, a pile of manure, a cow chip, and the Boss doesn't catch the insult.
summary: Pushed to invent options nobody needs, an engineer drafts sarcastic alternatives that mock his idiotic employer and then insults his boss to his face.

file: 1994/1994-07-05_project cancelled_answer_task delegated_craft response_boss delegating job_do nothing boss_fraud.gif
title: Cancelled Project Question Delegated Downward

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you remember when the company president visited? You asked why your project had been cancelled.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He promised to get an answer. That task has been delegated all the way back down to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to craft a response for me. You'll have to put your new project on hold until this is done.

situation: The Boss reminds Dilbert that he once asked the company president why his project was cancelled. The president promised an answer, and the task was passed down through management until it landed on the Boss. The Boss then hands it to Dilbert, telling him to write the response himself and to pause his new project to do it.
punchline: Dilbert's question about why his project was cancelled gets delegated down the chain until he has to answer it himself, at the expense of his new work.
summary: A question sent up the chain of command bounces all the way back to the employee who asked it, along with extra work.

file: 1994/1994-01-12_converstaion_dilbert_faking through_velcro works_block oxygen_brain.gif
title: Trapped by Dilbert's Velcro Lecture

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Blah blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (thought)
transcript.text: He's explaining something that I already understand. I've got to stop him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Blah blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (thought)
transcript.text: I'll try vigorous nodding and agreeing, plus closed body language.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Right right right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And have I ever told you how "Velcro" works?

transcript.speaker: Coworker (thought)
transcript.text: Maybe if I block the oxygen to my brain...

setting: Office, in a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Dilbert holds a Velcro-strapped device and drones on to a coworker, who already understands what he is explaining. The coworker tries to end the lecture with vigorous nodding, agreement, and closed body language, but Dilbert just keeps going and moves on to a lecture about how Velcro works. The coworker ends up wishing he could cut off oxygen to his own brain.
punchline: The coworker's polite tactics to stop a boring explanation backfire, since agreeing only encourages Dilbert to talk more, leaving him desperate enough to contemplate self-induced unconsciousness.
summary: A worker's attempts to politely shut down a colleague's tedious explanation only fuel more rambling, driving him to consider passing out as an escape.

file: 1994/1994-08-04_commercial_show company cars_avoid pedestrians_message_we care_sell bloopers_dick clark.gif
title: Car Commercial Bloopers Sold Later

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The commercial will show company cars braking hard to avoid pedestrians.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The message is "We care about people we don't even know!"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Was it dangerous to film this?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll sell the bloopers to Dick Clark.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Thud

situation: Dogbert pitches a TV commercial to the Boss, pointing at a TV that shows company cars braking hard to avoid pedestrians. The Boss asks whether filming it was dangerous, and Dogbert cheerfully replies that the bloopers will be sold to Dick Clark, implying real people were hit. A thud is heard off-panel.
punchline: Dogbert's plan to sell the bloopers to a TV outtake show reveals that the filming actually ran over pedestrians, undercutting the "we care about people" message.
summary: An ad consultant's caring-themed car commercial turns out to have been shot with real casualties that he plans to monetize as outtakes.

file: 1994/1994-05-17_build_meeting_project kick off_project manager_super fast microchips_harder to saboatge_business.gif
title: Secret Project Purpose Prevents Sabotage

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming to the project kick-off meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As project manager I've decided to not tell you the purpose of the project. That way it will be harder for you to sabotage it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Does it require any super-fast microchips?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good Lord, no. Don't build any of those... by Tuesday.

setting: Conference room during a project kick-off meeting
situation: Dilbert, acting as project manager, opens a kick-off meeting and announces he will deliberately withhold the project's purpose so the team cannot sabotage it. A coworker asks whether the project needs super-fast microchips. Dilbert reacts with alarm and tells him not to build any, then adds a Tuesday deadline.
punchline: By hiding the project's purpose, the manager has made it impossible for the team to know what to build, yet he still imposes a firm deadline, exposing how absurd secretive management is.
summary: A project leader keeps his team ignorant of their goal on purpose, then answers their only sensible question with a nonsensical deadline-laden reply.

file: 1994/1994-07-09_dogumentray_engineer at work_director dog_directing dilbert_jumps into action_focus_moved mouse_screen saver_deactivated.gif
title: Dogumentary Captures Engineer Deactivating Screensaver

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As my dogumentary begins, we see the engineer hard at work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Suddenly he leaps into action! Years of training and experience come into focus!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The screen saver has been deactivated. But doubt sets in... Was there a better way?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I should have moved the mouse.

situation: Dogbert films a documentary (a 'dogumentary') of Dilbert at his desk, narrating in a nature-documentary voice. Dilbert's dramatic burst of action turns out to be nothing more than moving his mouse to turn off the screen saver, after which he second-guesses his method.
punchline: The supposedly heroic 'hard work' of an engineer is just idly sitting at a computer until he finally nudges the mouse to dismiss a screen saver, which he then agonizes over as if it were a major technical decision.
summary: A narrating Dogbert films a gripping documentary of Dilbert's big moment, which turns out to be waking up his computer.

file: 1994/1994-04-10_ammunition_automatic weapons_bazookas_citizens_conversation about guns_dog_gun ownership_no ammunition_right to own guns_rocket launchers_weapons of choice_charlton heston_animals.gif
title: Dogbert Controls All The Ammunition

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's your position on gun ownership, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I believe everybody should have the right to own guns.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about automatic weapons?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm all for them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Citizens should have bazookas and rocket launchers too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I believe that all citizens should have the weapons of their choice.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: However, I also believe that only I should have ammunition.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because frankly, I wouldn't trust the rest of you goobers with anything more dangerous than string.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about Charleton Heston?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd keep the string away from him.

situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert for his views on gun ownership while they walk through the grass. Dogbert endorses everyone owning every kind of weapon, up to bazookas and rocket launchers, then reveals that only he should be allowed to have ammunition. When Dilbert asks about Charlton Heston, Dogbert says he would withhold even string from him.
punchline: Dogbert supports unlimited weapon rights in name only while keeping all the ammunition for himself, and he is so distrustful of everyone else that he would even deny string to Charlton Heston, the gun-rights advocate.
summary: Dogbert cheerfully backs everyone's right to any weapon, provided he alone controls the bullets, and singles out a famous gun-rights champion as too dangerous even for string.

file: 1994/1994-08-20_ratbert_filberts cubcile_big eyes_interested.gif
title: Ratbert Fakes Interest With Big Eyes

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I discovered I can look interested in what people say by making my eyes big.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Go ahead - say something. I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to get some work done here.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Work, you say? Very interesting.

situation: Ratbert stands by Dilbert's desk and proudly explains that widening his eyes makes him look interested in what others say. He invites Dilbert to say something, but Dilbert, typing at his laptop, just says he is trying to work. Ratbert responds with wide eyes and a fake-enthusiastic remark, ignoring that he is interrupting.
punchline: Ratbert's feigned interest is a hollow performance that interrupts Dilbert's work, showing that looking attentive is not the same as being helpful or considerate.
summary: A small pet demonstrates his newly learned trick of appearing fascinated by widening his eyes, and uses it to pester a busy coworker.

file: 1994/1994-06-09_six months_project six months_one month_annual visit_doesn't understand_selfish boss_impossible tasks_time frames etc.gif
title: Six-Month Project, One-Month Deadline

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I start the project today and work nights and weekends it will take ... oh, six months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has to be done in ONE month so we can show it to our VP on her annual visit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to know; does it even cross your mind to handle this differently?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need daily status reports on why you're so behind.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that even with nights and weekends the project will take six months. The boss insists it must be finished in one month so it can be shown to the VP during her annual visit. When Dilbert asks whether the boss ever considers handling things differently, the boss responds by demanding daily status reports on why Dilbert is behind.
punchline: The boss ignores the impossible deadline entirely and instead punishes Dilbert in advance by demanding daily reports explaining his failure to meet it.
summary: A manager sets a deadline six times shorter than the estimate, then answers a plea for reason by adding paperwork about the inevitable lateness.

file: 1994/1994-07-12_qualified_technology_artcile_smarter_microsoft corportaion_most geniuses_millionaires_smart.gif
title: Dogbert Smarter Than Microsoft Columnist

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What makes you think you're qualified to be a technology columnist?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's easy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this article I explain why I'm smarter than the entire Microsoft Corporation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, they're mostly geniuses. And many are millionaires.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If they're so smart, why aren't they columnists?

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dilbert questions Dogbert's qualifications to be a technology columnist while Dogbert types on a laptop. Dogbert says he is writing an article claiming to be smarter than all of Microsoft. When Dilbert points out that Microsoft employees are geniuses and millionaires, Dogbert counters that they would be columnists if they were really smart.
punchline: Dogbert absurdly treats being a columnist as the ultimate measure of intelligence, mocking both pundits' arrogance and the idea that writing opinions beats actual success.
summary: A self-assured dog types a column boasting he outwits a software giant, then dismisses its brilliant millionaires for not having his job.

file: 1994/1994-10-16_combines two projects_not the same_boss doesn't undertsnd_too late_logical solition_eliminate your project_resourceful idiot.gif
title: Boss Merges Projects, Then Eliminates Dilbert's

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just had my annual meeting with our vice president.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We decided to combine your project with project "Big Foot" because they're basically the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They're NOT the same! It only seems like it to you because you don't understand either project!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh well. It's too late to do anything. I told him they were the same.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just call him and say you were wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can see why you're not in management.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The logical solution is to wait for the next budget cut and eliminate your project, thus solving two problems.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's nothing more dangerous than a resourceful idiot.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has merged Dilbert's project with another one because he thinks they are the same. Dilbert protests that they differ, but the Boss refuses to correct his mistake with the vice president. Instead he proposes quietly killing Dilbert's project in the next budget cut to cover up his error.
punchline: The Boss would rather destroy an employee's project than admit a mistake to his superior, which makes him a dangerously resourceful idiot.
summary: A manager's blunder leads him to plot the cancellation of his subordinate's work rather than own up to it.

file: 1994/1994-02-04_c computer lamguage_black hole_light can't escape_field gravity_ideas_escape_lack substance.gif
title: Boss Collapses Into Idea-Emitting Black Hole

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, "C" is a computer language, not the grade for my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's happening?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He turned into a black hole, so dense that light cannot escape his field of gravity.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ping

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Unfortunately, only his ideas can escape the gravity because they lack substance.

transcript.speaker: Black hole
transcript.text: What if you program in "B"?

situation: Dilbert explains to his boss that "C" refers to a programming language and not a grade for his project. The boss shrinks into a black hole, and Dilbert narrates in his thoughts that nothing can escape it. Then a suggestion pings out of the black hole anyway.
punchline: The only thing that escapes the boss's black-hole density is his ideas, because they are so insubstantial and useless, as shown by his clueless suggestion to program in "B".
summary: A clueless manager who mistakes a programming language for a grade is imagined as a black hole that can only emit weightless ideas.

file: 1994/1994-02-24_talking_glowing terms_flaming idiot_dynamite.gif
title: Glowing Terms Behind the Boss's Back

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shhh.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We were just talking about you, sir... in glowing terms.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He's a flaming idiot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One stick of dynamite - it's all I ask.

situation: Dilbert and Wally are discussing something privately when Dilbert hushes Wally because the Boss has walked up behind them. Wally covers by claiming they were praising the Boss. Once the Boss walks off, Wally calls him a flaming idiot, and Dilbert wishes for one stick of dynamite.
punchline: The 'glowing terms' were a cover story, and the real opinion of the Boss is so low that Dilbert would like to blow him up.
summary: Caught gossiping, two coworkers feign admiration for the boss, then drop the act the moment he leaves and fantasize about explosives.

file: 1994/1994-10-08_two people_focus group_loved prodcut_not statistically useful_free food_sandwhiches.gif
title: Doubling Production After Two Focus Group Fans

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Two people in a focus group loved our product. So we're doubling our production.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The opinions of two people are not statistically useful...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...especially if you're one of the two people.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I knew those free sandwiches were too good to be true.

setting: Conference room at a meeting table
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that two people in a focus group loved their product, so the company is doubling production. Dilbert points out that two opinions are statistically meaningless, and adds that this is especially true if the boss is one of the two people. The Boss then realizes the free sandwiches were probably what swayed the focus group's opinion, and he was one of the two.
punchline: The Boss based a major production decision on feedback from two people, one of whom was himself, and he only realizes how unreliable it was when he connects the glowing reviews to the free sandwiches.
summary: A manager commits to doubling output because two focus group participants liked the product, only to realize his own bias and the lure of free lunch skewed the result.

file: 1994/1994-12-23_telemarketing_bid to run_telemarketers pay themselves_rip[ off people_old people_no way to lose.gif
title: Telemarketing Bid Preys on Feeble-Minded

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my bid to run your telemarketing company. Basically, it's no cost to you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My telemarketers pay themselves. If they get a feeble-minded person on the phone they charge them triple and pocket the difference.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no way I can lose.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't answer your home phone for a few weeks.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, hands the Boss a bid to run his company's telemarketing operation at no cost to the company. He explains that the telemarketers earn their pay by overcharging feeble-minded people on the phone. The Boss happily concludes he cannot lose, and Dogbert warns him to stop answering his home phone.
punchline: Dogbert's plan only works by fleecing gullible people, and he implies the Boss is exactly the kind of feeble-minded target his telemarketers would exploit.
summary: A consultant pitches a free telemarketing service funded by swindling the gullible, then slyly warns his naive client to avoid his own phone.

file: 1994/1994-01-24_elbonian division_launching staellites_technology_elbonians.gif
title: Elbonians Launch Satellites With Slingshot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our Elbonian division was the low bidder for launching French satellites into orbit.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you personally in charge. Make sure they use the right technology.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I hope those things aren't expensive.

setting: Office, then a hillside in Elbonia
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the Elbonian division won the bid to launch French satellites into orbit and puts Dilbert personally in charge of making sure they use the right technology. In Elbonia, two villagers stand beside a giant wooden slingshot that has just flung something away, and one worries about the cost.
punchline: The Elbonians' idea of launch technology is a primitive slingshot, so the expensive French satellites are being flung rather than properly launched, which shows why the low bid was so low.
summary: A boss hands off a satellite contract won by the cheapest bidder, only for the foreign team to turn out to be using a primitive hillside slingshot.

file: 1994/1994-02-05_3d stereo_life like sound_high def_video_life yet.gif
title: Lifelike Gadgets, Still No Life

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got my 3-D stereo for life-like sound...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got high definition television for life-like video...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you have a life yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, but I'm darn close.

situation: Dilbert proudly shows off his new home entertainment gear, first adjusting a stereo speaker for lifelike sound, then switching on a high definition television for lifelike video. Dogbert, sitting on the floor, asks whether he has a life yet. Dilbert, seated in his armchair surrounded by electronics, answers that he is close.
punchline: Dilbert surrounds himself with gadgets that simulate real life while sitting alone at home, so he is no closer to actually having a life, which makes his claim of being 'darn close' sad and funny.
summary: A lonely engineer boasts about his lifelike audio and video equipment, only to be asked if he has a real life to go with it.

file: 1994/1994-04-11_device conforms_international standards_communications_not fault_less experineced_boss phone number_vendor_salesman.gif
title: Compliant Device Does Nothing Useful

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Our device conforms to all international standards for communications.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In other words, it doesn't do anything useful and it's not your fault.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Is there somebody less experienced I could talk to?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have my boss's number?

setting: Office desk, during a sales meeting
situation: A vendor's salesman pitches a communications device to Dilbert, boasting that it meets all international standards. Dilbert translates this as meaning the device is useless but not the salesman's fault. The salesman then asks to speak with someone less experienced, and Dilbert offers him the Boss's number.
punchline: Dilbert implies that only his clueless boss, the least experienced and most gullible person around, would actually buy a useless product.
summary: A salesman touting a standards-compliant gadget gets decoded by a skeptical engineer and is then sent to prey on the boss instead.

file: 1994/1994-11-21_dogbert the consultant_employee turnover_low rates_metrics_turnover rate_corporate health.gif
title: Low Turnover Means Unemployable Staff

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: A good way to judge corporate health is to look at your employee turnover rate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our turnover rate is very low. We only hire people who aren't skilled enough to work anyplace else.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe metrics aren't the way to go here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No metric has beaten me yet!!

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk
situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, suggests the Boss measure company health by employee turnover rate. The Boss cheerfully explains that turnover is low because he only hires people too unskilled to get jobs elsewhere. Dogbert backs away from metrics, but the Boss proudly insists no metric has beaten him yet.
punchline: The Boss treats low turnover as a sign of success while admitting it exists only because his employees are unemployable elsewhere, and he is proud of 'beating' the metric.
summary: A consultant proposes a health metric, and the boss boasts of gaming it by staffing the company with people nobody else would hire.

file: 1994/1994-12-21_quality award_dishonest parts_project lost budget_assume project failed.gif
title: Faking a Quality Award Submission

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have to submit my project for a "quality" award. I'll need your help on the dishonest parts.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The real story is that the project lost its budget because its acronym was similar to a project that was canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Assume your project would have failed and claim the savings from avoiding it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're spooky.

situation: Dilbert sits at his laptop preparing a quality award submission for his project and asks Dogbert to help with the dishonest parts. After he admits the project only lost funding due to an acronym mix-up, Dogbert suggests claiming the project would have failed and taking credit for the money saved. Dilbert is unnerved by how easily Dogbert comes up with this.
punchline: Dogbert instantly invents a way to turn a clerical budget mistake into an award-winning cost-saving success, showing how corporate awards reward spin rather than real quality.
summary: Seeking help to dress up an ordinary budget mishap as an achievement, Dilbert gets a frighteningly effective spin from his dog.

file: 1994/1994-11-22_dogbert the consultant_warranty replacements_customers_repeat customers.gif
title: Repeat Customers Are Warranty Replacements

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can gauge your success by the number of repeat customers you have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm proud to say that virtually every customer gets another unit within three months of buying the first one!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if you don't count warranty replacements?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh... Then we don't look so good.

setting: Boss's office, during a consulting session
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the Boss that repeat customers are a good measure of success. The Boss proudly claims that nearly every customer comes back for another unit within three months. Dogbert asks whether that still holds if warranty replacements are excluded, and the Boss realizes it doesn't.
punchline: The Boss's proud 'repeat customer' statistic is really just a measure of how often his defective products fail and get replaced under warranty.
summary: A manager brags about his customers' rapid repeat purchases until a consultant's simple question exposes that they are merely replacing broken products.

file: 1994/1994-08-01_boos_delegate work_mark compalins_throws a fit_complain_behind back_boss retreats.gif
title: Uranus-Hertz Company Rebranding Fiasco

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've hired the Dogbert Ad Agency to give our company a new image.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I used a computer to suggest a new hi-tech name for your company. The program randomly combines words from astronomy and electronics.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The first choice is "Uranus-Hertz"

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I like it.

situation: The Boss announces to a meeting that Dogbert's ad agency has been hired to give the company a new image. Dogbert explains he used a computer program that randomly combines astronomy and electronics words to generate a hi-tech name. The first result is a crude-sounding pun, and the Boss happily approves it.
punchline: The Boss is so impressed by the computer-generated hi-tech branding that he fails to notice the name is a juvenile joke ("Your Anus-Hertz").
summary: A consultant dog lets a random word generator name the company, and the oblivious boss approves an accidentally rude result.

file: 1994/1994-07-21_techno geek_shy_boring_gullible_spider on arm_controlling_manipulate_bust_fool.gif
title: Market Research Insults Plus Spider Prank

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In market research terms, you belong to the "techno geek" segment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're shy, boring, gullible and male. You prefer computers to people. There's always a spider on your arm.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Made you look.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert, perched on the back of the couch and reading from a sheet of paper, tells Dilbert that market research classifies him as a "techno geek". He recites a list of unflattering traits, ending with the claim that there is a spider on Dilbert's arm. Dilbert looks down at his arm and Dogbert gloats that he fell for it.
punchline: Dogbert's list of stereotypical techno geek traits includes "gullible", and Dilbert immediately proves it by falling for the oldest trick there is.
summary: A dog reads out a demographic profile calling his owner gullible, then proves it with a childish arm-spider trick.

file: 1994/1994-10-10_sales_two years_sudden surge_business case apporved_get promoted_accountability_business.gif
title: Fake Sales Surge Gets Promotion

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: I predict sales to be nothing for two years and then take a sudden surge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: The surge was added so I could get the business case approved. The two-year lag gives me time to get promoted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about accountability?

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: That's where you come in.

setting: Conference room during a business presentation
situation: A presenter shows a projected sales graph that stays flat for two years and then suddenly spikes. When Dilbert asks why, the presenter admits the surge was invented to get the business case approved, and that the delay gives him time to be promoted away. Dilbert asks about accountability, and the presenter says Dilbert will be the one left holding the bag.
punchline: The presenter cheerfully admits his forecast is fabricated and that by the time it fails he will have been promoted, leaving Dilbert to take the blame.
summary: A manager reveals that his rosy sales projection is pure fiction designed to win approval and buy time for his own advancement, with someone else left to answer for it later.

file: 1994/1994-11-28_bigger portion_success of team_pay depends on coworkers_priorities change.gif
title: Team-Based Pay Backfires Over Printer

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're changing the salary plan to make a bigger portion depend on the success of the team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We reason that if your pay depends on the success of co-workers, then your priorities will change.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now THAT's a pretty resume!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop hogging the good printer.

setting: Conference room, then office cubicle area
situation: The Boss announces a new salary plan in which more pay depends on the team's success, arguing that this will change employees' priorities. Afterward, Wally is seen printing out his resume on the good printer, and Dilbert complains that he is hogging it.
punchline: The new pay plan doesn't make employees care about team success; it makes them start job hunting, and Dilbert's only concern is getting access to the good printer.
summary: After management ties pay to coworkers' success, the staff's reaction is to update their resumes and fight over printer access.

file: 1994/1994-07-01_flying pigs_dilbert dating_insufficient light_heel froze over_rare occasion.gif
title: Hell Freezes Over Dilbert Dates

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I found a woman who likes me, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No way!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Heck just froze over.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is not my fault!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Tell them.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with a desk in the background
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he may have found a woman who likes him, and Dogbert is incredulous. Phil, dressed as a red devil and holding a giant spoon, appears to announce that Heck has frozen over. Pigs fly past in the sky as Dilbert protests his innocence and Phil tells him to take it up with them.
punchline: A woman liking Dilbert is so improbable that it has triggered the classic impossibilities of hell freezing over and pigs flying.
summary: News of a woman's interest in Dilbert is so unlikely that it causes a devil to report Heck freezing over and pigs to take flight.

file: 1994/1994-04-17_vision thing_boss_visions_donuts_coffee_big house_servents_over rated_gardener_everyone laid off.gif
title: Boss's Vision: Lots of Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As your leader it's my job to provide a vision.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But frankly, I'm not seeing anything.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have another donut. Sometimes the sugar helps.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's working. I'm getting something, but it's fuzzy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Quick! Try my coffee!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Mmph!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh yeah, there it is. Oh-oh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It looks like I'll be living in a big house with servants. And you'll all get laid off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This vision thing is overrated.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So, do you have a gardener lined up yet?

situation: The Boss announces that as leader he must provide a vision, but he can't see anything. Wally and Alice feed him a donut and coffee to help the vision along, and he finally sees a future in which he lives in a mansion with servants while his staff is laid off. Dilbert and Wally react with weary resignation.
punchline: The boss's long-awaited vision turns out to be purely selfish, with him getting rich while everyone else loses their jobs, and Wally's reaction is to ask about the gardener job.
summary: A struggling manager coaxes a visionary revelation out of sugar and caffeine, only to foresee personal luxury and mass firings for his team.

file: 1994/1994-01-21_pheromone cologne_women desries_reconcile mentally_wash cologne_aerobics class.gif
title: Pheromone Cologne Repels Women Mentally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The pheremone cologne is making women desire me physically but they can't reconcile it mentally.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: N-n-no

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't fair ... I'll have to wash the cologne off...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: POW

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right after my aerobics class.

setting: Office or public area, outdoors against a plain blue background
situation: Dilbert thinks that his pheromone cologne is attracting women physically while their minds reject him. A blonde woman backs away in panic, and then a POW cloud hits a second woman, leaving her dazed with frazzled hair. Dilbert reluctantly decides to wash the cologne off, but only after his aerobics class.
punchline: Dilbert admits the cologne must go, but keeps wearing it a while longer, since he is still hoping the physical attraction outweighs the mental rejection.
summary: A man convinced his cologne makes women helplessly attracted keeps wearing it despite visibly stunning them.

file: 1994/1994-09-29_new strategy_tech support_that customers_user manual_defective products.gif
title: Defective Products, Paid Tech Support

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new strategy is to make defective products and charge for technical support.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Heh-heh... Our user manual is totally incomprehensible. We didn't plan it that way - we were lucky.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm so proud to be here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It all came together when I realized I hate our customers.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his staff at a meeting table that the company's new strategy is to make defective products and then charge customers for technical support. He gleefully admits the incomprehensible user manual was an accident that worked in their favor, and says the strategy came from realizing he hates the customers. Dilbert responds with deadpan sarcasm.
punchline: The Boss cheerfully reveals a deliberately customer-hostile business strategy, and Dilbert's sarcastic 'I'm so proud to be here' underlines how absurd and cynical it is.
summary: A gloating manager outlines a plan to profit from broken products and baffling documentation, admitting it all stems from his contempt for customers.

file: 1994/1994-12-27_computer interface_hurt user_new sound designs_sound of puking_fingernails on blackboard_bird hitting window_disturbing sounds_visceral reactions.gif
title: Punishing Users With Disgusting Error Sounds

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My theory is that a computer interface should hurt the user.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I designed some new sounds into our product. We've got "sound of puking," "fingernails on blackboard" and "bird hitting window."

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Splat

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But suppose the user does something wrong. Then we have the sound of a puking bird hitting a blackboard.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Puke screech splat

situation: Dilbert stands behind a coworker at a computer and explains his design philosophy that a software interface should cause the user discomfort. He demonstrates the unpleasant sounds he has built into the product, and the coworker reacts with a flinch, then ends up with his legs in the air as the worst sound of all plays for user errors.
punchline: Dilbert's software punishes users for mistakes with a deliberately revolting combined sound, mocking the idea that interfaces should be hostile rather than helpful.
summary: An engineer proudly shows off nauseating error sounds he has built into software to discourage users from making mistakes.

file: 1994/1994-02-15_trying to please_fool_better please_crush you_selfish dogbert_justa thought_others_threatened.gif
title: Dogbert Speaks For All Others

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't live my life trying to please others.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I can speak for all others when I say "Fool! You'd better please us or we'll crush you!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was just a thought.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We "others" don't like to be threatened.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on and in front of a couch
situation: Dilbert sits and announces that he can't spend his life trying to please other people. Dogbert, perched on the couch, appoints himself spokesman for everyone else and menacingly warns Dilbert he'd better keep pleasing them or be crushed. Dilbert backs down immediately, and Dogbert says the 'others' dislike being threatened.
punchline: Dogbert, speaking as 'all others', threatens Dilbert for saying he won't please people, then complains that the 'others' don't like being threatened when Dilbert merely backs down, which exposes the hypocrisy of people who demand to be pleased.
summary: A man's declaration of independence from people-pleasing is shut down by his dog, who claims to represent everyone else and menaces him into backing down.

file: 1994/1994-07-26_judges were cruel_olympic competition_play_ratbert_scored a two_sofa_doves_rat on couch.gif
title: Ratbert's Olympic Couch Dive

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A hush comes over the crowd. This would be Ratbert's most difficult dive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I give it a two.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The judges were cruel. But Ratbert captured the hearts of the audience. Endorsements would follow.

setting: Living room with a red sofa
situation: Ratbert stands on the arm of a couch while a narrator hypes up his most difficult dive, as if it were an Olympic event. He flips through the air and lands, and Dilbert, standing by with a paper, scores it a measly two. Ratbert, lying flattened on the sofa, imagines that the judges were cruel but that the audience loved him and endorsements would follow.
punchline: Ratbert's delusional daydream of Olympic glory and endorsement deals contrasts with his crash landing on the couch and a dismal score of two.
summary: A tiny rat treats a leap off a sofa like an Olympic diving final and consoles himself with fantasies of fame after a poor score.

file: 1994/1994-07-25_unnatural_have girlfirend_star trek comaprison_falls in love_girl dies_shooting star_panic_weird_overthinking.gif
title: Dilbert's Girlfriend Dies Like Star Trek

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It seems almost unnatural for me to have an actual girlfriend.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's like when the captain on "Star Trek" falls in love, and you know the woman will die in an unlikely accident.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! We just saw our first shooting star!

setting: A grassy hilltop at night, stargazing
situation: Dilbert sits on a hill with his girlfriend and admits that having a real girlfriend feels unnatural. He compares it to Star Trek, where the captain's new love interest is always doomed to die in an unlikely accident. Just as he finishes, a meteorite crashes beside them, leaving the girlfriend scorched and dazed.
punchline: Dilbert's Star Trek-style prediction that his girlfriend will die in a freak accident is immediately borne out when a falling meteorite lands right next to her, which he cheerfully mislabels a shooting star.
summary: While stargazing with his girlfriend, a nerdy engineer jokes that she is fated to meet a freak end like a TV starship captain's romance, and a crashing meteorite nearly proves him right.

file: 1994/1994-03-07_customers_marketing_technical_feasible_business.gif
title: Customer Not Boss Feasibility Study

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We in Engineering think of the Marketing Department as our customer, Fred.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: That's great. I'd like you to do a technical feasibility study for me.

transcript.speaker: Fred
transcript.text: Would that require any work?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I said "customer," not "boss."

situation: Dilbert tells a marketing representative named Fred that Engineering regards Marketing as its customer. Fred responds by asking Dilbert to perform a technical feasibility study for him, and then asks whether it would require any work. Dilbert frowns and points out he said customer, not boss.
punchline: Dilbert's talk of treating Marketing as a customer is only a courtesy, and he refuses to do free work on demand as if Marketing were his boss.
summary: A friendly gesture toward a marketing colleague backfires when the colleague treats it as a license to assign work.

file: 1994/1994-08-07_new employee_new engineer_sarcasm_shows around_telephone_cubicle_hallway_every foot staep_bad points_office tour_crazy_bad conditions_employement.gif
title: Show the New Hire the Ropes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Laurie's our new engineer. Show her the ropes, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Dilbert holds up a noose.)

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I meant figuratively.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is your anti-productivity pod.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's equipped with a little device that rings anytime you try to concentrate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The top is open so none of the background noise is inadvertently muffled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you're on the main aisle, so you'll be haunted every minute by footsteps behind you . . . step... step... step...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need to talk.

situation: The Boss introduces Laurie, a new engineer, and tells Dilbert to show her the ropes. Dilbert takes it literally and produces a noose, then gives a brutally honest tour of her cubicle's design flaws: a ringing device, no sound muffling, and constant footsteps. By the end Laurie is standing on top of the cubicle wall with the noose, and the Boss wants a word with Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic, honest tour of the awful working conditions drives the new hire to attempt suicide with the literal rope he gave her.
summary: A literal-minded orientation turns grim when a new engineer is shown a noose and a cubicle designed to destroy concentration.

file: 1994/1994-06-14_bad schdeuling_careless_company cares_last tuesday_long hours_missed out_stress on workers_stress redcution expert_stressful_talk at lunch_too late.gif
title: Stress Talk Scheduled For Last Tuesday

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company cares deeply about the effects of long hours and stress on the workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So they're paying nearly $200 to have an expert on stress-reduction give a talk during lunch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just when you think they don't care, something like this comes along.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's scheduled for last Tuesday.

situation: The Boss announces to the staff that the company cares about the stress caused by long hours and is paying a small fee for a stress-reduction expert to give a lunchtime talk. Dilbert sincerely remarks that this shows the company does care. The Boss then reveals the talk was scheduled for last Tuesday, so it has already passed.
punchline: The company's supposed concern for employee stress is hollow, since the stress-reduction talk was scheduled for a date that had already passed and the workers missed it.
summary: A manager touts a cheap stress-relief lunch talk as proof of corporate compassion, only to let slip that it already took place days ago.

file: 1994/1994-07-31_boost morale_alpha project_atta boy certificate_lazy imposter_wallyina_indian name_gives award_alice gets award.gif
title: Boss Botches Wally's Attaboy Award

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd like to boost morale by presenting this "attaboy" certificate to Willy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's Wally, not Willy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "i" becomes an "a" with a dot over it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, this is for your good work on the Alpha Project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Thanks, but I didn't work on the Alpha Project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get out of my sight, you lazy impostor!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: With a little bit of luck, I can pull this out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I give you your Indian name: "Wallyina."

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tries to boost morale by handing out an 'attaboy' certificate, but gets Wally's name wrong and credits him for a project he never worked on. When Wally points this out, the Boss angrily snatches the certificate back and calls him a lazy impostor. He then tries to recover by awkwardly improvising a fake 'Indian name' for Wally.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to boost morale collapses through his own incompetence, and his desperate cover-up is an absurd, culturally clumsy made-up name.
summary: A manager's botched recognition ceremony turns into an insult and then a ridiculous improvised name as he scrambles to save face.

file: 1994/1994-12-22_quality contest_everything is a lie.gif
title: Quality Contest Entry Full of Lies

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished our write-up for the National Millard Bullrush "Quality" contest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It took two weeks of otherwise productive time. And everything but our address is a lie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you know what irony is?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I send my shirts to a service.

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss the finished application for a national quality contest and complains that it cost two weeks of productive work and is almost entirely fabricated. He asks the Boss if he understands irony. The Boss misunderstands, thinking it has to do with ironing, and replies that he sends his shirts to a laundry service.
punchline: The Boss confuses 'irony' with ironing clothes, missing the point that a quality contest entry built on lies is deeply ironic.
summary: A weary engineer points out the absurdity of falsifying a quality award submission, but his manager mistakes the word for laundry.

file: 1994/1994-11-05_right sizing_company_bright sizing_laughter_bananas at lunch_business.gif
title: Bright-Sizing Joke Over Banana Lunch

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Instead of "right-sizing," our company is "bright-sizing." That's when all the bright people leave!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hoo ha ha hee ha. Hee ha ha. Snort.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! We all brought bananas again.

setting: Lunch table in a break room
situation: Three coworkers eat brown-bag lunches together. One jokes that the company is 'bright-sizing' rather than right-sizing, meaning all the smart employees are leaving. Everyone laughs loudly, then Dilbert cheerfully points out that they all brought bananas again.
punchline: The staff laugh at the joke about smart people leaving, yet the ones who stayed are so unimaginative they all packed the same lunch, proving the point.
summary: A quip about the clever staff fleeing the company gets big laughs from the remaining workers, who then notice they have identical lunches.

file: 1994/1994-03-05_technical degree_obsolete_5 years_doohickey.gif
title: Dilbert Forgets His Technical Vocabulary

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to this, a technical degree becomes obsolete in five years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind? I'm trying to get some work done on the ...uh...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doohickey.

situation: Dogbert sits in a chair reading an article and informs Dilbert that a technical degree becomes obsolete in five years. Dilbert, busy at his computer, irritably asks him to stop interrupting while he works on something, but can't think of the technical term. He ends up calling it a 'doohickey', suggesting the article may be right.
punchline: Dilbert's inability to name the thing he's working on, falling back on the vague word 'doohickey', implies his technical knowledge has already gone obsolete.
summary: A dog reading about expiring degrees gets proof when the engineer he's pestering blanks on a technical term.

file: 1994/1994-09-08_telecommute_high paying_goals_measured_stay home_mail checks_direct deposit.gif
title: Dogbert Seeks Unmeasurable Telecommuting Job

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like a job where I can telecommute every day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It should be high-paying yet have goals which can't be measured.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you'd stay home and we'd mail you checks?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I was hoping for direct deposit.

setting: The Boss's office, during a job interview
situation: Dogbert, sitting in a chair facing the Boss's desk, describes his ideal job: telecommuting daily, high pay, and goals that can't be measured. The Boss summarizes the arrangement as staying home and being mailed checks. Dogbert replies that he'd prefer direct deposit.
punchline: Dogbert is not bothered by the Boss's summary of the arrangement as getting paid for doing nothing; he only quibbles about the payment method, showing he expects to be paid with no accountability.
summary: A canine job applicant lays out terms for a well-paid, work-from-home position with no accountability, and only objects to how he'd get paid.

file: 1994/1994-07-24_downtrodden cubicle workers_form union_working conditions_salaried workers_against law_no overtime_no security_spines_demand bigger cucbilce_union dues_long hours_strap on spines.gif
title: Union Organizer Sells Strap-On Spines

transcript.speaker: Union Organizer
transcript.text: Hear me, all downtrodden cubicle-workers!

transcript.speaker: Union Organizer
transcript.text: I have come to form a union to improve your working conditions!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We can't join a union. We're salaried.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think it's against the law or something.

transcript.speaker: Union Organizer
transcript.text: You've got long hours, no overtime pay, shrinking benefits, and no job security. You must act now!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're confusing us with people who have spines.

transcript.speaker: Union Organizer
transcript.text: Don't worry. I brought strap-on porta-spines for everybody.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I demand a bigger cubicle!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Nobody will take advantage of us ever again!

transcript.speaker: Union Organizer
transcript.text: Now, let's talk about union dues.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Fair enough.

situation: A union organizer stands on a desk urging cubicle workers to unionize over long hours, no overtime, shrinking benefits and no job security. Dilbert and Wally refuse, saying they lack the spines, so the organizer straps artificial spines onto everyone. The newly emboldened employees make timid demands, and the organizer immediately moves on to collecting union dues.
punchline: Employees who are too spineless to organize get fake spines, and the organizer's real aim turns out to be collecting their dues.
summary: A labor agitator cures timid office staff of their meekness with clip-on backbones, then promptly asks them to pay up.

file: 1994/1994-06-10_no work_invented code_accounting systems_mid 80s_undocumented spaghetti logic_holy grail_technology.gif
title: Irv's Undocumented Accounting Code Job Security

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never seen you do any real work around here, Irv. How do you get away with it?

transcript.speaker: Irv
transcript.text: I wrote the code for our accounting system back in the mid-eighties. It's a million lines of undocumented spaghetti logic.

transcript.speaker: Irv
transcript.text: It's the holy grail of technology!!

transcript.speaker: Irv
transcript.text: You boys may find a little extra in your envelopes this month.

setting: Office break room or lunch table
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker named Irv, who never seems to work, how he gets away with it. Irv explains he wrote the company's accounting system decades ago and it is a huge mess of undocumented code that only he understands. He boasts about it and hints that his colleagues may get a bonus.
punchline: Irv keeps his job by making himself indispensable through unmaintainable, undocumented legacy code, and he even calls it the holy grail of technology.
summary: A slacking programmer reveals that his job security rests on an enormous, tangled legacy system nobody else can maintain.

file: 1994/1994-10-23_staff meeting_suggestions_dumb ideas_leaving for another job_never held accountable_project caribou_team building exercise_people vanished_meeting over.gif
title: Restarting Projects to Avoid Accountability

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our project is six months behind schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meanwhile, our technology has become obsolete and the users' requirements have changed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any suggestions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's stubbornly plod along and deliver the useless product that was originally requested.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We should restart every time something changes. That way we'll never be held accountable for results!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You losers can work it out alone. I heard there's a job opening on Project Caribou.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next on the agenda: our weekly team-building exercise.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team the project is six months late, its technology is obsolete and requirements have changed, then asks for suggestions. Dilbert proposes delivering the useless original product, Wally calls that dumb and suggests restarting the project every time something changes so nobody is accountable, and Alice walks out to seek a job on another project. The Boss is left alone and cheerfully moves on to the team-building exercise.
punchline: After the team members bicker and Alice abandons them, the boss blithely announces a team-building exercise to an empty room, showing how oblivious management is to the real cause of the team's dysfunction.
summary: A late, outdated project meeting collapses into bickering and an escape to another team, leaving the boss to announce team building for nobody.

file: 1994/1994-12-11_employee of month_offered parking space_wally takes train_work hard to win_doesn't need prize_laughter_meeting_program_business.gif
title: Employee of the Month Parking Prize

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've implemented an "Employee of the Month Award."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The winner gets to park in a special space right behind the area reserved for managers!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's like saying the very best employee isn't as good as the worst manager.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, you're just as good but... uh... less important.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Personally, I'm feeling all charged up about this program!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm going to work day and night to increase my chances for better parking!!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ha ha ho ho hee ha ha ha

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But wait! I ride the train to work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're off to a rocky start.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces an Employee of the Month award whose prize is a parking space just behind the managers' spots. Dilbert points out the insulting implication, and the Boss clumsily confirms it. Wally enthusiastically vows to work day and night for the parking, then realizes he takes the train to work.
punchline: Wally's burst of enthusiasm for a worthless prize collapses when he remembers he doesn't drive, which perfectly sums up how pointless the incentive is.
summary: A manager launches a recognition program rewarding top staff with a parking spot, and the one eager employee has no car to use it.

file: 1994/1994-07-14_carpal tunnel_health care_money_surgery_constant agony_false alarm_medical.gif
title: Boss Only Wakes For Money

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So now I have carpal tunnel syndrome...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Zzzz

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't care about the health of your employees! All you care about is money!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Money?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need surgery! I'm in constant agony!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: False alarm.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Zzz

setting: Office, in front of the boss
situation: Dilbert, his wrists in braces, tells his boss he has developed carpal tunnel syndrome, but the boss sleeps through it. When Dilbert accuses him of caring only about money, the boss stirs at the word 'money' and perks up. Once Dilbert mentions he needs surgery, the boss decides it was a false alarm and goes back to sleep.
punchline: The boss ignores an employee's suffering and only wakes at the mention of money, then dismisses the whole thing as a false alarm when the topic turns out to be his employee's health, not profit.
summary: An injured employee can only rouse his dozing manager by accusing him of greed, and the manager promptly drifts off again when he realizes there is no money to be had.

file: 1994/1994-10-31_jar_soul of mail boy_shake hold to light_bargaining table_union rights_negotiating.gif
title: Boss Collects Mail Boy's Soul

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's in the jar?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's the soul of Willy the mail boy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you shake it real hard and hold it up to the light you can see it.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The union didn't do too well at the ol' bargaining table this year.

transcript.speaker: Willy the Mail Boy
transcript.text: These aren't our glory years.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss what is in the jar he is holding, and the Boss cheerfully says it contains the soul of Willy the mail boy, urging Dilbert to shake it and hold it to the light to see it. A caption explains the union fared poorly in bargaining this year, as the real Willy delivers mail with a dejected remark.
punchline: Management literally bottled the mail boy's soul after crushing the union in negotiations, and the defeated Willy glumly admits these aren't their glory years.
summary: After a lopsided labor negotiation, a gleeful manager shows off a jar supposedly holding a deflated mail clerk's soul.

file: 1994/1994-04-28_top priority_last month_dated.gif
title: Your Top Priority, Not Mine

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Take care of this immediately. It's your top priority.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Top priority?? This is dated last month. It's been on your desk for weeks and now it's your top priority??

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I said it's your top priority. I still don't care about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... okay then.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a document and tells him to handle it immediately as his top priority. Dilbert notices the paper is dated a month ago and has been sitting on the Boss's desk for weeks. The Boss clarifies that it is Dilbert's priority, not his own, and that he still doesn't care about it.
punchline: The Boss reveals he treats the task as urgent only for Dilbert, while personally ignoring it, showing how managers dump neglected work on subordinates and label it a priority.
summary: A manager offloads a long-neglected paper onto an employee, insisting it's urgent for the employee even though he himself never cared.

file: 1994/1994-08-17_customer service_downsize_improve service.gif
title: Downsizing Fixes Customer Service Problems

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our two goals this year are to downsize and to improve customer service.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: How can you improve service if you're getting rid of service people?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Who do you think is screwing up the customer service? Duh...

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The boss announces two goals for the year: downsizing and improving customer service. Dilbert raises his hand and asks how cutting service staff could possibly improve service. The boss answers dismissively that the service people themselves are the problem.
punchline: The boss's logic blames the very employees he plans to lay off for poor service, using a condescending 'Duh' to justify the contradictory goals.
summary: A manager sets contradictory yearly targets and justifies them by claiming the staff he wants to cut are the source of the trouble.

file: 1994/1994-03-18_organ donor_reorganizations_unwanted employees_what job.gif
title: Reorganization Lands Dilbert as Organ Donor

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sometimes I think these constant reorganizations are just excuses for getting rid of unwanted employees.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What job did you end up with?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Organ donor.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My shoulder is acting up. Do I talk to you or is there a form to fill out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think that's an "organ."

setting: Office, in front of a plain blue background
situation: Wally muses that constant reorganizations are really a pretext for dumping unwanted staff. He then asks Dilbert what job he ended up with after the latest shuffle, and Dilbert grimly answers that he is now an organ donor. Wally promptly asks whether he should talk to Dilbert or fill out a form about his sore shoulder, and Dilbert points out that a shoulder isn't an organ.
punchline: The reorganization has literally turned Dilbert into a body-part supplier, and Wally's only concern is how to get his own sore shoulder dealt with, showing both the grim absurdity of corporate reshuffles and Wally's self-interest.
summary: After a company shake-up, Dilbert's new role is supplying body parts, and a self-serving Wally tries to requisition a fix for his achy shoulder.

file: 1994/1994-06-17_ball_bonk_dilbert_head bounce_make goal_soccer game_strike_uses head bonk.gif
title: Dilbert Scores Goals With Head

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bonk

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gee, I've scored five goals that way.

transcript.speaker: Teammate
transcript.text: You've got a good head for this game.

situation: At a soccer game, a teammate kicks the ball and it bonks Dilbert in the head, sending it into the goal past the diving goalkeeper. Dilbert, dazed, remarks that he has scored five goals this way, and his teammate compliments his head.
punchline: Dilbert is repeatedly being hit in the head by the ball, so his 'good head for this game' is really just a convenient target, and the compliment ignores his pain.
summary: A soccer player's accidental head-hits keep sending the ball into the net, earning him praise for what is really just repeated injury.

file: 1994/1994-05-25_canceling project_cooler acronym_anticipated move_carry empty binders_less fullfilling.gif
title: Cancelled Project, Empty Binders Gloat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm canceling your project so I can give your funding to a project that has a much cooler acronym.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ha! The joke's on you! I anticipated this move from the beginning and have done nothing but carry empty binders for weeks!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Being good at your job is less fulfilling than you might think, Dogbert.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is cancelling his project so the funding can go to one with a cooler acronym. Dilbert triumphantly reveals that he saw this coming and has done no real work for weeks, just carrying empty binders around. He then reflects to Dogbert that competence is not as rewarding as it sounds.
punchline: Dilbert's smug victory over the boss is hollow, since being good at his job has meant dodging work entirely and finding no real fulfillment in it.
summary: Anticipating a pointless cancellation, an employee secretly stopped working and faked busyness, then finds his cleverness oddly unsatisfying.

file: 1994/1994-01-13_reincarnation_investment_fund_invest now_come back as cow_fortune in milk_invest until reincarnate.gif
title: Dogbert's Reincarnation Investment Fund Scheme

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call it "Dogbert's Reincarnation Investment Fund."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You give me your money now and I invest it until you reincarnate. The compound interest will make you rich!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What if I come back as a cow?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll save a fortune in milk.

situation: Dogbert pitches Dilbert on an investment fund in which Dilbert hands over his money now and Dogbert invests it until Dilbert is reincarnated, promising compound interest will make him rich. Dilbert, holding a brochure, asks what happens if he comes back as a cow. Dogbert replies that he will save a fortune on milk.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the obvious flaw in his scam by offering a ridiculous consolation prize, showing he has no intention of delivering real returns.
summary: Dogbert sells an absurd investment that pays out only after the customer's next life, and shrugs off the risk of rebirth as livestock with a quip about dairy savings.

file: 1994/1994-01-10_sharing meeting_project_pathetic series_poorly planned_random acts_emotional desparation_things are fine_need a hug.gif
title: Brutally Honest Project Status Update

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's go around the table and give an update on each of our projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My project is a pathetic series of poorly planned, near-random acts. My life is a tragedy of emotional desperation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's more or less customary to say things are going fine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I need a hug.

setting: Conference room during a project status meeting
situation: The Boss kicks off a meeting by asking everyone to go around the table and report on their projects. Dilbert, when his turn comes, bluntly describes his project as a pathetic series of poorly planned acts and his life as a tragedy. The Boss merely points out that people usually say things are going fine, and Dilbert responds by asking for a hug.
punchline: Dilbert's unfiltered honesty about his chaotic project and bleak life is met with the Boss's only concern being social convention, ignoring any real distress, which leaves Dilbert craving basic human comfort.
summary: Asked for a routine status report, a miserable engineer candidly confesses his project and life are a mess, and his boss only corrects him on etiquette.

file: 1994/1994-12-15_invite yourself_meeting_split donut_ratbert at meeting_no experience in marketing_advised_business.gif
title: Ratbert Crashes Meetings for Donuts

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I didn't get the job in marketing. They say I have no experience.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Try inviting yourself to meetings. Nobody ever says no. And they're too timid to kick you out once you sit down.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Does anybody want to split a donut? I'll just take half and leave the rest.

setting: Dogbert's lounging spot, then a conference room meeting
situation: Ratbert tells Dogbert he was rejected for a marketing job because of his lack of experience. Dogbert advises him to invite himself to meetings, since no one will object or dare to throw him out. Ratbert then shows up at a meeting and offers to split a donut from the box on the table.
punchline: Ratbert's first act as an uninvited meeting attendee is to take half a donut, showing that meetings are really just a free-food opportunity and that attending them requires no qualifications.
summary: A job-seeking Ratbert takes a cynical tip about gatecrashing meetings and promptly uses it to snag a share of the pastries.

file: 1994/1994-01-29_less you know_happier_struggle_computer_naked_clueless_annoying_feeling good_technology.gif
title: Ignorance Is Naked Bliss

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The less you know, the happier you are.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: While you struggle with that computer, I'm naked, clueless, and f-e-e-e-ling GOOD!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're really annoying me now.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Totally naked! Isn't that a hoot?

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk wrestling with a balky computer while Ratbert and Dogbert stand nearby taunting him. They gleefully point out that being clueless about technology leaves them carefree, and Dogbert boasts about being naked and feeling good. Dilbert, increasingly irritated, tells them they are annoying him.
punchline: The two bystanders mock Dilbert's computer struggles by celebrating their own ignorance and nakedness, which only makes his frustration worse.
summary: While a man battles his stubborn computer, two pets cheerfully brag that knowing nothing and wearing nothing is far more pleasant.

file: 1994/1994-05-10_ratbert the consultant_analytical mind_business consultant_socially dysfunctional_brought in_consulatant.gif
title: Ratbert's Consultant Job Requirements

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It takes more than a brilliant analytical mind to be a business consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You also need to be arrogant and socially dysfunctional.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Does anybody know why a consultant was brought in to do your thinking? Anybody? Anybody?

setting: Dogbert's coaching spot, then a conference room
situation: Dogbert coaches Ratbert on what it takes to be a business consultant, listing arrogance and social dysfunction as requirements.
