In the final panel Ratbert applies the lesson in a meeting, sitting at a conference table and berating the employees who hired him, including Dilbert and a bald man in glasses.
punchline: Ratbert immediately demonstrates the arrogant, socially dysfunctional consultant persona by insulting the people who hired him for not being able to think for themselves.
summary: After a quick lesson from Dogbert on the qualities of a good consultant, Ratbert promptly lectures a conference room of employees about their need for outside thinking.

file: 1994/1994-05-01_all day meetings_cutting staff_giving stats reports_layers_quality team meeting_root cause_slow computers_slow design_wild guesses.gif
title: Root Cause Meeting Blames Everything Except Computers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming to our engineering quality team meeting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today we'll try to identify the root cause of our slow design process.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me take some wild guesses here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Management keeps increasing our work and cutting our staff.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We spend all our time giving status reports to unnecessary layers of management!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Now we're having all-day meetings to talk about our inefficiency!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was kinda hoping for something that isn't anybody's fault.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our computers are too slow. We need new ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now we're getting someplace.

setting: Conference room during an engineering quality team meeting
situation: Dilbert leads a quality team meeting to find the root cause of the slow design process. Wally bluntly lists management's real failings: more work, fewer staff, endless status reports and all-day meetings about inefficiency. Dilbert says he hoped for a cause that isn't anyone's fault, and happily accepts a coworker's suggestion that the computers are too slow.
punchline: Dilbert only wants a root cause that blames no one, so he ignores the obvious management failures and embraces the harmless-sounding excuse of slow computers.
summary: A quality meeting about sluggish engineering ends with everyone dodging the managerial culprits and settling on a convenient equipment complaint.

file: 1994/1994-04-26_no raises_appliances_television_fridge_lava lamp_jar of mayonnaise_dog_boss_dilberet_animals_entertainment.gif
title: Appliances Instead of Raises, Lava Lamp

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This year, instead of raises we're giving appliances.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: High performers could get a color television or a new 'fridge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He called it a "lava lamp."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call it a jar of old mayonnaise.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then Dilbert's home
situation: The Boss announces that this year employees will receive appliances rather than pay raises, with top performers getting a color television or a refrigerator. Later Dilbert holds up the gift he received, which was described as a lava lamp, while Dogbert lounges on a couch and dismisses it.
punchline: The company's cheap consolation prize for no raise is so poor that even a supposed lava lamp looks like a jar of old mayonnaise, showing how little value the 'reward' has.
summary: Management swaps salary increases for household gadgets, and the worthless gift Dilbert ends up with is mocked as spoiled condiment.

file: 1994/1994-08-02_ad agency_dogberts_new slogan_essence_captures_we abuse employees_pass savings_squalid cubicles_wear that shirt.gif
title: Dogbert's Honest Company Slogan Pitch

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've developed a new slogan that captures the essence of this company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "We abuse our employees and pass the savings to you."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll film actual employees in their squalid cubicles.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wear that shirt.

setting: Dogbert's ad agency conference room, during a presentation using an overhead projector
situation: Dogbert, running an ad agency, pitches a client company a new slogan using an overhead projector. The slogan openly admits the company abuses its employees to save money, and Dogbert proposes filming real employees in their grim cubicles. The Boss, rather than being offended, tells Dilbert to wear that shirt for the commercial.
punchline: The Boss completely misses the damning honesty of the slogan and only worries about how the filming will look, showing his indifference to the actual abuse.
summary: A consultant dog pitches a brutally candid ad campaign about mistreated workers, and the client's manager happily approves it and starts casting.

file: 1994/1994-10-27_dogbert ethics advisor_prodcut_mail people_high fees_procedure_ethics advice_return stupid prodcut.gif
title: Dogbert Returns Her Trapping Product

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert: Ethics Advisor

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We mail our product to people and tell them it's free for one year.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Then we start nailing them with high fees because they'll forget the procedure for returning the product. They're trapped.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, did you have some ethics advice?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: No. I asked you here so I can return your stupid product.

setting: Office desk where Dogbert is consulting as an ethics advisor
situation: Dogbert, working as an ethics advisor, listens as a woman across the desk describes her company's scheme of mailing a supposedly free product and later charging high fees to customers who forget the return procedure. When Dogbert asks if she wanted ethics advice, she reveals she only invited him so she could return the product he sent her.
punchline: The woman's scheme is a trap for customers who forget the return procedure, but she turns it around by using Dogbert's visit to return the product he mailed, so she dodges the fees herself.
summary: A businesswoman cheerfully outlines a scheme to trap customers with fees, then reveals she summoned the ethics advisor only to send back the product he mailed her.

file: 1994/1994-12-18_dogbert teaches math_cut staff_bonus worth_expense requiremnets_calculated_budget_multiply by one_doctor_flashlight_projections come from_medical.gif
title: Dogbert's Twisted Business Math Lesson

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert teaches business math

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Grunts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #1 Any job that can be done by two people...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ...can be done by one person for half the cost.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #2 A bonus today is worth more than...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ...the whole company tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: #3 Your expense requirements for December can be calculated...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ...by taking what's left in the budget and multiplying by one.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Giraffe goes where?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next week, a doctor with a flashlight shows us where sales projections come from.

setting: Office, with a whiteboard lesson framing the strip
situation: Dogbert gives a lecture on business math, with three rules illustrated by the Boss. First, one employee does the work of two for half the cost while the other is tossed out. Second, the Boss grabs a bonus even though it destroys the company, and third, he sets December expenses by multiplying the remaining budget by one. Dogbert closes by promising a lesson on where sales projections come from.
punchline: Dogbert's 'math' mocks management logic: cutting staff, hoarding bonuses at the company's expense, and pulling sales projections from a body part.
summary: A cynical canine instructor explains how managers rationalize layoffs, selfish bonuses, and made-up budget and sales figures.

file: 1994/1994-08-24_boot camp_conquer the earth_genetic mutations_half man_sea monkeys_half cucumber.gif
title: Dogbert's Cucumber Mutant Army

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What are you planting?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm growing an army of genetic mutants to do my bidding.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Half man, half giant cucumber. These unthinking brutes will help me conquer the Earth!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Didn't you try this with sea monkeys last year?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: None of them survived boot camp.

setting: A table or garden bench with small pots, a watering can and seeds
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert what he is planting, and Dogbert proudly explains he is growing an army of half-man, half-giant-cucumber mutants to conquer the Earth. Dilbert points out that Dogbert already tried a similar scheme with sea monkeys. Dogbert admits that none of those soldiers survived boot camp.
punchline: Dogbert's world-conquering plans are a repeat of past failures, as his previous army of tiny sea monkeys was too fragile to survive even basic training.
summary: Dogbert cultivates a vegetable-human hybrid army for world domination, but his track record with fragile pet-store soldiers suggests it won't go well.

file: 1994/1994-02-27_dog collar_keep track_employee slaves_final humiliation_cubicles_gerbils_rationalization_mechanisms_collar_6 foot extension cord_dog_adapting_animals.gif
title: Employee Dog Collar With Extension Cord

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's your employee locator device.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sensors in the building will be able to track you at all times.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll know how many times you use the restroom and how long.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a dog collar... the final humiliation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Once you got used to working in cubicles, like gerbils, we knew anything was possible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My conformance rationalization mechanisms are kicking in.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not so bad. A collar is simply an efficient design. Everyone is doing it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's powered by this six foot long extension cord.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert an employee locator device that tracks his location and restroom usage, and Dilbert realizes it is a dog collar. The Boss gloats that cubicles prepared workers for this, and Dilbert talks himself into accepting it. Just as he does, the Boss reveals the collar is powered by a six-foot extension cord, tethering him like a pet.
punchline: Just as Dilbert finishes rationalizing the humiliating dog collar, the Boss reveals it comes with a six-foot leash-like power cord, proving there is always a worse indignity.
summary: A manager outfits an engineer with a tracking collar, and the engineer's self-soothing excuses collapse when a short power cord turns it into a leash.

file: 1994/1994-02-11_dogbert_hit man for mob_get away with murder_cute_self complimentary_conversation.gif
title: Dogbert Plans Cute Mob Career

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have you ever noticed how incredibly cute I am?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Look at this little black nose, soft furry ears, adorable little tail...with these looks I could get away with murder.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking of becoming a hit man for the mob.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm glad we have these talks.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair and Dogbert perched on the footrest
situation: Dogbert sits on Dilbert's footrest and admires his own cuteness, listing his nose, ears and tail. He concludes that his looks would let him get away with murder and announces he is considering a career as a mob hit man. Dilbert, who has barely reacted, ends by saying he is glad they have these talks.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan 'I'm glad we have these talks' is sarcastic, treating Dogbert's absurd, menacing career plan as a normal chat while hinting he'd rather not hear it.
summary: After gushing over his own adorable looks, a small dog muses that they could shield him from consequences as a mob assassin, and his owner responds with dry sarcasm.

file: 1994/1994-07-11_new career_technology pundit_columnist_angry opinions.gif
title: Dogbert's Career as Angry Tech Pundit

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting a new career as a technology pundit and columnist.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This mostly involves forming angry opinions about things I haven't got the time to understand.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is the RISC processor appropriate for senior citizens? Hello!! Is anybody home?!!

setting: Dilbert's home office, with Dogbert typing on a laptop at a desk
situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he has become a technology pundit and columnist, typing away on a laptop. He explains the job is forming angry opinions on topics he has no time to understand. In the last panel he shouts a nonsensical question about RISC processors and senior citizens, as if demanding an answer from an unseen person.
punchline: Dogbert's pundit column shows that tech commentary can be loud, angry and ill-informed, as he combines a technical term with an irrelevant demographic and rages at being ignored.
summary: A dog takes up tech punditry by venting furious opinions on subjects he never bothered to learn about.

file: 1994/1994-12-31_self mangled team_vital tasks_staus report_kiss some butts_track your time.gif
title: Self-Managed Team Means Management Chores

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm going to make your group a "self-managed team."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All of the vital management tasks that I've been doing will now be shared among you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop your work and give me a status report!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I'll kiss some butts.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Track your time.

situation: The Boss announces that the group will become a self-managed team and that his vital management tasks will now be shared among the employees. The team members immediately take on the stereotypical management duties: Dilbert demands a status report, Wally decides to suck up to people, and Alice orders everyone to track their time.
punchline: The employees reduce 'vital management tasks' to demanding reports, brown-nosing, and time tracking, implying that is all the boss's job ever consisted of.
summary: When a manager hands his duties to his staff, they instantly pick up the most pointless and annoying parts of management.

file: 1994/1994-03-26_device_dogcart scam_end of world_evil be gone_evil money_give money_scammer_take money.gif
title: Dogbert's Evil-Be-Gone Money Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The end of the world is coming in year 2000. Therefore, you should give me your money before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It is written that money is evil. I'll keep your money in Dogbert's special "Evil-Be-Gone" device.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And it's completely deductible ... from your savings.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So I'm actually making money!

setting: Dogbert's office, a fake religious or financial consulting business
situation: Dogbert, wearing a yellow beehive-shaped hat, warns a man that the world will end in the year 2000 and asks for his money. He claims money is evil and that it will be safe in his special "Evil-Be-Gone" device, which is just a piggy bank. The man hands over his cash, convinced the deal is a tax deduction that earns him money.
punchline: The customer is so thoroughly fleeced by Dogbert's nonsense that he thinks handing over his savings means he is making money, since a deduction taken "from your savings" is just a loss.
summary: A scheming dog talks a gullible man into surrendering his savings to a piggy bank with the promise of apocalypse protection and a tax break.

file: 1994/1994-06-07_video conference_desktop_telecommuting_level of professionalism_share document_next time.gif
title: Telecommuting Dilbert Plays With Toy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This desktop video conference thing is great!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Even though you're telecommuting, you still maintain a level of professionalism.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's share a document next time.

setting: Boss's office and Dilbert's home, connected by desktop video conference
situation: The Boss, seen from behind at his desk, praises a new desktop video conferencing system and compliments Dilbert for staying professional while telecommuting. The camera then shows Dilbert at home, wearing pajamas and absently playing with a small toy figure on his hand. The Boss suggests sharing a document next time, unaware of what Dilbert is really doing.
punchline: The Boss praises Dilbert's professionalism only because the video shows a small window of Dilbert, while Dilbert is actually in pajamas playing with a toy, and the Boss's suggestion to share a document shows he doesn't see the real situation.
summary: A manager raves about video conferencing and his remote employee's professionalism, while the employee is actually at home goofing off in pajamas.

file: 1994/1994-07-20_head of market research_120k salary_value opinions_refrence_honesty_pay these days.gif
title: Dogbert's Market Research Job Offer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got a job as the head of market research at your company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be pulling down $120K per year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't value other people's opinions so I'll just use my own.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just for reference, how much does honesty pay these days?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up.

situation: Dogbert announces to Dilbert that he has landed a $120K job heading market research at the company. He explains that his research method is to ignore everyone else's opinions and rely only on his own. He then asks Dilbert what honesty pays these days, and Dilbert tells him to shut up.
punchline: Dogbert's market research consists of ignoring customers' opinions entirely, and he cheekily asks what honesty pays because he is clearly earning a big salary by being a fraud.
summary: A self-assured dog lands a lucrative research post by making up his own findings, then taunts his honest coworker about the poor pay of integrity.

file: 1994/1994-11-17_paperless office concept_restroom situation.gif
title: Paperless Office Saves Ten Percent

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Since implementing our "paperless office" concept, we've saved...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh... ten percent!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Next on the agenda: the restroom situation...

situation: The Boss presents the results of the company's paperless office initiative to Wally and Dilbert, hesitating before offering a vague savings figure that he appears to have scribbled on his arm. The meeting then moves on to the next agenda item, the restroom situation, implying that the paper isn't really gone.
punchline: The boss has to read a made-up savings figure off his hand, and the next agenda item, the restroom situation, suggests the paper is still being used, just for a different purpose.
summary: A manager boasts about savings from going paperless but has to peek at his hand for a number, and the meeting turns to bathroom trouble.

file: 1994/1994-11-10_business process_well designed porcess_compensate_apathy.gif
title: Consultant Insults Clients, Promises Fun

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As your consultant, I'll tell you how to improve your business processes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll show you how a well-designed process can compensate for your sloth, apathy and all-around incompetence.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But most important: let's have fun.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, addresses a conference table of managers and Dilbert about improving their business processes. He cheerfully explains that a well-designed process can make up for their laziness, apathy and incompetence. He then ends by saying the most important thing is to have fun.
punchline: The consultant openly insults his clients' incompetence to their faces, and they sit there accepting it, then he casually moves on to having fun.
summary: A canine consultant calmly tells his clients that his process improvements exist to cover for their laziness and ineptitude, then suggests everyone enjoy themselves.

file: 1994/1994-05-30_mister dork_surnamed dork_dorkage_demands apology_put behind us.gif
title: Dogbert Apologizes to the Dorks

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recently received this angry letter from a Mister "Dork".

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Mr. Dork informs me that the many people surnamed Dork are not amused that I once used the word "dorkage." He demands an apology.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I apologize to all the Dorks who were offended. I hope we can put this behind us.

setting: Dogbert's desk, shown in a plain orange-background panel
situation: Dogbert reads out an angry letter from a Mr. Dork, who complains that people with the surname Dork are upset by Dogbert's earlier use of the word "dorkage." Dogbert then writes a formal public apology to all offended Dorks and hopes the matter can be put to rest.
punchline: Dogbert's formal apology to "all the Dorks" and his hope to "put this behind us" repeatedly use the word in its offensive sense, so the apology is itself a pun that keeps the insult going.
summary: A pooch addressing a complaint about a silly word responds with a stiff, official-sounding apology that sneaks the same joke back in.

file: 1994/1994-09-25_personal uses_office fax_boss hassles dilberet_fax paper_phone lines_electricity_sent some over_dilbert busts boss_busts boss.gif
title: Faxing Electricity to the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It has come to my attention that you used the fax for personal business.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I sent the fax during lunch. It was a local call.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're using up all of our fax paper.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I sent a fax. The paper doesn't travel through the phone lines.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You used the company's electricity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had a friend fax us a wad of extra electricity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm using it right now to power my PC.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you get any extra electricity? My PC is out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Press the button on the back and I'll fax you some.

situation: The Boss accuses Dilbert of using the company fax machine for personal business and wasting fax paper. Dilbert points out that paper isn't transmitted over phone lines, then claims a friend faxed him extra electricity to cover his power use. The gullible Boss believes him and asks for some electricity for his own dead PC.
punchline: Dilbert exploits the Boss's technical ignorance by claiming electricity can be faxed, and the Boss falls for it completely, asking for a transmission of his own.
summary: Caught using the office fax for private reasons, an engineer talks his clueless manager into believing power can be sent down a phone line.

file: 1994/1994-11-26_new name for group_engineering science research_designed business cards_long name_complicated.gif
title: Absurdly Long Department Name

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I came up with a new name for our group.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on we're the "Engineering Science Research Technology Systems Information Quality and Excellence Center."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You should throw "Efficiency" in there too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I designed the business cards myself.

situation: At a meeting, the Boss proudly announces a new name for the group, a ridiculous string of buzzwords. Wally sarcastically suggests adding 'Efficiency' to the pile, and the Boss responds by boasting that he designed the business cards himself.
punchline: The bloated name is the opposite of efficient, and the Boss misses Wally's sarcasm entirely, instead fixating on the business cards he made himself.
summary: A manager unveils an endless buzzword-laden group name, and a sarcastic suggestion for more words goes right over his head.

file: 1994/1994-09-23_bob the dinosaur_double fee_triple fee_infinity plus one_childish men_hired to beat_tail_project requiremnets.gif
title: Bidding War Over Dinosaur Beatings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Coworker
transcript.text: I hired Bob the Dinosaur to beat you with his tail until you give me the project requirements.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Coworker
transcript.text: Ha!!! I'll double your fee if you thump Dilbert instead.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll triple your fee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He can't really pay you "infinity plus one."

transcript.speaker: Bob the Dinosaur
transcript.text: I wonder how much that is on an hourly basis.

situation: A coworker hires Bob the Dinosaur to beat Dilbert with his tail until Dilbert hands over the project requirements. Dilbert's coworker and Dilbert then get into a bidding war, each offering to pay the dinosaur more to thump the other. Dilbert's bid escalates to "infinity plus one", leaving the dinosaur calculating what that would be worth per hour.
punchline: The two men escalate their childish bidding war so far that the dinosaur mercenary is promised an impossible fee and cheerfully wonders what it works out to hourly.
summary: Two feuding coworkers try to outbid each other for a dinosaur's violent services, ending with an absurdly infinite offer.

file: 1994/1994-01-30_large dart_preservation_spotted chipmunk_tranquilize male_write newsletter_dead chipmunk_jokes.gif
title: Dead Chipmunk Newsletter Jokes

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I joined the "Spotted Chipmunk Preservation Society."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're going to tranquilize the last known male and unite it with a female.

transcript.speaker: Society member (bald man)
transcript.text: There he is!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pow

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thunk!

transcript.speaker: Society member (bald man)
transcript.text: When you think about it, that's an awfully large dart to use on a chipmunk.

transcript.speaker: Society member (blonde woman)
transcript.text: It's Dilbert's turn to write the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Trust me. Humor is the way to go. It eases tension.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah, but a whole issue of dead chipmunk jokes?

setting: A wooded outdoor spot under a tree, then Dilbert's desk at home
situation: Dilbert and two fellow members of a chipmunk preservation society aim a rifle loaded with a tranquilizer dart at the last known male spotted chipmunk so it can be paired with a female. After the shot, a member remarks the dart was awfully large, and it becomes Dilbert's turn to write the newsletter. Dogbert advises him to use humor, and Dilbert realizes that means a whole issue of dead chipmunk jokes.
punchline: The oversized dart evidently killed the last male chipmunk, so the preservation society's newsletter now has nothing to write about except dead chipmunk jokes.
summary: A rescue mission to save an endangered rodent ends with an accidentally lethal shot and a newsletter-writing assignment that is awkward at best.

file: 1994/1994-03-04_voting_opposite positions_cancel out_republican_dogs don't vote_democrat.gif
title: Dogbert's Flawed Stay-Home Voting Logic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you remember last Election Day... and how you convinced me to not vote?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You argued that since we disagreed on all issues, we could both stay home and the outcome would be the same as if we both voted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogs can't vote!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, not directly.

situation: Dilbert recalls how Dogbert talked him out of voting last Election Day, using the argument that two people who disagree on everything cancel each other out. Dilbert then realizes the flaw: Dogbert never could have voted at all. Dogbert coolly replies that he doesn't vote directly.
punchline: Dogbert's cancel-out argument was a con, since only Dilbert's vote was ever removed, and Dogbert's 'not directly' hints he influences elections through other, shadier means.
summary: A man realizes too late that his dog's neat excuse for skipping the election quietly deleted only his own ballot.

file: 1994/1994-09-20_trade show registration_rental beards_not allowed_pipe scented suspenders_portly attendees.gif
title: Rental Beards Required at Trade Show

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Trade show registration

transcript.speaker: Registration Clerk
transcript.text: Men without facial hair are not allowed on the exhibition floor.

transcript.speaker: Registration Clerk
transcript.text: We have rental beards for your convenience.

transcript.speaker: Registration Clerk
transcript.text: That model comes with pipe-scented suspenders. It's very popular with our portly attendees.

situation: Dilbert arrives at a trade show registration desk and is told that clean-shaven men are not allowed on the exhibition floor. The clerk offers him a rental beard and he tries one on, and she points out that the model he picked comes with pipe-scented suspenders, a favorite of heavier attendees.
punchline: The trade show enforces an absurd beard requirement that turns attendees into a stereotype of a portly, pipe-smoking, bearded industry veteran, complete with scented accessories.
summary: A trade show insists on facial hair for entry, so Dilbert is fitted with a rental beard and a matching set of accessories.

file: 1994/1994-08-12_still single_shower_recoup money_wedding gifts_baby showers_bitter_election hut_registered.gif
title: Still Single Shower Gift Registry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, you're invited to a "still single" shower in my honor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to recoup all the money I've blown on wedding gifts and baby showers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Someone's feeling a little bitter today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a pattern registered at "Electron Hut."

situation: Dilbert hands Wally an invitation to a "still single" shower being held in his own honor. He explains that he wants to recoup the money he has spent on wedding gifts and baby showers for others. Alice remarks that he sounds bitter, and Dilbert replies that he has already registered a gift pattern at an electronics store.
punchline: Dilbert turns the bitterness of being the last single coworker into a gift-grab, mimicking wedding registries by registering for gifts at an electronics store, and he shows no embarrassment when Alice calls him bitter.
summary: A perpetually single engineer throws himself a mock shower so coworkers will finally repay him for all the presents he has bought them.

file: 1994/1994-05-20_good inertia_marketing department_project_under funded_uniformed decision_take blame.gif
title: Doomed Project, Scheduled Uninformed Decision

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How's your project coming along?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's under-funded and doomed. But I've got some good inertia going and I'm setting the marketing department up to take the blame.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I feel like I should be doing something here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got you planned to make an uninformed decision next week.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how his project is going, and Dilbert cheerfully admits it is under-funded and doomed while he lines up the marketing department as scapegoats. The Boss, feeling he ought to contribute something, is told that Dilbert has already scheduled him to make an uninformed decision next week.
punchline: Dilbert has so thoroughly planned for failure that even his manager's meddling is a scheduled, predictable part of the project's downfall.
summary: An employee candidly briefs his manager on a doomed project, including who will be blamed and when the manager will weigh in ignorantly.

file: 1994/1994-06-21_most talented_technical professional_dogbert_professional head hunter.gif
title: Headhunter Dogbert Calls Worried Employee

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello, this is Dogbert's professional headhunting service.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I find jobs for the most talented technical professionals. Several people mentioned your name.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, is it true they'll be looking for somebody to fill your job soon? Hello?

setting: Dogbert's desk with a phone, and an office cubicle with a computer
situation: Dogbert, running a headhunting service, phones a bald, bespectacled office worker and flatters him with talk of finding jobs for talented professionals. He then casually asks whether the man's job is about to be vacated. The man has apparently hung up by the end.
punchline: Dogbert's flattering pitch is really a fishing expedition for gossip about layoffs, and the man hangs up the moment he realizes it.
summary: A scheming dog posing as a recruiter sweet-talks an employee, then gives away that he really wants to know if the man is about to be fired.

file: 1994/1994-11-29_lowest bid_technical support hotline_other bidders.gif
title: Lowest Bidder Plans Support Hotline

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You submitted the lowest bid to run our new technical support hotline, Mister Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The other bidders would love to know how you plan to handle twelve thousand calls a day by yourself.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tell them to call me.

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk
situation: The Boss tells Dogbert that his bid to run the company's new technical support hotline was the lowest. He then relays that competing bidders are curious how Dogbert will handle twelve thousand calls a day alone. Dogbert, slumped in his chair, replies that they should call him.
punchline: Dogbert's plan for handling an impossible call volume is to treat the competitors' question as just another call, and he answers it by being as unhelpful as a bad support line.
summary: A consultant who undercut every rival to win a support contract brushes off questions about his one-dog operation by inviting his competitors to phone him.

file: 1994/1994-11-24_flicking fingers_joyous celebration_linked to pay_success sounds like_snappy sounds.gif
title: Celebrating Pay Unlinked From Performance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look, Ted! We get paid the same as you but all we're doing is standing around and flicking our fingers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Come join us and flick your fingers in joyous celebration that our performance is not linked to our pay.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Flick flick

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Flick flick flick flick flick

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't know what success sounds like, but I'll bet this isn't it.

setting: Office cubicle area and the Boss's desk
situation: Dilbert, Alice and Wally stand around flicking their fingers in a mock celebration, taunting hard-working Ted that they earn the same pay as him for doing nothing. The sound of the flicking carries to the Boss, who sits at his desk and muses about what he hears.
punchline: The employees celebrate that pay is unrelated to performance, and the Boss unwittingly hears the sound of his own pay system failing, noting that this surely isn't the sound of success.
summary: Staff snap their fingers in glee because their salaries don't depend on how well they work, leaving their manager puzzled by the noise.

file: 1994/1994-06-01_diveristy_sensitivity training_seek better understanding_dumpy white guy section.gif
title: Diversity Training's Dumpy White Guy Section

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't believe we have to go to "diversity sensitivity" training.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally, I don't see how it could be bad to seek a better understanding of others.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take a seat in the "dumpy white guy section." I'm ready to start.

setting: Office hallway leading to a training room
situation: Wally grumbles about having to attend mandatory diversity sensitivity training while walking there with Dilbert and a coworker. Dilbert optimistically says that seeking to understand others can't be bad. When they arrive, Dogbert, the trainer, directs them to sit in the "dumpy white guy section."
punchline: Dilbert's naive optimism about the training is undercut when the trainer immediately singles out him and Wally by their stereotype, showing the training will cast them as the targets.
summary: Two coworkers heading to mandatory sensitivity training get an unwelcome lesson in being categorized the moment the session begins.

file: 1994/1994-02-10_delight customers_fire everybody_price of products_slogan_stop meetings_we waste your money.gif
title: Delight Customers: Stop Meetings Instead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must constantly ask ourselves what we can do to delight our customers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We could stop having these meetings, fire everybody in the room and lower the prices of our products.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was thinking more along the lines of a slogan.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: How 'bout "We waste your money"?

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks what the company can do to delight its customers. Alice answers sincerely that the company should end these meetings, fire everyone in the room and cut prices. The Boss dismisses this and says he wanted a slogan, and a colleague suggests a brutally honest one.
punchline: Management wants a catchy slogan rather than real improvements, and the only honest slogan on offer admits that the company wastes its customers' money.
summary: A manager seeking ways to please customers shrugs off a blunt cost-cutting answer and asks for marketing copy, which invites a candid but damning tagline.

file: 1994/1994-11-27_south wing_cubicle_improve communication_project team_pawn in the game_new dress code_dressed like pawns.gif
title: Moved Like a Chess Pawn

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm moving you to a cubicle in the South Wing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Umm... It's more efficient if my group is all in one place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not for me. The people on my project team are all in this wing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will improve communication in our group.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't need to communicate with my group. I only need to work with my project team.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll bet another manager wants that same cubicle in the South Wing. I think I'm just a pawn in your little game.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You move tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: By the way, there's a new dress code.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're in my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Other Pawn
transcript.text: You can only move to a diagonal cubicle.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's doorway
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to move to a cubicle in the South Wing, offering weak justifications about efficiency and communication. Dilbert objects that his project team is in his current wing and suspects he is merely a pawn in the Boss's political game with another manager. The next day the Boss imposes a new dress code, and Dilbert arrives in the new cubicle dressed as a chess pawn, where another pawn-costumed worker tells him he can only move diagonally.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint that he is just a pawn becomes literal when the dress code turns employees into chess pawns who must obey pawn movement rules.
summary: After a pointless cubicle relocation that Dilbert calls a power play, everyone shows up dressed as chess pawns, making his metaphor literal.

file: 1994/1994-01-31_patron saint_technology_heal broken hearts_demons_stupidity_spiritual side.gif
title: Dogbert, Patron Saint of Technology

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I declare myself the patron saint of technology.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I heal broken technology with my right paw and I use the scepter to drive out the demons of stupidity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think I've seen your spiritual side before.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Out! Out!

situation: Dogbert, wearing a bishop-style hat and carrying a scepter, stands on Dilbert's desk and proclaims himself the patron saint of technology. He claims to heal broken technology with his paw and drive out the demons of stupidity. Dilbert remarks that he has never seen this spiritual side of Dogbert, while Dogbert shouts "Out! Out!" and jabs the scepter at Dilbert's phone.
punchline: Dogbert treats ordinary tech support like a religious exorcism, performing a pious ritual on a phone while Dilbert is left observing the absurd display.
summary: A self-anointed canine saint performs an exorcism on office gadgets to cast out the demons of stupidity while his human coworker looks on bemused.

file: 1994/1994-05-26_rat_mouse_politically incorrect_named in rats honor_scuzzy_suggestion.gif
title: Ratbert Demands a Computer Peripheral

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Why is that thing called a mouse and not a rat?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: At the risk of being labelled, quote, politically correct, unquote, I must object.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I demand to have something named in my honor!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What about the "scuzzy" interface?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hee hee.

situation: Ratbert sits on Dilbert's chair and asks why the computer pointing device is called a mouse rather than a rat. He objects on grounds of political correctness and demands that something be named after him. Dilbert suggests the SCSI interface, pronounced "scuzzy."
punchline: Dilbert offers Ratbert a dig disguised as an honor: the computer interface pronounced "scuzzy" (SCSI), which sounds like an insult to a rat, and Ratbert's gleeful laugh suggests he doesn't realize it.
summary: A pet rat insists computing should honor him the way it does mice, and Dilbert slyly proposes a name that sounds like an insult.

file: 1994/1994-08-22_engineers_filberts job security_menacing statements_one option_reducing headcount_works hard_finish project.gif
title: Threatening Dilbert Instead of Adding Engineers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The only way to finish the project on time is by adding four engineers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's one other option. You could make menacing statements about Dilbert's job security until he works five times as hard.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just kidding. Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I've been thinking about reducing headcount.

setting: Conference room during a project meeting
situation: Dilbert tells a meeting that finishing the project on time requires four more engineers. The Boss cheerfully suggests an alternative: threatening Dilbert's job security until he works five times as hard. After saying he is joking, an executive across the table remarks that he has been thinking about reducing headcount.
punchline: The Boss's 'joke' about threatening Dilbert's job is immediately undercut when another manager seriously raises layoffs, showing the threat is real and management is willing to use it.
summary: A manager prefers intimidating an engineer into superhuman effort over hiring help, and a colleague's layoff comment makes the intimidation genuinely credible.

file: 1994/1994-10-07_never managed_marketing people_do marketing things_segments_focus groups_segmenting_dominate industry_motivated.gif
title: Boss Orders Vague Marketing Things

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've never managed marketing people before. But a good manager can manage anything.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... I order you to go do marketing things... like segmenting and focus groups...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And keep on focusing and segmenting until we dominate the industry!!!

transcript.speaker: Marketing employee
transcript.text: Well, I'm motivated.

situation: The Boss, who has just been put in charge of the marketing staff, admits he has never managed marketing people but insists a good manager can manage anything. He then issues vague orders to do 'marketing things' like segmenting and focus groups, and ends by shouting that they should keep at it until the company dominates the industry. One of the employees sarcastically says he is motivated.
punchline: The Boss's empty buzzword-filled orders are so meaningless and absurd that the employee's deadpan 'I'm motivated' is clearly sarcastic.
summary: A manager with no marketing knowledge barks out jargon-laden commands to his new team and expects world domination as a result.

file: 1994/1994-10-24_confidential_ethics offcie_weasel boy_ethics expert.gif
title: Ethics Hotline Isn't Really Confidential

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company hired an ethics expert to help us through the gray areas.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your calls to the Ethics Office are completely confidential.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks for sharing that. I own you now, Weasel-Boy.

setting: Conference room, then Dogbert's ethics office
situation: In a meeting, the Boss announces that the company has hired an ethics expert to guide staff through gray areas. The expert, Dogbert, assures employees that calls to the Ethics Office are confidential. The final panel shows Dogbert at his computer surveillance setup, having listened to the Boss's call and now using it to blackmail him.
punchline: The ethics expert promises confidentiality but is actually spying on callers and exploiting their confessions for his own power, making the ethics office itself deeply unethical.
summary: A newly hired corporate ethics consultant reassures staff about privacy, then uses a secretly monitored call to take control of the manager who confided in him.

file: 1994/1994-10-21_3 hour meeting_doesn't apply_highly paid contractor_oxygen to brains_multimedia developer.gif
title: Contractor Skips Meeting, Gains Skills

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: It looks like you're off to a three-hour staff meeting that doesn't apply to me.

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: I'm glad I'm a highly paid contractor. I'll be increasing my skills while you fight to get oxygen to your brains.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Three hours later

transcript.speaker: Contractor
transcript.text: I became a multimedia developer. How was YOUR day?

setting: Office hallway outside a meeting room
situation: A smug contractor in a bathrobe holding a coffee mug watches Dilbert and Alice head off to a three-hour staff meeting that he doesn't have to attend. He boasts that he will use the time to improve his skills while they suffer. Three hours later he announces he has become a multimedia developer and asks how their day was.
punchline: The contractor gloats that his time is spent profitably learning new skills while employees waste three hours in a pointless meeting, and he rubs it in afterward.
summary: A relaxed, well-paid outside worker mocks two employees heading into a marathon meeting, then returns hours later having gained a whole new career skill.

file: 1994/1994-07-07_ratbert_birds and bees_get stung_birds_humming bird_sex with birds_words to say.gif
title: Ratbert's Confused Birds and Bees Talk

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Dogbert told me about the birds and the bees.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The bee part confuses me. It seems like I'd get stung.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: And as for birds, I just wouldn't know the words to say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try a humming bird.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, at a desk with a computer
situation: Ratbert sits at a computer next to Dilbert and explains that Dogbert gave him a garbled version of the birds and the bees. He takes it literally, worrying about getting stung by bees and not knowing what to say to birds. Dilbert deadpans a pun suggestion about a hummingbird.
punchline: Ratbert has taken the birds-and-bees talk literally as interspecies romance, and Dilbert's reply plays along with a pun on a hummingbird, since you could hum when you don't know the words.
summary: A naive little lab rat misreads a euphemism for the facts of life as literal advice about courting insects and birds, and gets a punny tip from his coworker.

file: 1994/1994-05-09_dogbert_consulting company_new course_business_extra brains_liver_ratbert.gif
title: Consultants With Extra Brains Strapped On

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company will plot a new course for your business.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My consultants are so smart that their brains don't fit in their heads. They have to strap the extra brains to their torsos.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Why do I need a piece of liver strapped to my torso?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got a little carried away at the pitch meeting.

situation: Dogbert pitches his consulting company to The Boss, claiming his consultants are so brilliant that their oversized brains have to be strapped to their torsos. A consultant then complains that he has a piece of liver strapped to his torso. Dogbert admits he made the claim up in the pitch and then faked the evidence.
punchline: Dogbert's exaggerated sales pitch was a lie, and he covered it by strapping a piece of liver onto his consultant to pass as an extra brain.
summary: A consulting pitch built on an absurd boast ends up with a hapless employee wearing organ meat to back it up.

file: 1994/1994-10-14_2004_cheaper than dating_date at door_dogbert_future_holodeck_virtual reality_writing article_money_male hormones.gif
title: Virtual Reality Cheaper Than Dating

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can predict the future by assuming that money and male hormones are the driving forces for new technology.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Therefore, when virtual reality gets cheaper than dating, society is doomed.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Year 2004

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Is Dilbert available?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He's been in the holodeck since March.

setting: Dogbert's desk and a doorway, with the final panel set in 2004
situation: Dogbert types on a laptop and explains his method for forecasting technology trends, concluding that society is doomed once virtual reality costs less than dating. In the final panel, set in 2004, a woman comes to the door asking for Dilbert, and Dogbert says Dilbert has been in the holodeck for months.
punchline: Dogbert's prediction comes true almost immediately, as Dilbert has chosen a virtual reality holodeck over real dating and has been gone since March.
summary: A scheming dog forecasts the downfall of civilization through cheap virtual reality, then a visitor discovers his predicted future has already claimed his lonely owner.

file: 1994/1994-01-11_small group_young_funny_single people_socialize_romances_ski trips.gif
title: Excluded From the Office Clique

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm forming a small clique of all the young, funny, single people in the department.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We'll have drinks during lunch, talk about ski trips, and have romances within the group.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please... just shoot me now.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: No, no... we need you to do our work.

situation: A coworker tells Dilbert she is forming a social clique of young, funny, single people who will drink at lunch, talk about ski trips and date each other. Dilbert assumes he is being invited and begs to be shot, but she explains that she only wants him around to do the group's work.
punchline: Dilbert is not invited into the cool clique; he is only valued as the dependable drudge who will do everyone else's work while they socialize.
summary: A coworker describes her fun-loving social circle to Dilbert, then reveals his only role is to pick up their workload.

file: 1994/1994-06-12_aa meeting_ratbert_fear of computers_technophobe_wrong meeting_alcoholics anonymous_interupt_elaborate excuses_avoid computers_web of deception.gif
title: Ratbert Confesses at Wrong Support Group

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My name is Ratbert. I fear the information superhighway.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Like most of you, my problem started because I never learned to type.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I thought only secretaries needed to type.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Then the computers came. At first I dismissed them as mere toys for men with no social skills.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Soon they were everywhere.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I would invent elaborate excuses to avoid computers. I was caught in my own web of deception!

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: This is "Alcoholics Anonymous."

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I didn't interrupt you.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Can we talk about me now?

setting: A support group meeting in a room with folding chairs
situation: Ratbert sits in a circle of folding chairs and tearfully confesses his fear of computers and the information superhighway, explaining how he avoided them with excuses. Only at the end does a man in the group point out that this is an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting. The man then politely asks to take his turn, since he didn't interrupt Ratbert's long story.
punchline: Ratbert has been pouring out his technophobia at the wrong support group, and the real alcoholic patiently waited through the whole thing before asking for his own turn.
summary: A little rat bares his soul about his computer phobia, unaware he has wandered into a meeting for people with entirely different problems.

file: 1994/1994-03-15_new management layer_middle mangemnet_new boss_harfurd_idiot_unqualified_fool.gif
title: New Boss Misspells Harvard

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm creating a new layer of management so I don't have to talk to you in person anymore.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Richard is your new boss. He has an MBA from Harfurd University.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean "Harvard" don't you?

transcript.speaker: Richard
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

setting: Office, in front of Dilbert's workspace
situation: The Boss announces he is adding a layer of management so he can avoid speaking with Dilbert directly. He introduces Richard as Dilbert's new boss and brags about Richard's MBA from 'Harfurd University.' Dilbert politely corrects the name to Harvard, and Richard's thought bubble reveals he is nervous, hinting his credentials are fake.
punchline: The new manager's MBA is from a university whose name even he and the Boss can't spell, implying his qualification is bogus and the new management layer is pointless.
summary: A boss inserts a middleman manager to dodge his own employee, but the man's supposed Ivy League degree looks fishy when his school's name is misspelled.

file: 1994/1994-08-11_tough year_special team_much smaller team.gif
title: Go Team, Then Layoffs Revealed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This will be a tough year for the company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will take a special kind of team to get by.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Go team!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Team! Team!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Specifically, it will take a much smaller team.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss tells his staff in a meeting that the company faces a tough year and needs a special kind of team. His employees cheer enthusiastically, pumping their fists and chanting. The Boss then clarifies that what is needed is a much smaller team.
punchline: The employees cheer for team spirit without realizing the Boss is announcing layoffs, so their enthusiasm is misplaced.
summary: A manager's rousing talk about teamwork turns out to be a warning that many of the people cheering will lose their jobs.

file: 1994/1994-04-22_broadcasted_dsn_identify_jobs_movie_take over_takeover.gif
title: Takeover Staff Are Unnecessary Jobs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on you'll be working full time on our takeover of DSN.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You must also identify any unnecessary jobs that can be cut after the takeover.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would be the people who worked on the takeover.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh, I broadcasted that move.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to work full time on the company's takeover of DSN, and also tells him to identify unnecessary jobs that can be cut once the takeover is finished. Dilbert points out that the redundant jobs would be those of the people who carried out the takeover. The Boss reacts as if he has just been outplayed.
punchline: Dilbert points out that the people who worked on the takeover, including Dilbert himself, would be the ones made redundant afterward, and the Boss sees it as a clever move rather than a threat to Dilbert's job.
summary: After being told to find jobs to eliminate once a corporate acquisition is complete, an engineer observes that the staff who carried out the deal will be the redundant ones.

file: 1994/1994-10-06_managing_marketing group_previous manager killed_parking lot_run down_murder_apathy to murder_body on bumper.gif
title: Marketing Manager Run Over, Promoted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In addition to my current duties, I'll be managing the marketing group.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The marketing job opened because the previous manager got run down in the parking lot.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When they needed a good manager, they knew where to look.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Under your bumper?

characters: Coworker with glasses and green tie
situation: At a meeting, the Boss announces he will take over the marketing group on top of his current duties. He explains the job opened up because the previous manager was run down in the parking lot. Dilbert suggests the Boss is the one who ran him over.
punchline: Dilbert implies the Boss killed the previous marketing manager with his car, since the Boss is oblivious enough to describe the vacancy cheerfully and the only 'good manager' found was under his bumper.
summary: A boss gleefully inherits a dead colleague's job while Dilbert drily suggests the vehicular culprit is sitting right there.

file: 1994/1994-12-12_disoriented_entire career_environmental hazards_feeling tired_nervous_run for exit.gif
title: Environmental Inspector Describes Dilbert's Career

transcript.speaker: Inspector
transcript.text: I'm checking the building for environmental hazards.

transcript.speaker: Inspector
transcript.text: Have you been feeling tired, nervous and disoriented?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You just described my entire career.

transcript.speaker: Inspector
transcript.text: If you start feeling good, run for the exit.

situation: A masked inspector carrying a detector device sweeps the office for environmental hazards and asks Dilbert if he has been feeling tired, nervous and disoriented. Dilbert replies that this describes his whole career, and the inspector warns him to flee if he suddenly starts feeling good.
punchline: The symptoms of toxic building exposure are exactly how Dilbert always feels at work, so the only abnormal sign would be feeling good, which implies the job itself is as unhealthy as a hazard.
summary: A hazard inspector's checklist of poisoning symptoms turns out to match one engineer's ordinary working life.

file: 1994/1994-12-30_paintball tournament_next team building exercise_easy sport_employees unhappy.gif
title: Boss Announces Paintball Team-Building Tournament

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided that our next team-building exercise will be a paintball tournament.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This is not a good thing.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This is not a good thing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is not a good thing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a deceptively easy sport.

situation: The Boss announces to Dilbert, Alice and Wally that the next team-building exercise will be a paintball tournament. The three employees all think the same worried thought. In the last panel, the Boss stands in the cubicles wearing goggles and holding a paintball gun, thinking that it's a deceptively easy sport.
punchline: The Boss treats team building as a chance to shoot his own employees, and he is confident that paintball is easy, which hints he is about to underperform and that the employees are in for trouble.
summary: A manager's plan to turn team building into an armed paintball battle fills his staff with dread while he arms himself.

file: 1994/1994-09-28_cartoon_cartoon on back_hurts morale_joke_management decions_take it down_improvement.gif
title: Boss Bans Cartoons, Gets Cartoon Taped

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This cartoon seems to be saying that management decisions are a joke.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cartoons are not allowed on cubicles. It hurts morale. I don't want to see this when I return.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've noticed a real improvement in morale since you removed the cartoon.

situation: The Boss points at a cartoon posted on Dilbert's cubicle wall and complains that it implies management decisions are a joke. He orders Dilbert to take it down, claiming cartoons hurt morale. Later, the Boss compliments Dilbert on improved morale, not noticing the cartoon is now taped to his own back.
punchline: The Boss cannot see that the cartoon mocking management decisions is now stuck on his back, and he ironically credits its removal for improved morale.
summary: A manager who bans a cartoon mocking his decisions ends up unknowingly wearing it, proving its point.

file: 1994/1994-05-04_bumper sticker_cops are wuses_house_staff meeting_tasteless hovel_dilberts home.gif
title: Staff Meeting Guests Insult Dilbert's Home

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The staff meeting at Dilbert's house ends

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I guess we're done abusing your tasteless hovel.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Burp

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It was somewhat dim-witted of you to invite us to your house. Let's do it again real soon.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wondered if I'd ever get to use my "Cops are wusses" bumper-stickers.

setting: Dilbert's house, at the front door
situation: After a staff meeting held at Dilbert's home, the departing coworkers file out past him, one after another, insulting his house while thanking him. In the last panel, Dogbert comments from the floor about his bumper stickers, tying in with the meeting having been unwelcome and disastrous.
punchline: The coworkers' backhanded 'thanks' are all insults, and Dogbert's odd remark about finally using his anti-cop bumper stickers implies the gathering was so rowdy it might have brought the police.
summary: Departing colleagues lob left-handed compliments at their host's home while a smug dog muses about finally getting use out of some provocative stickers.

file: 1994/1994-09-07_bungee boss_incoming_made a difference_mentor_sprong!_bouncing bungee.gif
title: The Bungee Boss Arrives and Leaves

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll be getting a new "bungee boss" sometime today.

transcript.speaker: Bungee Boss
transcript.text: Hi-I'm-your-new-boss-let's-change-every-thing-before-I-get-reassigned-oops-too-late-goodbye.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sproing

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: He was like a mentor to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think he made a difference.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Incoming!

situation: The Boss announces that a temporary 'bungee boss' will be arriving that day. The new manager appears, rattles off a rushed announcement about changing everything before he gets reassigned, and is yanked away on a bungee cord. Afterward, the employees solemnly reflect on his brief influence, just as another bungee boss comes flying in.
punchline: Managers are rotated through so quickly that each one is gone almost as soon as he arrives, yet employees treat their fleeting tenure as meaningful, while the next one is already bouncing in.
summary: A manager on an elastic tether is snapped away mere seconds after introducing himself, and his staff mourn him before the next one springs into view.

file: 1994/1994-07-08_philosophy of life_gives you lemons_big pitcher_ice_few glasses_no napkins.gif
title: Lemonade Philosophy Needs Better Supplies

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: My philosophy is "If life gives you lemons, make lemonade."

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Of course, the whole thing depends heavily on life also providing a big pitcher with ice and a few glasses.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: What? No napkins?!

setting: Outdoors on a dirt path with a hedge in the background
situation: Ratbert walks beside Dogbert and shares his philosophy about turning lemons into lemonade. He then qualifies it by noting that life must also supply a pitcher, ice and glasses. When a pitcher, glasses and lemons appear, he complains that there are no napkins.
punchline: Ratbert's optimistic philosophy quickly reveals itself as a demanding wish list, and even when life delivers the supplies he finds something else to complain about.
summary: A little lab rat tweaks the famous lemon proverb with a list of necessary extras, then grumbles when the spread still falls short.

file: 1994/1994-09-27_pulling rank_vice president_teaching himself banjo_wait in hallway_offcie_feet on desk_making wait.gif
title: Vice President Makes You Wait

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: I'm running late. But since I'm a vice president you'll have to wait in the hallway.

transcript.speaker: Vice President
transcript.text: You'll be able to judge your relative worth by observing what things I do while you wait.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's teaching himself the banjo.

setting: Office hallway outside a vice president's office
situation: Dilbert and the Boss are told by a vice president that he is running late and they must wait in the hallway. The vice president says they can gauge their importance by what he does while they wait. Peeking through the doorway, Dilbert reports that the executive is teaching himself the banjo.
punchline: The vice president's smug claim that his waiting-time activities reveal your worth backfires, since he is merely idling with a banjo, implying he considers them (and his time with them) unimportant.
summary: A pompous executive keeps two employees waiting and boasts that his behavior will show how much they matter, only to be caught noodling on a banjo.

file: 1994/1994-02-17_forgiveness_seek permission_personal risk_next reorganization_sound stupid_ask permission.gif
title: Better to Seek Permission, Reorganization

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I say it's easier to ask forgiveness than to ask permission.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I say it's better to seek permission, thus delaying your personal risk until it all becomes moot in the next reorganization.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That makes mine sound kinda stupid.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Get over it.

setting: Office conference room during a lunch meeting
situation: Three coworkers eat lunch at a meeting table. One coworker states the familiar maxim that it is easier to ask forgiveness than permission, and another counters with a cynical alternative: seek permission and stall until a reorganization wipes out any accountability. The first admits the second take makes his own sound stupid and gets a curt brush-off.
punchline: In a company that reorganizes constantly, the smartest way to avoid blame is to stall by asking permission until the reorg makes the whole issue irrelevant.
summary: A lunchtime debate about risk-taking is upended by a coworker whose cynical strategy relies on reorganizations erasing all accountability.

file: 1994/1994-10-19_algorithim_higest salries_overstatement_reduce headcount_scientific algorithm_who goes.gif
title: Scientific Algorithm Just Means Highest Salaries

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to reduce headcount.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: To be fair about it I created a scientific algorithm to decide who goes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought you were firing the people with the highest salaries.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, maybe "algorithm" is an overstatement.

setting: Dogbert's office, behind a large desk
situation: Dogbert, sitting at a desk as a manager, announces he has been told to cut headcount and boasts that he built a scientific algorithm to choose who gets laid off. Dilbert points out that the actual method is simply firing the highest-paid employees. Dogbert concedes that calling it an algorithm was a stretch.
punchline: The supposedly fair, scientific layoff algorithm is really just cutting the most expensive people, so calling it an algorithm is a pretentious overstatement.
summary: A canine executive dresses up a crude cost-cutting rule as rigorous science until an employee calls out the truth.

file: 1994/1994-01-26_emphasize positive_french staellite_trending downward_upbeat_war with france_project staus.gif
title: Positive Spin on War Report

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Project status: We accidentally destroyed the French satellite and are now at war with France.

transcript.speaker: Bearded Man
transcript.text: Maybe you should be a little more upbeat in your report. Emphasize the positive.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "...On a positive note, our headcount expenses are trending downward."

setting: A rocky desert hillside, with a cutaway to the boss's office
situation: Dilbert sits outdoors typing a project status report on a laptop while two bearded, hooded men stand beside him. He reports that they accidentally destroyed a French satellite and are now at war with France. One of the men advises him to be more upbeat, so Dilbert revises the report, which the boss reads in his office.
punchline: Told to emphasize the positive, Dilbert cheerfully spins the war casualties as lower headcount expenses, mocking corporate euphemism that hides disasters behind good-news framing.
summary: A status report about a satellite blunder and a resulting war gets a sunny rewrite that celebrates the staff cost savings from the casualties.

file: 1994/1994-03-09_assurance_value_average employee_less of us_more work_downsizing_layoffs_warning_fewer employees.gif
title: Employee Value Rises After Layoffs

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can assure you that the value of the average employee will continue to increase.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that because there will be less of us, doing more work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm right, aren't I?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Except for the "us" part.

situation: The Boss tells a group of employees that the value of the average employee will keep increasing. Dilbert deduces that this means fewer staff doing more work. The Boss confirms it, quibbling only over Dilbert's use of the word "us".
punchline: The Boss's only objection is to the word "us", revealing that he knows layoffs are coming but sees himself as safe, since the cuts will fall on the employees and not on management.
summary: A manager's upbeat promise about rising worker value turns out to be code for staff cuts that he himself won't suffer.

file: 1994/1994-04-29_making faces_holding ears_little fort_friday meetings.gif
title: Childish Behavior at Friday Meetings

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thp-p-p-p-p

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: I can't hear you! La-la-la-la-hm-hm-la-la

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendee
transcript.text: He's right! It is just like a little fort!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Friday meetings.

situation: Around a conference table, the attendees act like small children: one sticks out his tongue and waggles his hands at his ears, another covers his ears and sings to drown out the others, and in the last panel several hold papers over their heads like a makeshift fort. Dilbert sits quietly, taking it all in.
punchline: Dilbert's closing thought, 'Friday meetings', implies that this kind of childish behavior is a regular occurrence at the weekly meeting.
summary: Grown professionals regress to playground antics around the conference table while Dilbert resignedly notes this is par for the course at the weekly meeting.

file: 1994/1994-02-26_cut budget_spinning_flung_space_locusts_fling locusts.gif
title: Cutting Both Projects, Flinging Locusts

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: According to you, if I cut your budget the world will abruptly stop spinning and we'll be flung into space.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Whereas, the risk of cutting Dilbert's project is "...a plague of locusts o'er the land."

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'll cut both projects. With any luck, we'll fling the locusts into space.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: Locusts. Real good.

situation: At a budget meeting, a woman weighing cuts reads out the dire warnings each side has given her: one predicts the world will stop spinning, the other a plague of locusts. Rather than choose between the two, she decides to cut both projects, while a bald man at the table mutters a glum remark about locusts.
punchline: The budget decision-maker, faced with absurdly exaggerated doomsday claims from both sides, simply cuts both and hopes the two disasters cancel each other out.
summary: Faced with two wildly overblown predictions of catastrophe, a budget holder slashes both projects and hopes the disasters collide harmlessly.

file: 1994/1994-12-29_horse drink_lead a horse to water_stick a hose_tape hose  in mouth_horse drink water.gif
title: Leading a Horse to Water, Literally

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Remember the old saying, Ratbert: You can lead a horse to water...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...But by the time you got there you'd smell like a horse and your butt would hurt.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: If you stuck a hose in a horse's mouth and taped it there, could you make the horse drink?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, I've tried it.

setting: A red couch in Dilbert's home
situation: Dogbert recites the proverb about leading a horse to water to Ratbert, then cynically mocks it by pointing out the unpleasant reality of riding a horse there. Ratbert asks whether taping a hose in a horse's mouth would force it to drink, and Dogbert admits he has already tried it.
punchline: Dogbert's deadpan admission that he has actually tried taping a hose into a horse's mouth reveals his willingness to use absurd, forceful methods to defeat a proverb about the limits of coercion.
summary: Dogbert undermines a famous proverb with crude practicalities, then confesses to a bizarre hands-on experiment in forcing a horse to drink.
keywords: you can lead a horse to water

file: 1994/1994-02-21_back of neck_humane_layoffs_tranquilizer_unemployment offcie_wake up_shooter_gun_knocked out.gif
title: Humane Layoffs By Tranquilizer Dart

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The layoffs will be handled in the most humane way possible.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Pow!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Shtk!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How long does the tranquilizer last?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He'll wake up at the unemployment office.

situation: The Boss assures a group of employees that layoffs will be handled in the most humane way possible. A hidden hunter in safari gear then shoots a coworker in the back of the neck with a tranquilizer dart and he drops. Dilbert asks how long the drug lasts, and the Boss says the man will wake up at the unemployment office.
