punchline: The 'humane' layoff is just knocking employees unconscious and dumping them at the unemployment office, treating laid-off workers like captured animals.
summary: Management's idea of a kind firing involves a sedative dart and a free delivery to the jobless line.

file: 1994/1994-07-13_career criminlas_jail_sentences_don't reduce crime_commit crimes_others commit crimes_statistics.gif
title: Statistics Don't Lie, Unless Jailed

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I oppose putting career criminals in jail for life. There's no evidence that longer sentences reduce crime.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, your theory is that when career criminals are in jail, other people commit more crimes to keep the average up...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Statistics don't lie, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unless bad statistics went to jail - then the others would lie.

setting: Outdoors on a walk, then sitting by a log in a hilly landscape
situation: Dilbert argues against life sentences for career criminals, claiming there is no evidence that longer sentences reduce crime. Dogbert mocks the reasoning by suggesting Dilbert believes other people commit extra crimes to keep the average up. When Dilbert insists statistics don't lie, Dogbert counters with a twisted joke about statistics being jailed.
punchline: Dogbert turns Dilbert's faith in statistics into absurdity by imagining statistics themselves as criminals whose imprisonment would make the remaining ones start lying.
summary: A man defends a data-driven stance on sentencing, and his dog skewers it by treating statistics as prisoners who might be locked away.

file: 1994/1994-04-02_chicken to dinosaur_vegatables_vegetarian.gif
title: Vegetarian Dinosaur Eyes Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like some chicken, Bob?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I told you I'm a vegetarian. I eat vegetables.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about fish? Do you eat fish?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Fish are not vegetables.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about clams? Do you eat clams?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: No, but you're starting to look good.

situation: Dilbert is having a meal with Bob, a green dinosaur, and keeps offering him food. Bob insists he is a vegetarian and rejects chicken, fish and clams in turn. Dilbert's persistent questions finally prompt Bob to say Dilbert himself is starting to look appetizing.
punchline: Bob's claim to be a vegetarian is undercut by his hint that he might eat Dilbert, whose annoying questions make him look like a meal.
summary: A dinosaur guest who refuses all meat and seafood runs out of patience with his host's repeated offers and ends up eyeing the host instead.

file: 1994/1994-08-03_best assets_competitions worst_employees on job_hidden camera_imply_they work for competition_ad agency_dogbert's ad agency.gif
title: Dogbert's Deceptive Comparative Advertising Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Ad Agency

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your commercials should compare your best assets to the competition's worst.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll use a hidden camera to film your employees on the job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I missed something here...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll imply that they all work for the competition. This isn't a documentary.

setting: Dogbert's ad agency office, across a desk
situation: Dogbert, running an ad agency, advises a client (the Pointy-Haired Boss) to make commercials comparing his best assets to the competition's worst. He explains they will secretly film the Boss's own employees and falsely imply they work for the competitor.
punchline: Dogbert's 'comparison' advertising is really just deception: filming the client's own staff and passing them off as the competition's, because ads don't need to be truthful.
summary: A scheming dog ad executive coaches his client on making misleading comparison commercials by passing off the client's own staff as a rival's workforce.

file: 1994/1994-07-23_market research_customers age_proposal study_funding_no answers_half above_half below.gif
title: Shocking Median Age Market Research

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My market research indicates that 50% of your customers are above the median age.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But the shocking discovery was that 50% were below the median age.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What percent are exactly the median age?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm proposing to study that in phase two.

setting: Boss's office during a slide presentation
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, uses an overhead projector to present market research to the Boss. He announces obvious statistical facts about the median age as if they were shocking discoveries. When the Boss asks a follow-up question, Dogbert proposes a second, paid phase of study to answer it.
punchline: The consultant presents the mathematical definition of a median as a startling finding, then uses the Boss's naive question to justify billing for more research.
summary: A consultant dog dazzles his boss with the self-evident meaning of a median, then angles for a follow-up contract.

file: 1994/1994-12-10_effects pay_employee survey_grumpiest employee_morale_touchy feely stuff.gif
title: Firing the Grumpiest Employee for Morale

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The employee surveys indicate some dissatisfaction in my group. That affects my pay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're my grumpiest employee, so I'm going to fire you to bring up my average score for morale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I'm getting better at all the touchy-feely stuff.

situation: The Boss explains to a scowling employee that low morale scores in employee surveys affect his pay. He decides to fire the grumpiest employee so the group's average morale score goes up. He then congratulates himself on getting better at the people-skills side of management.
punchline: The Boss thinks firing an unhappy employee is a way to improve morale, which shows he completely misunderstands what morale is and is only motivated by his own pay.
summary: A manager tries to fix poor survey results by dismissing his most disgruntled worker and then feels proud of his emotional intelligence.

file: 1994/1994-10-22_computer_academy award winner_next years award_best actor_technology.gif
title: Software Wants Future Oscar Winner

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: To configure the software, enter the name of next year's Academy Award winner for best actor.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Please wait.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his desk in front of a computer
situation: Dilbert is installing software, and the computer's configuration prompt demands the name of next year's Academy Award winner for Best Actor. Dilbert types away in the second panel, apparently trying to comply, and the computer responds by telling him to wait.
punchline: The software asks for information that is impossible to know yet, so Dilbert has to sit and wait a year for the winner to be announced, mocking absurd and poorly designed software setup requirements.
summary: A computer's setup wizard asks for a piece of information that cannot exist until next year, leaving its user stuck waiting.

file: 1994/1994-04-23_new wealth_build amusement park_thrilling rides_wedgie_restrooms_customers_build park.gif
title: Dogbertland: Amusement Park Hostile to Customers

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I plan to use my new wealth to build an amusement park.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbertland will have thrilling rides like "The Wedgie" and I'll have a maze in front of the restrooms.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The customers will hate this.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If they want fun they can build their own park.

situation: Dogbert, newly wealthy, tells Dilbert his plan to build an amusement park called Dogbertland. Dilbert studies the blueprints as Dogbert describes a ride called The Wedgie and a maze blocking the restrooms. Dilbert warns that customers will hate it, and Dogbert dismisses the concern.
punchline: Dogbert's smug refusal to care about customer satisfaction, suggesting unhappy visitors should just build their own park if they want fun, reveals his contempt for the people he plans to profit from.
summary: A newly rich Dogbert unveils plans for a deliberately miserable theme park and shrugs off his engineer friend's warning that guests won't enjoy it.

file: 1994/1994-09-16_throwing out cat_no value_widen demograohic_make you immortal_bargaining_wants to stay.gif
title: Cat Pitches Demographic Appeal, Immortality

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You have to go, Cat. You have no value to us.

transcript.speaker: Cat
transcript.text: Actually, my mere existence will widen your demographic appeal and make you immortal.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Oh... a cat. That's original.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Give it a rest, "Mickey."

transcript.speaker: Cat
transcript.text: Purr

setting: Blank pink background, a cartoon stage with no office furniture
situation: Dogbert drags a cat away by its tail, telling it that it has no value and must leave. The cat argues that its presence will broaden the strip's demographic appeal and make it immortal. Ratbert sarcastically complains that adding a cat is unoriginal, and Dogbert retorts that Ratbert is just a Mickey Mouse knockoff while the cat purrs, staying.
punchline: The cat justifies its existence in marketing terms, and the sarcastic jab at Ratbert as a derivative "Mickey" shows that cartoon characters are valued for merchandising appeal and longevity rather than originality.
summary: A mistreated stray wins a place among the cast by pitching itself as a smart marketing move, while another character gets mocked for being a copycat.

file: 1994/1994-02-07_approved underwear list_blue jeans_forbidden clothes_morale_new casual dress code_shorts_tanktops.gif
title: Casual Dress Code Underwear Appendix

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought it necessary to provide detailed guidelines to our new casual dress code.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Forbidden clothing includes: shorts, tank tops, tee shirts, shirts with slogans, blue jeans, sneakers, and sandals.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My morale is soaring.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Appendix "A" is the approved underwear list.

situation: The Boss visits Dilbert at his desk and reads aloud a long list of clothing banned under the company's new casual dress code. Dilbert sarcastically says his morale is soaring, and the Boss responds by mentioning there is also an appendix listing approved underwear.
punchline: A casual dress code meant to boost morale has been turned into a rigid, micromanaging rulebook so thorough that it even regulates underwear.
summary: A supposedly relaxed dress policy is buried under so many prohibitions and appendices that it becomes more restrictive than the formal rules it replaced.

file: 1994/1994-04-13_committed to buy_cost justify_ethical_execuitve_translate_vendor_weasel_words.gif
title: Cost-Justifying an Executive's Bad Purchase

transcript.speaker: Mole-like Consultant
transcript.text: Tell me about your project and I'll translate it into weasel words for the business case.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... an executive had lunch with a vendor and committed to buy some stuff that doesn't work. Our job is to cost-justify the decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I quit.

transcript.speaker: Mole-like Consultant
transcript.text: Don't get all ethical on us.

setting: A conference room or office table
situation: A small mole-like consultant offers to turn Dilbert's project into weasel words for a business case. Dilbert explains that an executive got wooed by a vendor at lunch and committed to buy defective products, and his team must now justify the cost after the fact. Dilbert says he quits, and the consultant tells him not to get ethical about it.
punchline: The consultant treats ethics as an unreasonable obstacle, showing that fabricating a business case to cover a bad purchase is simply routine corporate practice.
summary: A weasel-word consultant helps rationalize a worthless purchase made by a lunching executive, and brushes off Dilbert's moral objection as a nuisance.

file: 1994/1994-11-19_job performance_reflects on boss_balance of power_get fired_low job perfromance_wally hold hostage.gif
title: Wally Threatens Boss With Underperformance

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I suddenly realized that MY job performance reflects on YOUR career.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The balance of power has shifted. Unless I get what I want, I'll lower my performance until you get fired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha! There's no way you could lower your job performance.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Curse your eyes!

situation: Wally stands before the Boss's desk and announces that his own work performance reflects on the Boss's career. He threatens to deliberately lower his performance until the Boss gets fired unless his demands are met. The Boss laughs and points out that Wally's performance is already so low it can't get any worse.
punchline: Wally's blackmail fails because he is already so unproductive that he has no lower performance to threaten with.
summary: An employee tries to hold his manager hostage with a threat of doing worse work, only to be told he already does as little as possible.

file: 1994/1994-10-15_dating scene_reprodcue_cell division_steer clear.gif
title: Wally Plans Asexual Reproduction

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I've given up on the whole dating scene. I've decided to reproduce by asexual cell division.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't realize that was an option.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You never know until you try.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'll steer clear of here for a while.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Divide! Divide!

situation: Wally sits at his desk and tells Dilbert he has given up on dating and will instead reproduce by asexual cell division. Dilbert is bemused by the idea. As Dilbert decides to stay away for a while, Wally is seen straining and muttering 'Divide! Divide!' in his cubicle.
punchline: Wally is actually trying to split himself in two at his desk, so Dilbert wisely decides to avoid the area.
summary: A lonely coworker abandons romance and tries, absurdly, to multiply himself like a single-celled organism while his colleague backs away.

file: 1994/1994-06-16_bank off head_coach_field_game_glasses_goal_soccer_strike_team players_sports.gif
title: Soccer Team Uses Dilbert's Head

transcript.speaker: Kid Coach
transcript.text: Dilbert, you'll be playing the left striker position.

transcript.speaker: Kid Coach
transcript.text: One of our good players will try to strike you in the head with the ball and bank it in the goal.

transcript.speaker: Girl Teammate
transcript.text: "It" being the ball, not your head.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better take off my glasses.

transcript.speaker: Girl Teammate
transcript.text: No, don't. I included their dampening effect in my calculations.

setting: A kids' soccer field with a goal in the background
situation: Dilbert joins a youth soccer team and is assigned the left striker position. The coach explains that the plan is for a teammate to hit Dilbert in the head with the ball so it ricochets into the goal. Dilbert offers to remove his glasses, but the teammate says she has already factored the glasses into her calculations.
punchline: The team treats Dilbert's head as a calculated billiard-style bank shot, and his glasses are just another variable in their physics, so his safety is irrelevant.
summary: A children's soccer team casually plans to use the new player's skull as a rebound surface, complete with precise math that accounts for his eyewear.

file: 1994/1994-02-13_insensitive_dogbert_dog bashing_born this way_no campassion_feel bad_who cares_insensitive about insensitivity.gif
title: Dogbert Defends His Insensitivity Proudly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That joke was not funny. You're insensitive, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, here we go with the "insensitive dog bashing."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it my fault I was born without the ability to sense the feelings of others?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh, sure, I wish I could be like you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Somehow you know exactly what it feels like to be a different gender, race, lifestyle or body.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But I'm insensitive. All I know is how I feel!! And I'm proud of it!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But you'd understand that, if you weren't insensitive about insensitivity!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When you put it like that, I feel kinda bad.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who cares?

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair and Dogbert on a cushion
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert that his joke was not funny and that he is insensitive. Dogbert turns this into a complaint about being bashed for something he was born with, and Dilbert sarcastically replies that Dogbert seems to know how others feel. Dogbert then accuses Dilbert of being insensitive about insensitivity, making Dilbert feel bad, and Dogbert dismisses his feelings.
punchline: Dogbert co-opts the language of identity and victimhood to defend his own insensitivity, and then proves his point by callously asking "Who cares?" about Dilbert's hurt feelings.
summary: A dog turns a scolding for being tactless into a claim of being unfairly persecuted, then brushes off the human's hurt feelings.

file: 1994/1994-10-20_dress codes don't apply_fireing_hire back_more money_reverence package_telecommute_two weeks vaction.gif
title: Fired, Then Rehired As Contractor

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great news-- you're fired!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You get a generous severance package, two weeks' vacation, AND we hire you back as a contractor for more money!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I can telecommute if I want, but since dress codes don't apply to me...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Aargh!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bonk Bonk

setting: Dogbert's office, with a desk and a doorway outside
situation: Dogbert, acting as a boss behind a desk, tells an employee he is fired and then lists the perks: severance, vacation, and being rehired as a contractor at higher pay. In the last panel, Dogbert, who is not bound by the dress code, appears in a bathrobe holding a coffee mug, while Wally grabs Dilbert by the tie and bonks his head against the door.
punchline: The benefits of being fired and rehired as a contractor are so good that the employees violently fight over who gets laid off, while the boss enjoys perks like telecommuting and ignoring the dress code.
summary: A canine executive makes getting laid off sound so lucrative that coworkers start brawling for the privilege.

file: 1994/1994-03-20_better comoritively_dread_fixed income_health problems_pre meeting meeting_retirement_shrink_wrinkles_complaints.gif
title: Looking Forward to Retirement Misery

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: I'm looking forward to retirement.

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: I can't wait! I'll have my tiny fixed income, barely enough to survive!

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: ...and a new health problem almost every day!

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: I'll have wrinkles everywhere, and I'll actually shrink!

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: Ha ha! I'll produce nothing and I'll complain constantly!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're looking forward to all that??

transcript.speaker: Balding Coworker
transcript.text: Well... compared to working here...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's time for the pre-meeting meeting on employee productivity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm... fixed income... health problems.

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: A balding coworker cheerfully lists the grim realities of retirement to Dilbert: a tiny fixed income, constant health problems, wrinkles, shrinking, and complaining without producing anything. When Dilbert asks if he really looks forward to that, he says it's still better than working here. A colleague then announces a pre-meeting meeting on employee productivity, and Dilbert starts to see the appeal of retirement.
punchline: Even a retirement of poverty, ill health and bodily decline sounds preferable to the pointless meetings and drudgery of this workplace.
summary: A coworker gleefully anticipates the miseries of old age because they still beat his current job, and Dilbert is nearly persuaded after hearing about yet another meeting.

file: 1994/1994-05-06_user rep_stupid_new paradigm.gif
title: Stupidest User Contest Becomes Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My user representative is the stupidest...

transcript.speaker: Software Engineer
transcript.text: No way! My user is the stupidest.

transcript.speaker: Software Engineer
transcript.text: Oh yeah?! Let's have a little wager. Go get your user and I'll get mine!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're on!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have another scone, Tom.

transcript.speaker: User
transcript.text: You're right. They do look just like Styrofoam cups.

transcript.speaker: Another User
transcript.text: It's a new paradigm...

setting: Conference room with a meeting table
situation: Dilbert and a fellow engineer argue over whose user representative is the stupidest and agree to a wager, each fetching their user. The two users then sit at a table with scones and Styrofoam cups, saying baffling things that apparently settle the contest.
punchline: The users' absurd remarks, such as noting that scones look like Styrofoam cups and calling it a new paradigm, prove the engineers' contempt for their users is well earned.
summary: Two engineers bet on whose user is dumber, then bring them together and let the users' nonsensical chatter speak for itself.

file: 1994/1994-12-03_dogberts tech support_three menu_read a memo.gif
title: Dogbert Mocks Caller's Memo Authority

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So... there are three menu choices and the first two didn't work...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Some people would have recklessly tried the third choice before calling for help. But I can tell you're different.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's be honest with ourselves, Dave. Do you think anybody is going to read a memo from you?

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk, on the phone
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line, listens to a caller named Dave who tried two of three menu options and then called for help instead of trying the third. Dogbert sarcastically calls him 'different' for his caution, then bluntly tells him nobody would read a memo from him, dismissing the idea of Dave writing up his problem or advice.
punchline: Dogbert insults the caller twice over: first by mocking his timidity in not trying the obvious third option, then by telling him he has so little influence that no one would even read his memo.
summary: A tech support dog gently ridicules a timid caller for phoning in before exhausting his options, then crushes his hopes of being taken seriously.

file: 1994/1994-02-01_saint dogbert_technology_demons_stupidity_make command_easy to remeber_software developer.gif
title: Saint Dogbert Exorcises Stupid Software

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Saint Dogbert seeks out technology that has been possessed by the demons of stupidity.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: He happens across a software developer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll make the command easy to remember, like "Ctrl-Alt-F4-Del".

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And if they forget that they can just edit the source code in "command.com"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Perfect.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Out! Out!

setting: A dirt path outdoors, then an office cubicle with a computer
situation: Dogbert, dressed as a saint with a papal-style hat and wand, wanders in search of technology possessed by the demons of stupidity. He finds a software developer (Dilbert) designing a clumsy key-combination command and suggesting users can just edit the source code if they forget it. Dogbert waves his wand and tries to exorcise the demon from the computer.
punchline: The developer's absurdly convoluted 'easy to remember' command and the suggestion that users edit the operating system's source code show the demon of stupidity is in the developer himself, so the exorcism is aimed at the wrong target.
summary: A holy dog goes hunting for cursed technology and finds a programmer whose idea of user-friendliness is the real source of the evil.

file: 1994/1994-08-06_goldfish_hair on cat_hairless cat_dilbert spray.gif
title: Dogbert Sprays Hairless Cat Furry

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Thanks for inviting me over, Dogbert. We little hairless cats are usually shunned.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Fsss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would have bet anything that that wouldn't work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now the goldfish.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Hair!!

setting: Outside Dilbert's front door, on the doormat
situation: A hairless cat thanks Dogbert for inviting him over, noting that hairless cats are usually shunned. Dogbert sprays him with an aerosol can, covering him in a thick coat of hair. Dilbert, amazed the product works, watches as Dogbert announces his next target, the goldfish.
punchline: Dogbert's spray-on hair product actually works, so he immediately plans to use it on a goldfish, with the cat horrified at his new fur and Dilbert astonished that it worked at all.
summary: Dogbert tests a can of instant hair on a trusting hairless cat, then eyes the goldfish as his next experiment.

file: 1994/1994-06-18_no ring_dilbert asks liz_date_pizza date_after game_big ring_eunuchs_special van_flop sweat_kidding_joke_gullible_likes gullible.gif
title: Dilbert Falls for Liz's Giant Ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Liz, I noticed you're not wearing a ring. Would you like to go for a pizza after the game?

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Oh, I do have a ring. It's so big I can't wear it. A team of eunuchs follows me around with it in a special van.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Flop-sweat time.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: You're gullible. I like that.

setting: Outdoor soccer field during a game
situation: Dilbert, standing at a soccer game, asks Liz, who is holding a soccer ball, whether she'd like to get pizza after the game, having noticed she wears no ring. Liz claims she owns a ring so enormous that a team of eunuchs follows her in a special van carrying it. Dilbert panics and sweats, then Liz reveals she was joking and says she likes his gullibility.
punchline: Dilbert believes Liz's absurd claim about her huge ring and eunuch entourage, panics, and she reveals she was kidding and finds his gullibility appealing.
summary: A nervous suitor is rattled by an outlandish boast about a jewel so big it needs its own escort, only for the woman to confess she was teasing and likes how easily he was fooled.

file: 1994/1994-02-09_engineers_good tatse_home to change_shut up wally_casual dress.gif
title: Bell-Bottoms Violate Casual Dress Day

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I realize that casual dress day isn't easy for you engineers...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But you've exceeded the bounds of good taste. I've got to send you home to change.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Shut up, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I heard they were back! I swear!

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert and Wally that casual dress day is hard for engineers, then says they have gone too far and must go home to change. In the last panel the two walk away wearing green shirts and orange bell-bottom trousers, with Dilbert telling Wally to shut up.
punchline: The engineers wore bell-bottoms because Wally heard that the trend was back, and it clearly is not, so they are sent home for violating good taste.
summary: Two engineers are sent home for outrageous retro flared pants after a rumor that the fashion had returned.

file: 1994/1994-12-08_iso 9000 certfication_create boring_poorly written document_big binder_copies to dept. heads_dead racoon.gif
title: ISO 9000 Certification Binder Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's the basic plan for getting our "ISO 9000" certification.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Each of you will create an insanely boring, poorly written document. I'll combine them into one big honkin' binder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll send copies to all department heads for comment. They will treat it like a dead raccoon and route it to the first passerby.

setting: Conference room with an overhead projector
situation: Dilbert presents a flowchart on an overhead projector, explaining his plan for ISO 9000 certification. Team members will each write a deliberately dull, poorly written document, which he will merge into a giant binder. He then predicts that department heads will pass the binder along to the nearest bystander rather than read it.
punchline: The certification process is pure bureaucratic paperwork that nobody wants to write or read, so the binder will be passed around like a dead raccoon that no one wants to handle.
summary: A presenter lays out a certification scheme built on tedious paperwork that every manager will quickly offload onto someone else.

file: 1994/1994-08-16_difference_entire day_hamster on wheel_new assignements_finish work_explaining.gif
title: Hamster on a Wheel Futility

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I spent the entire day getting new assignments which left no time to actually work on anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll spend the entire day explaining why I didn't finish yesterday's work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I don't know the difference between me and a hamster on a wheel.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hamsters don't depress me.

setting: Office or Dilbert's workspace, with Dilbert holding a briefcase and Dogbert lounging nearby
situation: Dilbert complains that a whole day of receiving new assignments left him no time to do any actual work. He predicts the next day will be spent justifying the unfinished work. He then compares himself to a hamster on a wheel, and Dogbert coolly replies that hamsters don't depress him.
punchline: Dogbert dryly implies that, unlike hamsters, Dilbert's pointless busywork is depressing to watch, which is a deadpan insult to his misery.
summary: A weary engineer likens his endless cycle of assignments and excuses to a rodent running in circles, and his pet dog declares the rodent the less depressing of the two.

file: 1994/1994-11-23_existential problem_dilbert reconciling work_paid_salary_what do for money_flick fingers_get paid_money.gif
title: Paid Regardless, Dilbert Flicks Fingers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just lost the subtle mental connection between my performance and my salary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get paid the same no matter what I do. I can stand here and flick my fingers and still get paid.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flick flick flick

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you realize what this means??!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flick flick

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey! You're getting paid for that!

situation: Dilbert stands in the office and realizes his salary has no connection to how well he performs. He tests this by flicking his fingers, then announces his realization to two coworkers. One of them, a balding man in glasses, angrily points out that Dilbert is being paid to do nothing.
punchline: The coworker misses Dilbert's point and is merely outraged that he's paid for flicking his fingers, which confirms that pay really is unrelated to useful work.
summary: A worker discovers that pay is detached from effort, demonstrates it by doing something pointless, and a colleague's indignation proves him right.

file: 1994/1994-06-05_engineer_shut down factory_ethical_make film_empowered_more women in management_down for day_ego booster_endangered bird_parking lot_engineering.gif
title: Engineers Empowered To Shut Down Factory

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, any engineer can shut down our factory for any reason.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Later we'll film a commercial about how ethical and empowered you are.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ha! Give me a raise, Tubby, or the factory's going down!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You can't shut it down; I'm shutting it down until more women are in top management!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to shut it down for a day, just as an ego booster. Is Tuesday good?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Didn't any of you hear that there's an endangered bird living in the parking lot??

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Silent panel: the engineers sit quietly at the table.)

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think I parked on it this morning.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can we get back to the point?

situation: The Boss announces that any engineer may shut down the factory for any reason, then adds that it's all for a PR commercial. Wally demands a raise, Alice demands more women in top management, and Dilbert asks for a day off to boost his ego. The Boss ends it by mentioning an endangered bird in the parking lot, and Wally admits he may have parked on it.
punchline: The engineers immediately abuse their new shutdown power for petty personal gain, and when a genuinely legitimate reason appears, the only response is that one of them probably ran over the bird.
summary: Handed a free pass to halt production, the engineers turn it into a bargaining chip for selfish demands until the one real ethical issue turns out to be their own fault.

file: 1994/1994-10-03_consulting comany_executive compensation_ninety percent_overpaid_repeat business.gif
title: Consultant Recommends Slashing Executive Pay

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The Dogbert Consulting Company has reviewed the executive compensation plan as you requested.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My conclusion is that you're already hideously overpaid. I'm recommending ninety percent pay cuts and a whack in the head for each of you.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: I'll bet you don't get much repeat business.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh yeah, as if I'd want to spend more time with you.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents his review of the executive compensation plan to a table of executives. He concludes they are hideously overpaid and recommends ninety percent pay cuts plus a whack in the head for each. One executive snipes that he won't get repeat business, and Dogbert fires back that he doesn't want any.
punchline: Dogbert is so contemptuous of his executive clients that he doesn't care about losing their business, since he'd never want to spend more time with them.
summary: A dog consultant tells a roomful of executives they earn far too much and then shrugs off the threat of losing their future contracts.

file: 1994/1994-09-01_macro economics_diagram_flood victim_mechanical pencil_erase.gif
title: Economics Professor's Incomprehensible Diagram

transcript.speaker: Professor
transcript.text: Let's start with a brief refresher in macro economics.

transcript.speaker: Professor
transcript.text: This diagram explains why I'm an expert in money yet I dress like a flood victim.

transcript.speaker: Professor
transcript.text: You'll have no trouble with the rest of the course unless your mechanical pencil jammed...let's erase...

situation: An economics professor, wearing a rumpled blue suit, begins a lecture with a refresher in macro economics. He presents a chaotic whiteboard diagram full of arrows, squiggles, a skull and crossbones, and random labels like Lottery, GNP and Luck. Dilbert, sitting among the students, frantically fiddles with a jammed mechanical pencil while the professor prepares to erase the board.
punchline: The diagram is meaningless scribble that explains nothing, and the professor erases it before anyone can copy it down, so the only note-taking trouble is a jammed pencil.
summary: A scruffy economics professor reveals a nonsensical diagram and then wipes it away before a flustered Dilbert can write any of it down.

file: 1994/1994-08-05_final design_zebra_fisnih on time_canceled project_month ago_legal_binder_dont travel.gif
title: Weeks of Work on Canceled Project

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's the final design for Project "Zebra." I worked day and night for weeks to finish it on time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I canceled that project a month ago. I meant to tell you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In some countries it would be legal to kill you with this binder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's why I don't travel.

setting: Office, in front of the Boss
situation: Dilbert proudly hands the Boss the final design binder for Project Zebra after weeks of overtime. The Boss casually reveals he canceled the project a month ago and forgot to tell him. Dilbert threatens him with the binder, and the Boss deadpans that he avoids travel for exactly that reason.
punchline: The Boss's obliviousness to wasted work is so profound that he answers a murder threat by noting he simply avoids countries where it would be legal.
summary: After burning himself out finishing a design, an employee learns his manager scrapped the whole effort weeks earlier and never mentioned it.

file: 1994/1994-12-17_make a suggestion_idea rat_multi disciplinary forces_processes.gif
title: Idea Rat Pitches Buzzword Task Forces

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Excuse me... I'm only an intern, but may I make a suggestion?

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Let's form multi-disciplinary task forces to reengineer our core processes until we're a world class organization!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sounds good. Go do it.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: I'm more of an idea rat.

characters: Intern (small orange creature in the chair)
situation: A small furry intern at a conference table humbly asks to make a suggestion, then proposes forming multi-disciplinary task forces to reengineer core processes. The Boss immediately approves and tells the intern to go carry it out. The intern protests that he only comes up with ideas and doesn't do the work.
punchline: The Boss treats any suggestion as an assignment for whoever proposed it, and the intern, who spouted pure management buzzwords, wants to be the one who has ideas without doing any of the implementation.
summary: A meeting newcomer rattles off consultant-speak about reengineering and is promptly told to execute it himself, which he declines on the grounds that he only supplies ideas.

file: 1994/1994-12-01_dogberts tech support_online data base_compatible_computer_software_red blotches_poison ivy_technology_engineering.gif
title: Tech Support Delivers Bad News

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: According to my online database, our product isn't compatible with your computer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's also incompatible with all other computers and all other software including our own.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And those red blotches on your hands - that's because our box is made of poison ivy.

situation: Dogbert, working a tech support phone line, tells a customer that the product is incompatible with their computer. He then adds that it is incompatible with every other computer and all software, even the company's own. He finishes by explaining that the customer's red blotches come from the product's box being made of poison ivy.
punchline: The tech support call escalates from a routine compatibility problem to the product being totally useless and even physically harmful, delivered in a casual, unapologetic tone.
summary: A deadpan support dog gives a customer a steadily worsening diagnosis of a thoroughly useless and rash-inducing product.

file: 1994/1994-11-06_project approved_budget giveaway_doomed_hyped up_marketing dept_snatched porject_reverse psychology.gif
title: Hyping a Doomed Project Away

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I got your project approved by our president!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But he gave your budget to another project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's pretty much doomed from the get-go.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I hyped it up at the executive meeting so somebody else will try to take it over.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager
transcript.text: Step aside, fools! This project belongs to Marketing now!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, please don't take our project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever worry that you're finding joy in the wrong places?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nope.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert his project was approved but had its budget given away, making it doomed. To get rid of it, he hyped it at the executive meeting so another department would take it over. When Marketing storms in to claim the project, the Boss pretends to protest, then high-fives Dilbert in celebration.
punchline: Dilbert and the Boss gleefully celebrate successfully dumping a doomed project on another department, and the Boss shows no shame about taking joy in this petty office victory.
summary: A manager cleverly tricks a rival department into stealing a hopeless project, and he and his employee celebrate with a high five.

file: 1994/1994-12-14_marketing_offcie_opening in security_rat is insulted_ratbert_suited career_gnaw on cord_business.gif
title: Ratbert's Marketing Interview Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Outwardly, yes, I'm a rat. But my bubbly personality and my utter lack of skill make me well-suited for a career in marketing.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Would you mind terribly if I gnawed on your phone cord?

transcript.speaker: Interviewer (off-panel)
transcript.text: We have an opening in lobby security.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm insulted!

setting: An office, during a job interview
situation: Ratbert, sitting in a chair at a desk, pitches himself for a marketing job by admitting he is a rat with no skills but a bubbly personality. He then politely asks if he may gnaw on the interviewer's phone cord. The interviewer offers him a lobby security position instead, and Ratbert takes offense.
punchline: Ratbert is offended at being offered a security job, even though he has just proudly admitted he has no skills and wants to chew on the phone cord, as if marketing were the only place that rewards such traits.
summary: A rat applying for a marketing job cheerfully admits he is useless, asks to chew a phone cord, and then is indignant when offered a lesser post.

file: 1994/1994-12-09_high income group_can afford product_rich_tasteless_easily amused_located a cluster_dog_golf course_animals.gif
title: Dogbert's Rich Tasteless Target Market

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your target market is the high income group. They're the only ones who can afford your product.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: More specifically, they must be rich, tasteless and easily amused. I've located a cluster of them to study.

transcript.speaker: Golfer
transcript.text: That dog's watching us golf again.

setting: Conference room presentation, then a golf course
situation: Dogbert, acting as a marketing consultant, presents a slide deck to Dilbert and a coworker, narrowing the target market to people who are rich, tasteless and easily amused, shown as a Venn diagram. He says he has found a group of them to study. The final panel shows two golfers noticing a dog watching them from the bushes, revealing where Dogbert is doing his research.
punchline: Dogbert's research subjects are golfers, implying that golfers are the rich, tasteless and easily amused people he is studying.
summary: A consulting dog defines the ideal customer as wealthy, tacky and simple to entertain, then goes off to observe them at the country club.

file: 1994/1994-03-06_business_competition_control_deadbeats_for scuccess_mangers_reorganize_subgroup_thrown out window_whiners.gif
title: Dogbert's Treacherous Reorganization Seminar

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: How to reorganize for success

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Put all your deadbeats and whiners in one subgroup.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We don't want to be a subgroup.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Give them a project that duplicates work being done by more competent people elsewhere in the company.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Soon, the manager of the competent people will find out you're duplicating his work.

transcript.speaker: Competent Manager
transcript.text: You're on my turf.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Boo hoo

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: He'll make a play to get your project under his control.

transcript.speaker: Competent Manager
transcript.text: They should be transferred to my control.

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Big Boss

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Before you transfer the deadbeats, give them high performance reviews to conceal your treachery.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Godlike? Wow!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll miss you.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: In time, the manager who took your losers will fail, thus decreasing competition for promotions.

transcript.speaker: Falling Manager
transcript.text: Aaiil!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Next week I'll discuss teamwork, the manager's obstacle to success.

situation: Dogbert lectures on how to reorganize a company for success. He instructs managers to group their worst employees into a subgroup, assign them duplicate work, and then let a rival manager take them over after giving them glowing reviews. The rival manager eventually fails and falls from a building, eliminating promotion competition.
punchline: Dogbert's 'reorganization for success' is really a scheme to sabotage rival managers and clear your own path to promotion, ending with the dismissal of teamwork as an obstacle.
summary: A scheming canine consultant teaches managers to dump their worst workers onto a rival with fake praise so the rival collapses and promotions open up.

file: 1994/1994-03-21_dilbert date_asks lunch date_cheryl_full of lunch_rejection_next week_turned down_lame excuse_office_co worker.gif
title: Lunch Invitation Met With Absurd Excuses

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Cheryl. Would you like to have lunch with me next week?

transcript.speaker: Cheryl
transcript.text: I... uh... already ate lunch. I'm not hungry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm talking about next week!!

transcript.speaker: Cheryl
transcript.text: I don't think I could have another bite. All full.

situation: Dilbert approaches coworker Cheryl at her desk and asks her to lunch next week. She replies that she has already eaten and isn't hungry. When Dilbert clarifies he means next week, she doubles down with an even more ridiculous claim that she is completely full.
punchline: Cheryl is so determined to turn Dilbert down that she uses an obviously illogical excuse, claiming she's too full to eat lunch a week from now.
summary: A hopeful coworker's lunch invitation is rebuffed with a flimsy excuse that gets more absurd when he points out the date is a week away.

file: 1994/1994-05-16_important project_marked man_other employees_throw bricks_keep persepctive_suck ups_brick to the head.gif
title: Funded Project Attracts Suck-Ups and Bricks

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm putting you in charge of an important project which is fully funded.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gasp!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm a marked man. The other employees will either try to suck up to me for money or throw bricks at me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Buddy!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The trick is to keep a protective ring of suck-ups around at all times.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Zip!

setting: Dilbert's office, with the Boss speaking from off-panel
situation: The Boss off-panel assigns Dilbert an important, fully funded project, and Dilbert gasps. He reasons that coworkers will either flatter him to get money or throw bricks at him. A friendly coworker rushes up calling him 'buddy' just as a brick flies in, hinting the plan to be surrounded by suck-ups is already being tested.
punchline: Dilbert's cynical plan to be shielded by suck-ups is immediately undercut when a brick is thrown at him anyway, showing that funding turns coworkers into either flatterers or attackers.
summary: Handed a well-funded project, Dilbert predicts jealous colleagues will either fawn over him or attack him, and a brick promptly proves him right.

file: 1994/1994-07-28_gerard depardieu_ceo_productive work_overhead transparencies_exaggerate value_uglier coworkers_actors.gif
title: Faking Productivity For The CEO Visit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO will visit here next week. You all know what to do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We should stop all productive work and create overhead transparencies that exaggerate our value.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And a few of our uglier co-workers will be replaced by actors.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As long as it's not Gerard Depardieu.

situation: The Boss announces that the CEO will visit next week and tells everyone they know what to do. Dilbert dryly summarizes the expected routine: stop real work and produce overhead transparencies that inflate the team's value. The Boss adds that uglier co-workers will be replaced by actors, and Dilbert quips about which actor he hopes won't be used.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically accepts the absurd plan to fake a good impression, joking that the replacement actors shouldn't be the famously rugged-looking Gerard Depardieu.
summary: Ahead of an executive visit, the staff are expected to ditch real work and put on a staged show, even swapping in actors for unattractive employees.

file: 1994/1994-02-19_computer_deluxe_state of the art computer_feel happy_song_sing a song_no need people_technology.gif
title: Dilbert Sings About Needing No People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: 35 inch monitor, 20 megs of RAM, 1.2 gigabytes of hard disk space...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel a song coming on.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People... who don't need people... are the ha-a-a-ppiest people.

situation: Dilbert sits at his desk admiring his new high-end computer, thinking about its impressive specifications. Delighted, he feels a song coming on and then bursts into song with arms spread wide, singing that people who don't need people are the happiest people.
punchline: Dilbert is so thrilled with his powerful computer that he sings a parody of 'People' (people who need people) to say he no longer needs human company, which pokes fun at tech-obsessed isolation.
summary: A man overjoyed by his souped-up new computer joyfully serenades himself with a twisted love song about not needing anyone else.

file: 1994/1994-11-16_project report_thick binder_foot rest_annual performance_appraisel.gif
title: Project Report Becomes Boss's Footrest

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you see my project report yet? It's in a big thick binder.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm using it as a foot rest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You never want to hear the words "foot rest" the day before your annual performance appraisal.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss whether he has looked at the project report Dilbert put in a big thick binder. The boss casually reveals he has been using the binder as a foot rest. Dilbert, standing with his briefcase, grimly notes that this is a bad sign the day before his annual performance appraisal.
punchline: The boss's use of Dilbert's hard work as a foot rest shows he values it as little more than furniture, which bodes poorly for Dilbert's performance review.
summary: A employee's carefully compiled report is treated by his manager as a place to rest his feet, just before review time.

file: 1994/1994-04-18_press release_dsn_bid 50 million_hollywood studio_providing static_channels_dogbert_static netowrk.gif
title: Dogbert's Static Network Acquisition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the press release about our bid to buy "DSN" for fifty billion dollars.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: DSN is the Hollywood studio that provides static to all the channels that would otherwise be blank.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The "Dogbert Static Network"?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Talk to me, babe.

setting: Office meeting area, then Dilbert's home
situation: The Boss hands out a press release announcing a fifty-billion-dollar bid to buy a Hollywood studio called DSN, explaining that it supplies static to channels that would otherwise be blank. Dilbert, carrying a suitcase, realizes the initials stand for the Dogbert Static Network. Dogbert lounges in sunglasses, answering with a Hollywood-style greeting.
punchline: Dogbert has built a ridiculous business selling TV static, and the company is about to pay fifty billion dollars for it.
summary: A company plans a massive purchase of a studio that sells empty TV static, only for Dilbert to discover his own dog is behind it.

file: 1994/1994-04-06_about co workers_donuts_get prompted_say bad things_weight_woman_medical.gif
title: Dilbert Insults Coworker, Gets Chair Thrown

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you want to get promoted, say bad things about your co-workers so you look better by comparison.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Geez, Lisa, it looks like you've been hitting the donuts pretty hard lately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heh-heh... Big things are coming my way soon.

setting: Office, at a desk and in a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Dogbert advises Dilbert that putting down coworkers will make him look better and get him promoted. Dilbert immediately tries it on a coworker named Lisa by mocking her weight. In the last panel he smugly thinks big things are coming his way, while an office chair flies at him.
punchline: The 'big things' coming Dilbert's way are not a promotion but a chair thrown at him in retaliation for his insult.
summary: After taking Dogbert's backstabbing career tip too literally, Dilbert insults a coworker and gets an airborne chair for his trouble.

file: 1994/1994-08-09_cranky_discover religion_physical until marriage_unitarian_liz_dilbert serene_dogbert talks liz.gif
title: Dilbert's Suspicious Serenity Explained

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't understand something, Liz. You told Dilbert you don't want to be physical until after marriage...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I would expect him to be cranky around the house, yet he's quite relaxed... serene. I don't see how...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Unless...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Did you discover religion?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'm a Unitarian.

setting: A park bench outdoors, then Dilbert seated in a pink-background scene
situation: Dogbert sits on a park bench beside Liz and puzzles over why Dilbert is so calm when she has told him she wants to wait until marriage to be physical. Dogbert hints at an explanation, then asks Dilbert if he has found religion. Dilbert answers that he thinks he is a Unitarian.
punchline: Dilbert's unexpectedly peaceful mood is implied to come from private self-gratification, and he disguises the admission with a pun on 'Unitarian' (sounding like 'urinarian' or a solo act).
summary: A suspiciously relaxed boyfriend gives a euphemistic answer when his dog asks why abstinence hasn't made him cranky.

file: 1994/1994-11-12_donuts_contains memo_fired_termination notice_humane_ate the memo_wally_3 donuts.gif
title: Donut Lottery Layoff Memo

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: One of these donuts contains a memo which fires the recipient.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This seemed like the most humane way to reduce head count.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How was your donut?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The first two were great. The third was papery.

setting: Conference room and hallway outside it
situation: The Boss gathers the staff around a table and offers a box of donuts, one of which hides a memo firing whoever gets it. He calls this the most humane way to cut head count. Afterward, Dilbert asks Wally about his donut, and Wally reveals he took three and the last one was papery.
punchline: Wally, who is always eager for free food, ate three donuts and apparently swallowed the termination memo without noticing, so the firing failed or went unnoticed.
summary: A manager hides a pink slip inside one donut as a gentle layoff method, but a greedy employee accidentally eats it.

file: 1994/1994-07-19_areodynamic_blow on me_handy_ratbert_smart_attractive.gif
title: Ratbert Claims To Be Aerodynamic

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I may not be smart and I may not be attractive...

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: But I AM aerodynamic!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That might come in handy in a minute.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Blow on me.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, on the couch
situation: Ratbert stands on the back of the couch next to Dilbert, who is typing on his laptop. Ratbert admits he is neither smart nor attractive but proudly strikes a streamlined pose and declares himself aerodynamic. Dilbert says that might be useful soon, and Ratbert asks to be blown on, apparently expecting to be sent flying.
punchline: Ratbert's only self-proclaimed virtue is aerodynamics, which he cheerfully offers up as a reason to be blown across the room, implying he expects to be thrown or launched.
summary: A self-deprecating little rat brags about his one strength, being streamlined, and invites his owner to send him sailing through the air.

file: 1994/1994-03-17_constant reorgnizing_needs of employees_spare parts_liver_jose in accounting.gif
title: Boss Harvests Dilbert's Liver Preemptively

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: These constant reorganizations do not take into consideration the needs of the employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to use you for spare parts. Your liver will be sent to José in accounting, immediately.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: José has a bad liver?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, but why take a chance?

situation: Dilbert complains to the Boss that constant reorganizations ignore employees' needs. The Boss responds by announcing that Dilbert will be used for spare parts, with his liver going to José in accounting. When Dilbert asks if José is ill, the Boss admits he isn't, but says he wants the organ transplanted just in case.
punchline: The Boss literally treats employees as disposable resources, harvesting an organ for a coworker who doesn't even need it, proving the point that management ignores employees' needs.
summary: A worker's gripe about reshuffling gets a grimly absurd answer when his manager decides to give his organs away as a precaution.

file: 1994/1994-08-15_management fast tracker_deliver big report_ceo_fax_shredder_tricked_punked_contempt.gif
title: Fast-Tracker Faxes Report Into Shredder

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, Matt. How's our favorite management fast-tracker?

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: Great! I've got two minutes to deliver my big report to our CEO. Can you tell me where the fax is?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oops, I'm wrong. That's the shredder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He'll go far in this company.

situation: A coworker greets Matt, an ambitious young manager, with mock friendliness. Matt says he has two minutes to get his big report to the CEO and asks where the fax machine is. The coworker sends him to the shredder, which destroys the report, and Dilbert sarcastically comments on Matt's prospects.
punchline: Matt's gullibility, which gets his report shredded, is exactly the trait that wins promotions in this company, so Dilbert sarcastically predicts he'll go far.
summary: A rising young manager is misdirected to a paper shredder instead of the fax machine, and Dilbert quips that such a person is destined for corporate success.

file: 1994/1994-04-30_senior executive_bad deciosn_end careers_challenging_decison_great idea_mixed signals_pull neckties_hurts.gif
title: Challenging The Executive's Bad Decision

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If we know our senior executive is making a bad decision, shouldn't we tell her?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hmm, yes. Let's end our careers by challenging a decision that won't change. That's a great idea.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting mixed signals here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And let's pull our neckties until it hurts!

situation: Dilbert asks a coworker whether they should warn their senior executive about a bad decision she is making. The coworker replies with heavy sarcasm, saying that doing so would only end their careers since the decision won't change. When Dilbert says he's getting mixed signals, the coworker sarcastically adds that they should also yank their neckties until it hurts.
punchline: The coworker sarcastically equates challenging an executive's unchangeable decision with self-harm, implying that speaking up is pointless and career-ending.
summary: A coworker mocks Dilbert's honest impulse to question a superior by comparing it to pointlessly hurting yourself.

file: 1994/1994-02-12_baby dogbert_ceramic figurine_first aid_vomiting_focus group_disater_inmate cuteness_profit.gif
title: Baby Dogbert Figurine Induces Vomiting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I found a way to profit from my inate cuteness.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Introducing the limited edition "Baby Dogbert" ceramic figurine!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see — it's a first aid device to induce vomiting.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The focus group was a disaster.

situation: Dogbert announces he has found a way to profit from his cuteness and shows off a ceramic figurine of himself as a baby. Dilbert examines the figurine and concludes it is a first aid device for inducing vomiting. Dogbert admits the focus group went badly.
punchline: The 'cute' Baby Dogbert figurine is so unappealing that Dilbert sees it as something that would make you vomit, which is exactly how the focus group reacted.
summary: Dogbert tries to cash in on his adorableness with a collectible figurine, but it turns out to be nauseating rather than charming.

file: 1994/1994-12-02_dogberts tech support_dog_rat_phone call_customer_question_compensate tiny brain_to busy_play dead_animals.gif
title: Tech Support Dodges Work With Transfers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Please wait while I consult with somebody who has your exact same problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How do you compensate for a tiny brain, Ratbert?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I just say I'm way too busy to learn. Then I get somebody else to do my work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to transfer you to an expert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I pretend to be dead.

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center office, at desks with phones
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support line, puts a caller on hold, supposedly to consult someone with the same problem. He instead asks Ratbert, a fellow support worker, how he copes with having a tiny brain. Ratbert explains he avoids learning and offloads work to others, then Dogbert transfers the caller while Ratbert adds that he sometimes plays dead.
punchline: The tech support staff have no real expertise, so they survive by stalling customers, passing them along to someone else, and feigning incapacity to avoid doing any actual work.
summary: Two clueless help desk employees swap tricks for avoiding customers' problems, revealing that nobody there actually knows how to fix anything.

file: 1994/1994-01-20_synthetic pheremone_irresitable_cafe_waiter_paid off_kill_mace myself.gif
title: Pheromone Date Needs Waiter Insurance

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing a synthetic pheremone scent that makes me irresistible. It should kick in any minute.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Uh-oh

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Waiter! Here's three hundred dollars. If I start to flirt with him, kill him!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far so good

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I've got to... mace... myself...

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert proudly tells his date at a restaurant that he is wearing a synthetic pheromone scent that makes him irresistible. Alarmed, she hands the waiter three hundred dollars and tells him to kill her if she starts flirting with him. The pheromone ends up affecting the waiter, who is smitten with a heart over his head, while Dilbert optimistically thinks things are going well and the date reaches for mace to defend herself from her own attraction.
punchline: Dilbert's pheromone does work, but on the waiter and the date's own reaction, not in the way he hoped, and the date is so afraid of becoming attracted to him that she plans to mace herself.
summary: A man's attempt to seduce his dinner companion with a lab-made attraction scent backfires when she bribes the waiter to stop her and the scent affects the wrong person.

file: 1994/1994-06-13_emergency assignment_critical_moot_crisis_moots.gif
title: Everything Is Urgent Until Moot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Emergency assignment!! Urgent! Urgent!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's only critical because everything sits on your desk until it either becomes moot or a crisis.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I'm giving him the moots.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and the Boss's desk
situation: The Boss rushes up to Dilbert waving a paper and shouting that it is an urgent emergency assignment. Dilbert points out that the task only became critical because the Boss let work pile up until it was either moot or a crisis. The Boss, seated at a desk with stacks labeled Aging, Crises and Moot, resolves to hand Dilbert the moot pile from now on.
punchline: Instead of fixing his habit of procrastinating, the Boss takes Dilbert's criticism as a cue to dump the useless 'moot' work on him.
summary: A boss who lets tasks rot until they become emergencies responds to criticism by deciding to assign his employee the already-pointless ones.

file: 1994/1994-08-14_boyfriend-girlfreind_buddies_close freinds_friends explined_mans best freind_platonic friends_work friends.gif
title: Friends Explained: Many Kinds of Friendship

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Friends" explained

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A very special "Dilbert"

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Close friends

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: May I borrow your gum?

transcript.speaker: Friend
transcript.text: Sure. Reach in and take what you need.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Buddies"

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Can I borrow your hammer?

transcript.speaker: Buddy
transcript.text: Why not use your forehead as usual?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Work friends

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, how's your wife?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Dead. Same as last week.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Boyfriend/Girlfriend (stereotypical view)

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Love

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Lust

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Boyfriend/Girlfriend (modern correct view)

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Lust

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Television

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Platonic friends

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Television?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Lust

transcript.text: Man's best friend

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: By my estimate there are 2.6 billion females who do not desire you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Name them.

setting: Series of vignettes in homes, couches and a conference table at work
situation: Dogbert presents a special Dilbert strip explaining different kinds of friendship through a series of short vignettes. Close friends and buddies trade barbed insults, work friends are callous about a dead wife, and couples and platonic friends have mismatched thoughts of love, lust and television. In the final panel Dogbert, as man's best friend, tells Dilbert how many women don't desire him.
punchline: Every kind of friendship is defined by insults, indifference or mismatched desires, and even man's best friend gleefully points out Dilbert's romantic hopelessness.
summary: A tour of friendship types reveals that each one is built on mockery, apathy or crossed wires, ending with Dogbert gently crushing Dilbert's love life.

file: 1994/1994-02-23_potluck lunch_bring bags_salt_ice_beverage_mineral water.gif
title: Potluck With Only Ice and Salt

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We've reached a new low in the "potluck lunch" sign-up.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Twelve people signed up to bring bags of ice and one person is bringing salt.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I need one of you to at least bring a beverage.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Put me down for one bag of sparkling mineral water.

situation: Carol, holding the sign-up sheet for the office potluck lunch, complains that nobody has signed up to bring real food, with twelve people bringing ice and one bringing salt. She asks someone to at least bring a drink. Wally cheerfully volunteers a bag of sparkling mineral water, which is a minimal-effort contribution.
punchline: Even when asked for a real contribution, Wally offers the laziest possible option, showing how little effort anyone will put into the potluck.
summary: A frustrated organizer finds that her potluck is shaping up to be all ice and salt, and the one volunteer for drinks picks the easiest store-bought item.

file: 1994/1994-04-21_big money_deal_dog_dogbert_executive_mercury dimes_negotiate_static network_stock_static for sale_animals.gif
title: Selling Static for Worthless Stock

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: We'll give you sixty billion for the "Dogbert Static Network." Half of that will be stock in our company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Who would want stock in a company that would pay sixty billion for static?

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Not us. That's the point.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like it all in Mercury dimes.

situation: An executive in a suit offers Dogbert sixty billion for his "Dogbert Static Network," with half of the payment in stock in the executive's own company. Dogbert points out that nobody would want stock in a company foolish enough to pay that much for static. The executive admits that is exactly why they are paying in stock, so Dogbert asks for the whole amount in Mercury dimes instead.
punchline: The buyer cheerfully admits their own company stock is worthless, so Dogbert demands payment in valuable Mercury dimes (collectible silver coins) rather than the overvalued shares.
summary: A buyer tries to pay an absurd price for nothing in inflated shares, but Dogbert sees through the scheme and insists on real, collectible coins.

file: 1994/1994-07-29_summarized accomplishments_ceo_converts waste into penicillain_calirovoyant_invented wool_sheep_believe me.gif
title: Dilbert's Accomplishments Include Inventing Wool

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you summarized your accomplishments for our CEO?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Almost done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay — my body converts toxic waste into penicillin, I'm clairvoyant, and I invented wool.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought sheep invented wool.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who are you going to believe, them or me?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he has written up his accomplishments for the CEO. Dilbert reads out an absurd list of fabricated achievements, including turning toxic waste into penicillin and inventing wool. When the Boss points out that sheep invented wool, Dilbert brazenly dismisses the objection.
punchline: Dilbert exaggerates his accomplishments to ridiculous, easily disproved extremes and then asks the Boss to trust him over the sheep, mocking self-promotional performance reviews.
summary: Asked to write up his career highlights, Dilbert claims outlandish feats and cheekily challenges his boss to doubt him over a flock of sheep.

file: 1994/1994-02-03_evil demons_stupidity_saint dogbert_image_protect and wathc_career change_out demons of stupid.gif
title: Saint Dogbert Exorcises Workplace Stupidity

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is your job plagued by the evil demons of stupidity?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Simply affix this image of Saint Dogbert to every document, cubicle or computer you want to protect and watch your career begin to change!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Out out!! You demons of stupidity!!

setting: Plain tan background, no office shown; Dogbert as a saint figure
situation: Dogbert, dressed as Saint Dogbert in a tall yellow mitre and holding a small scepter, pitches a protective talisman like a TV infomercial. He tells viewers to stick his image on documents, cubicles or computers, then waves the scepter to banish the demons of stupidity.
punchline: Dogbert is selling a superstitious charm to cure workplace stupidity, mocking people who look for magical rather than practical fixes to organizational incompetence.
summary: Playing a holy figure, Dogbert hawks a sticker-sized blessing that supposedly drives idiocy away from your work.

file: 1994/1994-08-28_acute_acute design flaw_crucial_feminist questions word_other monitor_poor choice_sexist puns_word means_words_apology.gif
title: Acute Design Flaw Sparks Accusation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The image is fuzzy because the monitor has an acute design flaw.

transcript.speaker: Woman co-worker
transcript.text: Acute? That's an unusual choice of words.

transcript.speaker: Woman co-worker
transcript.text: Would you have said "acute" to a male co-worker? I think not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It means crucial, that's all!!

transcript.speaker: Woman co-worker
transcript.text: I know what the word means! Do you think I don't see right through your sexist puns?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No! I swear, it was just a poor choice of words!!

transcript.speaker: Woman co-worker
transcript.text: Well... okay. I accept your apology. This time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, what's wrong with the other monitor?

transcript.speaker: Woman co-worker
transcript.text: Which?

setting: Office cubicle with a computer monitor
situation: Dilbert tells a female co-worker that a monitor's fuzzy image is caused by an acute design flaw. She takes offense, accusing him of making a sexist pun on 'a cute' and refusing to accept his explanation that the word means crucial. He ends up apologizing, then asks about the other monitor, and she replies with a single word that turns it into another pun.
punchline: After being scolded for an accidental pun on 'a cute', Dilbert asks about the other monitor, and her reply 'Which?' is itself a pun on 'witch', turning the accusation back on her.
summary: A harmless technical remark gets treated as a hidden insult, and the accuser then makes a pun of her own.

file: 1994/1994-04-15_delay_beta trial_exploding_engineers_pessimists_foucs_positive aspects_trial_hassle_non disclosure_agreements.gif
title: Exploding Beta Has Positive Aspects

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've got to delay the beta trial with customers until we figure out why it keeps exploding!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You engineers are such pessimists. Just once, try to focus on the positive aspects of the trial!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We won't need to hassle with "non-disclosure agreements."
