situation: Dilbert tells his boss that the beta trial must be delayed because the product keeps exploding. The boss accuses engineers of pessimism and tells Dilbert to focus on the positives. Dilbert, thinking it over at his computer, finds a grim upside: no one will survive to need a non-disclosure agreement.
punchline: The only 'positive' about a product that explodes on customers is that they won't be around to need non-disclosure agreements, implying the customers would be killed.
summary: When ordered to look on the bright side of a dangerously exploding product, an engineer darkly concludes that dead customers can't leak secrets.

file: 1994/1994-03-11_no raise_engineers wuit_the goal_reduce headcount_smart people leave_organize pot luck.gif
title: Layoffs Disguised as Raise Freeze

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm telling you — if nobody gets a raise, half of the engineers will quit!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the goal. We're trying to reduce headcount by fifty percent.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But all the smart people will leave!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you mind organizing a goodbye potluck lunch for them?

situation: Dilbert warns his boss that denying everyone a raise will cause half the engineers to quit. The boss calmly says that is exactly the intention, since the company wants to cut headcount by fifty percent. When Dilbert points out the smart people will be the ones to leave, the boss asks him to organize a goodbye potluck for them.
punchline: Management is deliberately using a raise freeze to force out staff, ignores that the best talent will leave first, and then casually asks Dilbert to throw the departing employees a farewell lunch.
summary: A boss welcomes the mass resignations that a pay freeze will trigger and then asks the warning employee to plan the send-off party.

file: 1994/1994-05-11_project leader_dogcart consulting_shall do bidding_endless variety_expediations_slab of liver_external brain pack_career low.gif
title: Ratbert Leads With External Brain

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm the project leader for the Dogbert Consulting Company. You simple employees shall do my bidding.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'll be sending you on an endless variety of data-gathering expeditions. That will keep you busy while I do the thinking.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: By the way, this may look like a slab of liver but it's an external brain pack.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My career just reached an all time low.

situation: Ratbert, wearing a strange pack on his back, announces at a conference table that he is project leader for Dogbert's consulting company. He tells Dilbert and Wally they will do his bidding and run data-gathering errands while he does the thinking. He then reveals that his 'brain' is an external pack resembling a slab of liver, leaving Dilbert to reflect on how low his career has sunk.
punchline: Dilbert's career has sunk so far that he is now taking orders from a rat whose thinking is done by a slab of liver strapped to his back.
summary: A tiny rodent boss delegates all the legwork to his human underlings and admits his intellect comes from a strapped-on organ.

file: 1994/1994-07-22_market research_market segment_wild fungi_pencil erasers_head rubbed_piece of paper.gif
title: Ratbert Surveyed as Pencil Eraser

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like your opinion for my market research, Ratbert.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Me?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've lumped you in the market segment that includes wild fungi and pencil erasers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Question one: Would you enjoy having your head rubbed vigorously on a piece of paper?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Who wouldn't?

setting: A living room with a green couch
situation: Dogbert holds a clipboard and conducts a market research survey on Ratbert, who is sitting on the couch. Dogbert explains that Ratbert has been grouped into a market segment with wild fungi and pencil erasers. The first survey question asks whether he would enjoy having his head rubbed vigorously on paper, and Ratbert answers enthusiastically.
punchline: Ratbert is so naive that he cheerfully agrees to a question that treats him like a pencil eraser, showing how absurd and demeaning market segmentation can be.
summary: Dogbert surveys Ratbert after sorting him into an absurd consumer category, and the little guy happily plays along with a ridiculous question.

file: 1994/1994-03-16_blind ambition_chips & dips_food services_new name_procurement_the unled_new department.gif
title: Naming the Reorganized Department

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll need a name for the newly reorganized department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The name should reflect how I've seamlessly integrated engineering with food services and procurement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about "Chips and Dips"?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Blind Ambition"

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: "The Unled"

setting: Conference room during a department meeting
situation: The Boss tells his team that the newly reorganized department needs a name, one that celebrates how he merged engineering with food services and procurement. Dilbert and two coworkers respond with suggestions that mock the absurd reorganization and the boss's leadership.
punchline: The employees' name suggestions "Chips and Dips," "Blind Ambition," and "The Unled" openly ridicule the nonsensical merger and the boss's incompetent management while he expects praise.
summary: After mashing unrelated groups into one department, a manager asks for a flattering name and gets sarcastic jabs from his staff instead.

file: 1994/1994-06-30_does not meet needs_publishing needs_plot was lame_hated characters_association_insulting author_mean publisher_insulting publisher.gif
title: Dogbert's Brutal Rejection Letter

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Publisher

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dear Tim, your book does not meet our current publishing needs.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your plot was lame and I hated your characters. And by association I have come to hate you too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For safety reasons, I hired an illiterate person to rip up your manuscript. I would use the return envelope you provided but I'm afraid you might have licked the stamps.

setting: Dogbert's publishing office, at a computer
situation: Dogbert, acting as a book publisher, types a rejection letter to an aspiring author named Tim. The letter starts with the standard polite line, then turns into a personal attack on the plot, the characters and Tim himself. It ends with Dogbert explaining that the manuscript was destroyed and not returned because Tim might have licked the stamps.
punchline: A normally polite form-rejection letter becomes a stream of insults, ending with the claim that the author is too disgusting to touch his own stamps.
summary: A canine publisher turns a routine manuscript rejection into a nasty, germ-fearing takedown of the hopeful writer.

file: 1994/1994-05-02_meeting_bathroom_business.gif
title: Staff Meeting At My House

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: We could have our next all-day staff meeting at my house.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Do you have actual furniture?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Somebody will have to sit in the bathroom.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I call bathroom.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: At a staff meeting, a coworker suggests holding the next all-day meeting at her house. Alice asks whether she has real furniture, and Dilbert notes that someone will have to sit in the bathroom. Wally immediately claims the bathroom for himself.
punchline: Wally eagerly volunteers for the bathroom seat because it would let him escape the all-day meeting in private.
summary: A proposal to host a marathon meeting at someone's home leads to a scramble for the one seat where nobody can see you.

file: 1994/1994-04-27_upgrade boss computer_cardboard prop_came with desk_new mother board_new desk_needs_no actual computer.gif
title: Boss's Cardboard Computer Needs Desk

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to help me upgrade the computer in my office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The computer in your office is a cardboard prop that came with your desk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, I need a new motherboard, right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, you need a new desk.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to help him upgrade the computer in his office. Dilbert reveals that the machine is merely a cardboard prop that shipped with the desk. The Boss, still missing the point, asks if he needs a new motherboard, and Dilbert tells him he needs a new desk.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he has never noticed his computer is fake, and he still thinks a hardware component would fix it, when the only real remedy is replacing the desk the prop came with.
summary: A manager wants his computer upgraded, only to learn it was never a real computer at all.

file: 1994/1994-12-04_restaurant trip_distractions_people disperse_alice bathroom_wally calls_ted mail letters_eat dinner.gif
title: Simple Lunch Outing Falls Apart

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're waiting for Ted, then we can head for the restaurant.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: While we're waiting, I'll return a few phone calls.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Let's go! Hey, where's Wally?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The chain reaction has begun.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why can't we do this simple thing?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll be in the ladies room.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Where's Alice?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I've got to mail a letter. I'll take my car and meet you there.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can make some calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're the only one who knows which restaurant we're going to!

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Alice knows where it is. Tell her it's the one with the food.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Has your team finished engineering the new missile guidance chip?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think it's time to give peace a chance.

setting: Office hallway, just before a group lunch outing
situation: Dilbert tries to get a group of coworkers to leave together for a restaurant, but each person finds an excuse to wander off: Wally makes phone calls, Alice goes to the ladies room, and Ted goes to mail a letter. Ted's vague directions to the restaurant add to the chaos. Dilbert is so frustrated that when an engineer asks about a missile guidance chip, he suddenly turns pacifist.
punchline: After failing to organize even a simple lunch outing, Dilbert concludes that his team is too incompetent to build missile guidance and says it's time to give peace a chance.
summary: A trivial group lunch dissolves into scattered errands, leaving one man so disillusioned about his colleagues' abilities that he questions building weapons at all.

file: 1994/1994-06-27_book publishing_reject people_dismiss lifes work_gesture_witty comment_not a people person_dog_animals.gif
title: Dogbert Plans Rejecting Authors for Fun

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to start my own book publishing company so I can reject people all day long.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll dismiss their life's work with a gesture and a witty comment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bottom line, I'm just not a people person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch next to Dilbert and announces plans to start a book publishing company. His motivation is the chance to reject aspiring authors all day with a wave of the hand and a clever quip. He concludes that he is not a people person, and Dilbert dryly says he has noticed.
punchline: Dogbert's gleeful plan to crush authors' dreams proves he is unsuited to dealing with people, which Dilbert deadpans he already knew.
summary: Dogbert reveals he wants to run a publishing house purely for the joy of dismissing writers, then admits people skills aren't his strength.

file: 1994/1994-03-19_bad news_break gradually_budget worked on_build up_effort_reorganizing dept._worthless_you're fired.gif
title: Breaking Bad News Gradually, Then Firing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Susan, I'm reorganizing the department again. The budget you worked on for months is now worthless.

transcript.speaker: Susan
transcript.text: I think when you have bad news you should make an effort to break it gradually, maybe build up to it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, that reminds me: you're fired.

situation: The Boss tells Susan, an employee, that he is reorganizing the department and that the budget she spent months on is now worthless. Susan suggests he should deliver bad news gradually and build up to it. The Boss takes the advice literally and adds that she is fired.
punchline: The Boss treats Susan's request to soften bad news as a cue to deliver even worse news, firing her in a deliberately escalating fashion.
summary: A manager responds to an employee's plea for gentler bad news by piling on a termination as the next installment.

file: 1994/1994-09-30_after every typo_point and click_poorly documented commands_reboot_interface.gif
title: Hostile Interface Chosen Over Usability

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could design the product with a simple point-and-click interface...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or we could require the user to choose among thousands of poorly documented commands, each of which must be typed exactly right on the first try.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Bear in mind, we'll never meet a customer ourselves.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make it so they have to reboot after every typo.

setting: Dilbert's office, at his desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert presents his boss with two design options for a product: an easy point-and-click interface or a punishing command-line system with thousands of poorly documented commands. He adds that they will never have to meet a customer. The boss gleefully picks the worse option and asks for a forced reboot after every typo.
punchline: Because the company never has to face its customers, the boss deliberately chooses the most user-hostile design and even makes it worse.
summary: Offered a friendly design or a miserable one, the boss cheerfully opts for misery since nobody in the company will ever meet the people suffering through it.

file: 1994/1994-05-07_boss made pass_cat ate ring_family in coma_irs audit_seek relief_woes_anti woe cologne.gif
title: Anti-Woe Cologne Blocks Coworker's Complaints

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm going to seek relief from my many woes by sharing them with you.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: My entire family is in a coma... The cat ate my wedding ring... The IRS is auditing us... My boss made a pass at me...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: It isn't working. You aren't absorbing my woes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing anti-woe cologne.

situation: A coworker announces she will relieve her troubles by dumping them on Dilbert, who keeps typing at his computer. She rattles off a long list of calamities, including a family in comas, a cat that ate her ring, an IRS audit and a boss's advances. She complains that he isn't absorbing her woes, and he explains he is wearing anti-woe cologne.
punchline: Dilbert deadpans that he has protected himself from other people's problems with a fictitious cologne, showing how little he wants to be emotionally burdened by a coworker's venting.
summary: A distraught coworker unloads a catalogue of disasters on an unresponsive Dilbert, who blames his indifference on a repellent fragrance.

file: 1994/1994-12-25_time to go_working all night_extra work_not better off_fixed mistakes_duct tape_chair_uncanny_duck tape cureall.gif
title: Duct-Taping the Overeager Overworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's seven o'clock, Ed. Time to call it a night.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: I'm planning to work all night.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: I'm not very bright so I work long hours to compensate.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ed, we're not better off when you do extra work.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: I'm not quite following your logic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We all worked late undoing what you did yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We voted to duct-tape you to your chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's uncanny how many problems you can solve with duct tape.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sometimes I use it instead of underwear.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker named Ed it's time to go home, but Ed insists on working all night to make up for not being very bright. Dilbert explains that the team had to stay late fixing Ed's mistakes from the previous day. The team then votes to duct-tape Ed to his chair to stop him from doing more damage.
punchline: Ed's extra effort actually creates more problems than it solves, so his coworkers resort to physically restraining him with duct tape, with Wally adding an absurd quip about using duct tape as underwear.
summary: A well-meaning but error-prone employee is physically bound by his colleagues so he can't keep making extra messes after hours.

file: 1994/1994-04-05_corporate politics_waste basket_teach everything_promoted level.gif
title: Wastebasket Lessons in Office Politics

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want you to teach me everything you know about corporate politics so I can get promoted to your level.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: To truly understand office politics you must wear a waste basket on your head for one full day.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does this really work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It works for me.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss to teach him everything about corporate politics so he can be promoted to the Boss's level. The Boss tells him he must wear a waste basket on his head for a full day. Later, Dilbert, wearing the waste basket, asks if this really works, and the Boss says it works for him.
punchline: The Boss's own success in management is implied to come from being oblivious or having his head in a waste basket, suggesting that promotion rewards cluelessness rather than skill.
summary: Seeking a promotion, an eager employee follows his superior's absurd advice and learns that the boss's own career rests on dubious foundations.

file: 1994/1994-09-24_confidential questionnaire_management class_style of management_instructor sees_trusts me_sneaked a look_at answers_ratings.gif
title: Boss Reads Confidential Management Questionnaire

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I filled out the confidential questionnaire about your style of management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope it's useful for that management class you're taking. Only your instructor sees those, right?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I played that about right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh, good marks! And it says he trusts me too!

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a questionnaire rating his management style, saying it is confidential and only for his management class instructor. The Boss says 'right' while taking the envelope. In the last panel Dilbert thinks he played it well, while the Boss is heard reading the answers and gloating over the good marks.
punchline: Dilbert gave flattering ratings because he suspected the Boss would read the supposedly confidential questionnaire, and the Boss's delight proves him right.
summary: An employee deliberately flatters his manager on a supposedly private evaluation, correctly predicting the manager will peek at it.

file: 1994/1994-02-16_appointment_booked_every yahoo_set priorities_calendar.gif
title: Boss Prioritizes Nothing, Calendar Overbooked

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As the leader of this organization it's my job to set priorities.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Here's your calendar. I booked you through next year with every yahoo who could dial your number.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe I'll call this a priority.

situation: The Boss thinks to himself that setting priorities is his job as leader. His secretary Carol hands him a calendar she has filled for the next year with appointments from anyone who called. The Boss, seated at his desk, thinks he might call this a priority while an employee gestures at him.
punchline: The Boss's idea of setting priorities is to simply declare whatever his assistant has randomly scheduled to be the priority, showing he does no real prioritizing at all.
summary: A manager who claims leadership means choosing priorities is handed an indiscriminately packed schedule and decides to just label it his priority.

file: 1994/1994-07-06_benefits dept_retire now_haitian penny stocks_change in tone_letter about pension_contrarain investor.gif
title: Retire Now Or Haitian Penny Stocks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... It's never good when we get mail from the Benefits Department.

transcript.speaker: Letter
transcript.text: "Retire now or we'll invest your entire pension in Haitian penny stocks."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you noticed a change in tone lately?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Little do they know I'm a contrarian investor.

situation: Dilbert and Wally each receive a letter from the Benefits Department. The letter threatens that unless employees retire immediately, the company will invest their entire pension in Haitian penny stocks. Dilbert remarks on the hostile tone of recent company communications, while Wally smugly claims the threat won't bother him.
punchline: Wally claims the company's threat to gamble away his pension on junk stocks doesn't scare him because he's a contrarian investor, a way of spinning a terrible risk into a clever strategy while missing the point that it's the company forcing people out.
summary: A threatening pension letter tries to push employees into early retirement, but one coworker boasts that he'd actually welcome the doomed investments.

file: 1994/1994-11-07_dignity_creativity_precious earth_blood drive_three pint minimum.gif
title: Mandatory Blood Drive After Everything Taken

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This job has taken my dignity, my self-esteem, my creativity and my precious time on this earth.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You've taken all I have! There's nothing left to give!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The blood drive is next week. This year it's mandatory... and a three-pint minimum.

situation: At a meeting table, an employee complains that his job has stripped him of his dignity, self-esteem, creativity and time, then shouts that he has nothing left to give. The Boss, reading from a paper, calmly announces that the company blood drive is next week and is now mandatory with a three-pint minimum.
punchline: Just when the employee says he has nothing left to give, management finds something else to take: his blood, by force.
summary: A worn-down worker declares the company has drained him of everything, and his boss responds by announcing a compulsory blood donation.

file: 1994/1994-02-06_broken fax_copier_electronic mail_incompatible software_lan rewired_no toner_technology.gif
title: Technology Fails, Dilbert Must Read Aloud

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I tried to fax it but our fax machine is broken.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would send it by modem but my communication software is incompatible with my new system software upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... our electronic mail systems are incompatible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mail it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've only got one copy and our copier is out of toner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, normally I could print another one but our LAN is being rewired.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could just read it to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I describe how technology improves our lives by... Yeah, I'll hold.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dang.

situation: Dilbert is on the phone trying to get a document to someone, and every technological method fails: the fax is broken, his modem software is incompatible, the email systems don't match, the copier is out of toner and the LAN is being rewired. He finally resorts to reading the document aloud over the phone, only to be put on hold and then cut off.
punchline: The document is titled 'how technology improves our lives', yet technology fails at every step and even the low-tech phone fallback goes wrong.
summary: After every gadget in the office lets him down, a man ends up reading aloud a report praising technology, and even the phone call drops.

file: 1994/1994-09-21_losing life support_red alert_scanning_tractor beam_trade show.gif
title: Dilbert Trapped by Trade Show Vendor

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the trade show...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. A vendor is scanning me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm caught in a tractor beam! Red alert! Red alert!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Losing life support systems...

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: ... and it can even calculate fractions!

situation: Dilbert walks through a trade show crowd and notices a vendor scanning his badge. The vendor grabs him with the badge scanner's cord, which Dilbert imagines as a sci-fi tractor beam. By the end Dilbert is dozing off from boredom while the vendor pitches a product feature.
punchline: A vendor's sales pitch is so tedious that Dilbert feels like he is being abducted and his life support is failing, and the feature being touted (calculating fractions) is laughably unimpressive.
summary: A trade show salesman reels in an unwilling Dilbert with a badge scanner and bores him into a stupor with a feeble product boast.

file: 1994/1994-10-29_hate finance guy_rigid_inflexible_not team player_extra napkin_lunch room talk.gif
title: Hating the New Finance Guy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you started to hate the new finance guy yet?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Yeah. I started yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He seems so rigid.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Rigid and inflexible. Not a team player.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you have an extra napkin?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I won't really know until I'm done.

setting: Office lunch table or break room
situation: Dilbert and two coworkers eat lunch together at a table. Dilbert asks a bald, glasses-wearing coworker whether he has started to hate the new finance guy, and the coworker replies that he began yesterday while they trade complaints about the man's rigidity. Dilbert then asks for a spare napkin, and the coworker's answer shows he is still hung up on the finance guy's rigid, inflexible trait.
punchline: The coworker answers Dilbert's napkin request in the same stiff, literal way he just criticized the finance guy for, so he turns out to be rigid and inflexible himself, and the strip also suggests the office complaining is just lunchtime gossip.
summary: Two colleagues gripe about a rigid new hire over lunch, then one responds to a simple napkin request with equally stiff literalism.

file: 1994/1994-09-04_cute dog_dilbert attacks girl_dilbert exercises_flirt_mean_runs away_tease_the word no.gif
title: Dogbert Lures Women Into Dilbert's Path

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Pssst.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're probably noticing how soft and cute I am.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Aww! You're adorable! Let me give you a little pet on the head.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I couldn't. I'm too shy.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Shy? That is just so cute. I have to pet you now.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Come here, you little tease! You know you'll like it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't you understand the word "no"?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could do this all day long.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How about the redhead?

setting: A grassy park or jogging path
situation: Dogbert hides in the grass and calls out to a passing woman jogger, playing up how cute and soft he is. She insists on petting him despite his claims of shyness and chases him down, only for Dilbert to step in and angrily scold her for ignoring "no." Dilbert, happy with the arrangement, cheerfully suggests doing this all day, and Dogbert proposes the next target.
punchline: Dogbert is deliberately baiting women into pursuing him so Dilbert can lecture them about consent, turning a scheme into a repeatable game.
summary: A little dog lures an overeager stranger into chasing him, setting up his owner to give her a stern lecture about respecting boundaries.

file: 1994/1994-05-13_dogbert consulting_liver_slab of liver_harvard mba_good debaters_brains wrapped.gif
title: Consultant Brains Wrapped Around Torsos

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I hired the "Dogbert Consulting Company" he said his consultants were so smart they had to wrap their brains around their torsos.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that looks like a slab of liver.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This slab of liver has an MBA from Harvard, you pointy-hair fool!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow, you guys are good debaters.

situation: The Boss complains to Dogbert that the consultants he hired from Dogbert's consulting company, supposedly so smart their brains are wrapped around their torsos, look like a slab of liver. Dogbert angrily insists the slab of liver has a Harvard MBA and insults the Boss. The Boss, cowed, admires their debating skill.
punchline: Dogbert wins the argument by simply insulting the Boss, who mistakes bullying for skilled debate, while the joke also implies an MBA consultant is no more useful than a slab of liver.
summary: A boss doubts his new consultants' intelligence, and Dogbert bullies him into submission by claiming a hunk of organ meat holds a prestigious degree.

file: 1994/1994-04-14_project dew drop_test report_explodes_beta trial_friendly customers_killed_friendly ones_project ducky.gif
title: Beta Testing Exploding Product on Customers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I agreed to ship project "Dewdrop" to some customers for beta testing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Didn't you read my test report? Dewdrop explodes when you plug it in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll limit the beta trial to friendly customers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We killed all the friendly ones with project "Ducky."

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he has agreed to send the Dewdrop project to customers for beta testing. Dilbert points out that his test report says the product explodes when plugged in. The Boss proposes limiting the trial to friendly customers, and Dilbert replies that the previous failed product already killed all of those.
punchline: The company's earlier defective product, Ducky, was so dangerous that it wiped out every friendly customer, so the Boss's safeguard has nobody left to protect.
summary: A manager commits to shipping a dangerous prototype to customers and is reminded that his plan to use only the nice ones is no longer possible.

file: 1994/1994-07-27_broke code_can't be measured_cut pay_depend on meeting_own darn fault_sales targets.gif
title: Pay Cut Disguised as Sales Bonus

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, twenty percent of your pay will depend on the company meeting its sales targets.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In effect, we'll cut your pay and tell you it's your own darn fault.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will the sales target be based on a complex formula and involve numbers that can't be accurately measured?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You broke the code!

situation: The Boss announces to his staff that twenty percent of their pay will now depend on the company hitting its sales targets, then candidly admits it is really a pay cut they will be blamed for. Dilbert asks whether the target will rely on an unmeasurable, overly complex formula, and the Boss reacts as if Dilbert has uncovered a secret.
punchline: The Boss's own admission that the performance-based pay scheme is really a disguised pay cut, and his dismay that Dilbert saw through the management trick, exposes how such incentive plans work.
summary: A manager cheerfully reveals that a new performance-linked pay plan is just a salary reduction with blame attached, and congratulates an employee for seeing through it.

file: 1994/1994-05-19_difficult_cooperate_project success_head is full_birdseed_pants glued_soap carving.gif
title: Birdseed Head, Glued Pants, Soap Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your department has a reputation for being difficult to work with. But I know we can cooperate to make my project a success.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'd love to help but my head is full of birdseed and my pants are glued to this chair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll talk to your boss.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Good luck. He's a soap carving.

situation: Dilbert visits another department and politely asks a coworker to cooperate on his project. The coworker cheerfully offers absurd excuses, claiming his head is full of birdseed and his pants are glued to his chair. When Dilbert says he will go to the coworker's boss, the coworker warns that the boss is a soap carving.
punchline: The department's reputation for being difficult is earned by ridiculous excuses for not helping, and the uncooperative attitude goes all the way up, since even the boss is supposedly an inanimate object.
summary: A hopeful engineer seeking help is stonewalled by a smiling coworker with bizarre excuses, and escalating to management turns out to be hopeless too.

file: 1994/1994-06-20_behead_corporate head hunter_employee_new employees_staffing problem_you'd be flexible_go postal_post office employee.gif
title: Headhunter Offers Disgruntled Postal Worker

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We've never needed a corporate headhunter before, but now it's the only way to solve our staffing problem.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you aware that headhunters find new employees? We don't behead the ones you already have.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't suppose you'd be flexible...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I could find a disgruntled ex-post office employee for you.

situation: The Boss tells Dogbert, who is working as a corporate headhunter, that the company's staffing problem can only be solved by hiring a headhunter. Dogbert clarifies that headhunters recruit new people rather than 'beheading' existing staff, which is what the Boss apparently hoped for. When the Boss asks if Dogbert could be flexible, Dogbert offers to supply a disgruntled former postal worker instead.
punchline: Dogbert's offer of a disgruntled ex-post office employee is a dark 'going postal' joke, implying he'd supply someone who would violently eliminate the Boss's existing staff.
summary: A boss hoping his headhunter will get rid of current workers gets offered an angry former mail carrier as a workaround.

file: 1994/1994-03-02_process engineering consultant_totally objective_dont care_right attitude_flowing robe_cherubs.gif
title: Dogbert Pitches Heartless Reengineering Consulting

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You should hire me as your process reengineering consultant.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I would be totally objective about what jobs to eliminate. Frankly, I don't care about anybody at your company!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've got the right attitude.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'll wear a flowing robe and surround myself with cherubs.

situation: Dogbert, seated in a chair, offers his services as a process reengineering consultant, promising total objectivity about which jobs to cut because he doesn't care about anyone at the company. Dilbert approves of this attitude and then says he will dress in a flowing robe and surround himself with cherubs, as if he were a deity.
punchline: Dilbert's reaction implies that the ideal reengineering consultant is a callous, god-like figure who can decide who loses their job with no sympathy at all.
summary: A dog pitches himself as the perfect downsizing adviser because he cares about no one, and the man hiring him responds by imagining himself as a heavenly judge.

file: 1994/1994-11-30_dogberts tech support_dierctions_arrange parts_piles_stand on chair_above cubicle wall_shout to coworkers_read manual.gif
title: Dogbert Tells Caller to Shout

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I know what your problem is...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Take all the parts and arrange them in neat piles. Now stand on your chair so you can see above your cubicle wall...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now shout "Does anybody know how to read a manual?"

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk and a customer's cubicle
situation: Dogbert, working a tech support phone line, tells a caller to lay out all the parts in neat piles and then stand on his chair above the cubicle wall. He then instructs the caller to shout to his coworkers asking if anyone knows how to read a manual. The caller stands in his cubicle with the phone to his ear, following the instructions.
punchline: Dogbert's tech support advice is to publicly humiliate the caller for not reading the manual, implying the problem is simply that he never bothered to read it.
summary: A tech support dog has a clueless caller assemble his parts and then loudly announce to the office that he needs help reading the instructions.

file: 1994/1994-01-17_bugs_bugs are smater_cubcicle_dumb_permission denied_plastic_plastic plant_tell the difference.gif
title: Plastic Plant Denied by Cubicle Gestapo

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... I'd like permission to keep a plastic plant in my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Gestapo Officer
transcript.text: Permission denied! Plants attract bugs. If I can't tell it's plastic how are the bugs going to know the difference?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: With all due respect, bugs are way smarter than you.

transcript.speaker: Cubicle Gestapo Officer
transcript.text: Oh yeah? I'd like to see them do this job.

setting: Office of the cubicle gestapo officer
situation: Dilbert asks a uniformed cubicle-policing officer for permission to keep a plastic plant at his desk. The officer refuses on the absurd grounds that bugs wouldn't be able to tell it from a real plant, and Dilbert replies that bugs are smarter than the officer. The officer indignantly challenges the bugs to do his job.
punchline: The officer's feeble comeback inadvertently concedes the insult, since being able to do his pointless, nonsensical job is hardly a mark of intelligence.
summary: A petty enforcer rejects a fake houseplant request with bizarre logic and then defends himself badly when his intelligence is questioned.

file: 1994/1994-11-04_physical intimidation_smack face_stupid_manage by intimidation_mob menatlity_gets smacked.gif
title: Managing By Physical Intimidation Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to manage by physical intimidation. If somebody says something stupid I'll just smack them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the stupidest thing I've ever heard.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: On the other hand, maybe I should give it a chance.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Smack!

situation: The Boss announces a new management style in which he will physically smack anyone who says something stupid. Dilbert immediately tells him it is the stupidest thing he has ever heard. In the final panel the Boss has been knocked to the floor, and Dilbert reconsiders the idea.
punchline: The Boss's new smacking policy is itself stupid by his own standard, so he gets smacked first, and Dilbert decides the policy has some merit after all.
summary: A manager's plan to slap anyone who speaks foolishly is turned against him the moment an employee calls it idiotic.

file: 1994/1994-11-09_pile binders_have view_cubicle walls_everyone binders.gif
title: Binders Stacked for Window View

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: ...and if I pile enough binders on my chair I'll have a window view!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got to try that.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow! I've never seen so much interest in our business plan!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I have two?

situation: Wally shows Dilbert how he stacks binders on his chair to raise himself high enough to see out a window. Dilbert decides to try it, and soon the Boss notices employees clamoring for copies of the company's business plan binders. He mistakes their demand for genuine interest.
punchline: The Boss thinks employees are eagerly engaged with the business plan, when they actually just want the binders to use as chair boosters.
summary: A boss misreads a rush for his binders as enthusiasm for strategy, when staff just want them as seat cushions.

file: 1994/1994-07-16_dimly lit cucbicle_carpal tunnel_crippled_last job_coal miner_gas explosion_new cubcile_canary.gif
title: Canary for the Cubicle Coal Mine

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I guess it's time to go back to my dimly lit cubicle and see if my carpal tunnel has crippled me yet.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: This is a lot like my last job as a coal miner, but without the threat of a gas explosion.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm moving you to a new cubicle over by Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Better get a canary.

situation: A wrist-braced employee complains that returning to his dimly lit cubicle and risking carpal tunnel is just like his former job as a coal miner, minus the gas explosion risk. The Boss then announces he is moving the employee to a new cubicle next to Wally. Dilbert quips that the employee had better get a canary.
punchline: Being moved next to Wally is treated like entering a toxic mine, since Wally's presence is implied to be hazardous enough to need a canary as a warning system.
summary: A worker likens his gloomy, injury-prone cubicle to a coal mine, and when he is reassigned next to Wally, a colleague suggests he bring a canary to detect danger.

file: 1994/1994-05-24_the boss_dilbert_project_cooler_acronym_joke_anticipated_beginning_binders_fulfilling_dogbert_job.gif
title: Boss Edits Insult Into Wording

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I was just reading your project status report.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You say the project is delayed "due to the ongoing bungling of a clueless, pointy-hair individual."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Instead of saying "due to," it would read better as "facilitated by."

situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk holding his project status report. He reads aloud a line blaming the delay on a clueless, pointy-haired individual, which is obviously about him. His only feedback is a minor wording change, suggesting 'facilitated by' instead of 'due to'.
punchline: The Boss recognizes the insult is about himself but misses the point entirely, offering only a stylistic edit and proving his cluelessness.
summary: A manager critiques the phrasing of a report that mocks his own incompetence, fixing the grammar but ignoring the accusation.

file: 1994/1994-04-07_crash test dummies_dilbert gets political_dinner party_gourmet cooking.gif
title: Dilbert's Dinner Party Full of Dummies

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert gets political

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd love to have you and... what's-her-face come to my little dinner party.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to do a little gourmet cooking... when I'm not raising money to battle unpopular diseases.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it just me, or are the other guests crash dummies?

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: So, then I...

transcript.speaker: Guest
transcript.text: It's just you.

situation: Dilbert, in a 'Dilbert Gets Political' strip, invites a politician to a dinner party and boasts about his gourmet cooking and fundraising for unpopular diseases, as politicians do. At the dinner, Dilbert looks around the table and asks whether the other guests are crash dummies. A guest curtly replies that it's just him.
punchline: Dilbert acts like a polished politician cultivating a pleasant image, yet at the party he notices the other guests seem like lifeless crash dummies, and is told the problem is only him.
summary: A politically minded Dilbert hosts a fancy dinner party and wonders whether his stiff, odd-looking guests are crash test dummies.

file: 1994/1994-04-08_lottery tickets_sale_value_yesterdays lottery_half priced lottery_cheat_scam_dogbert_salesman_scammer_office dog_customer.gif
title: Half-Price Lottery Tickets for Yesterday

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: What makes these a "value"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They're half the normal price, and yet the chance of winning is only one in ten million less.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Hey! This is for yesterday's lottery!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And your point is...?

setting: Dogbert's lottery ticket stand, in front of a desk under a "Value Priced Lottery Tickets" sign
situation: A customer in a red knit cap asks Dogbert, who is selling lottery tickets from behind a desk, why the discounted tickets count as a bargain. Dogbert explains that the price is half but the odds are only slightly worse. The customer then notices the tickets are for yesterday's drawing, and Dogbert shrugs off the complaint.
punchline: The tickets are cheap because they are for a lottery that has already been drawn, so they can never win, and Dogbert shamelessly brushes off the customer's complaint.
summary: Dogbert pitches bargain lottery tickets to a buyer who only later realizes the drawing has already happened.

file: 1994/1994-05-03_all day meeting_bathroom_critique the decor_house_kitchen shoddy_sub teams.gif
title: Staff Meeting Invades Dilbert's House

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How foolish of you to host the all-day staff meeting at your house.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's form sub-teams to be more efficient. Ted will do accidental spills. Alice, you critique the decor. I'll be a floater.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Kitchen, shoddily done...

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I spilled mayonaise on the wall.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Where's the bathroom?

setting: Dilbert's house, at the front door and inside, during an all-day staff meeting
situation: The coworkers arrive at Dilbert's home for an all-day staff meeting that he is hosting. The Boss splits everyone into sub-teams for efficiency, assigning Ted to accidental spills, Alice to critiquing the decor, and himself as a floater. The staff then proceed to mess up and judge Dilbert's house while he stands there looking dismayed.
punchline: The Boss's corporate efficiency mindset turns a meeting at someone's home into a division of labor for insulting and damaging the host's house.
summary: A manager organizes his team into specialized groups whose jobs are to spill things and criticize the home hosting their meeting.

file: 1994/1994-01-22_opposites attract_beautiful women_drawing power_women  love pose_intellectually staimulating.gif
title: Opposites Attract Dating Advice

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're unsuccessful in love because you keep forgetting opposites attract.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Logically, the women who would be must attracted to you are beautiful and intellectually stimulating.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're right. I've been underestimating my drawing power.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And women love it when you pose like this for them.

setting: Outdoors on rocky ground, with Dilbert and Dogbert sitting on rocks
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert his love life fails because he forgets that opposites attract, suggesting that beautiful, intellectual women would be drawn to him. Dilbert is flattered and agrees he has underestimated his appeal. Dogbert then encourages him to keep sitting in a static pose, with his back to the viewer, as if it will impress women.
punchline: Dogbert's flattering logic is just a setup to get Dilbert to sit still in a ridiculous pose, implying the 'opposites attract' advice was insincere or a joke at Dilbert's expense.
summary: Dogbert persuades a hopeful Dilbert that his romantic prospects are brighter than he thinks, then nudges him into an odd posture he insists will charm women.

file: 1994/1994-10-28_new finance guy_hate automatically_justify photocopy_business case_make copies_pinch pennies_natural.gif
title: New Finance Guy Is Instantly Hateable

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ray's our new finance guy. He's got a face that makes you hate him automatically.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're right. I'm already hating him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wait until he opens his mouth!

transcript.speaker: Ray
transcript.text: From now on I want a business case to justify all of your photocopying.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is he a natural or what?!!

situation: The Boss introduces Ray, the new finance guy, to Dilbert and boasts that his face makes people hate him automatically. Dilbert agrees he already dislikes him, and the Boss says it gets worse once Ray speaks. Ray then demands a business case to justify all photocopying, and the Boss gleefully praises him as a natural.
punchline: The Boss treats being instantly hateable as a prized qualification for finance, and Ray's petty demand to justify photocopying proves the point.
summary: A manager proudly presents his newest bean counter as someone people loathe on sight, then gloats as the man immediately imposes an absurd paperwork burden.

file: 1994/1994-10-30_trap set_dogbert sniffs_thief found_set up_decoy lunch_synthetic female hormones_wally boobs_caught_busted_theif.gif
title: Dogbert Sniffs Out Lunch Thief

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exhibit "A" is my empty lunch bag, last seen full.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Only the people in this room had the motive and the opportunity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Inspector Dogbert will investigate.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sniff! You were in the supply room with Willy the mail boy all morning. You are innocent.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sort of.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sniff! I give you a "C+" for hygiene but you did not take the lunch.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sniff! Bologna... potato chips... carrot sticks... Ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This is the thief who took the decoy lunch... which we laced with synthetic female hormones!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You can't prove anything!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is there something you'd like to get off your chest?

situation: Dilbert gathers coworkers in a room to find who stole his lunch and appoints Dogbert as inspector. Dogbert sniffs each suspect, clearing Alice and another coworker, then identifies Wally by the smell of bologna, chips and carrots. Dogbert reveals the decoy lunch was laced with synthetic female hormones.
punchline: Wally is exposed as the thief not by evidence but by the hormone-laced lunch, and Dogbert's closing question mocks the chest enlargement Wally is presumably developing.
summary: A bait-and-trap sting using a doctored decoy lunch lets a dog detective catch the office food thief by sniffing, then taunt him about the side effects.

file: 1994/1994-03-24_dogbert_world will end_year 2000_compelling logic_news.gif
title: Dogbert's Round Number Doomsday Prophecy

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've become a doomsday prophet so I can scare gullible people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm telling everyone the world will end in year 2000. My compelling logic is that 2000 is a big round number.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's B-I-I-I-G and R-O-O-UND

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop it!!!

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert in an armchair
situation: Dogbert, wearing a yellow doomsday prophet hat, announces to Dilbert that he has become a doomsday prophet in order to frighten gullible people. He explains that his prediction of the world ending in the year 2000 rests only on 2000 being a big round number. He keeps drawing out the words 'big' and 'round' until Dilbert, who has been reading the newspaper, angrily tells him to stop.
punchline: Dogbert's entire 'compelling logic' for the apocalypse is that 2000 is a big round number, which is no logic at all, and he makes it more annoying by drawling the words.
summary: A scheming dog dons a prophet's hat and bases his end-of-the-world forecast on nothing more than a tidy-looking year, until his owner has had enough.

file: 1994/1994-07-04_baywatch_morale is low_talk of mutiny_project staus report_death to boss_pointy haired one.gif
title: Honest Status Report Reveals Mutiny

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my daily project status report.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Morale is low. There is talk of mutiny. We dream of quitting and becoming lifeguards on "Baywatch." Death to the Pointy-Haired One."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Holy cow! "Baywatch" is hiring??!

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss his daily project status report. The Boss reads it aloud, and it describes low morale, talk of mutiny, a dream of quitting to become Baywatch lifeguards, and a call for the Boss's death. The Boss ignores the threats and fixates on the idea that Baywatch is hiring.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he skips over the open hostility toward himself and only registers the offhand detail about job openings on Baywatch.
summary: A brutally candid status report is read out by a manager who misses everything except a throwaway mention of lifeguard jobs.

file: 1994/1994-02-28_reengineer_business processes_jump on band wagon.gif
title: Boss Assigns Reengineering, Offers Devilish Support

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just read this great book about how to "reengineer" our business processes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everybody's doing it. We'd better jump under the bandwagon before the train leaves the station! I'm putting you in charge.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you need any management support you know where to go.

situation: The Boss, holding a business book, announces he wants to reengineer the company's business processes because everyone else is doing it. He mixes up his clichés and puts Dilbert in charge of the effort. He then tells Dilbert to come to him for management support, while Dilbert imagines the Boss as a devil holding a pitchfork.
punchline: The Boss's offer of 'management support' is pictured as a literal devil in Dilbert's mind, implying that management is the source of the problem rather than a help.
summary: After reading a trendy book, a manager dumps a company-wide overhaul on his employee and promises backing that the employee sees as pure evil.

file: 1994/1994-11-13_promote district manager_technical knowledge_valuable_no promotions_promote al_no knowledge al_grumpy.gif
title: Promoting Al For Knowing Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need to promote one of you to the District Manager position.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, your technical knowledge is too valuable to lose.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ditto for Alice. Neither of you can be promoted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The only logical choice is to promote Al because he has no valuable knowledge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Al??! A Director??! He doesn't know what day of the week it is!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're just grumpy because it's Monday.

transcript.speaker: Al
transcript.text: It's Thursday.

situation: The Boss tells his staff he needs to promote someone to District Manager, then rules out Dilbert and Alice because their technical knowledge is too valuable. He decides to promote Al, who has no valuable knowledge. Dilbert is outraged, and Al shows he doesn't even know the day of the week.
punchline: The company promotes the least knowledgeable person because competent employees are too useful to move up, and Al's obliviousness about the day proves he is unfit for the job.
summary: A manager passes over his skilled workers for a promotion and rewards the clueless Al instead, since nothing of value would be lost.

file: 1994/1994-06-02_diversity training_respect differences_four groups_insults group_dog_teaching_workers_animals_education.gif
title: Diversity Training Four-Box Insult

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In "diversity sensitivity" training you will learn to respect those who are different.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People basically fall into these four groups.

transcript.speaker: Chart
transcript.text: Ugly smart. Cute smart. Ugly stupid. Cute stupid.

transcript.speaker: Unseen audience member
transcript.text: This is different than I expected.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I notice that all of you are in this box here.

setting: Conference room during a training session
situation: Dogbert leads a diversity sensitivity training seminar for office workers. He presents a two-by-two chart dividing people into ugly/cute and smart/stupid. When an attendee remarks that this isn't what they expected, Dogbert gestures at the chart and reveals which box the entire audience falls into.
punchline: The diversity training turns into an insult as Dogbert places everyone in the room in the box he clearly considers the worst, implying they are all ugly and stupid.
summary: A trainer dog sorts people into appearance and intelligence categories, then cheerfully informs his audience of colleagues that they all belong in the least flattering square.

file: 1994/1994-11-25_continue seeing dilbert_pass my test_dogs are superior_she devil.gif
title: Dogbert's Dogs-Versus-Cats Dating Test

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Liz, if you're going to continue seeing Dilbert, you'll have to pass my test.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Question one: Give seven hundred reasons why dogs are superior to cats.

transcript.speaker: Liz
transcript.text: Well, the first six hundred reasons have to do with the fact that you're cuter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Fingernails! She-devil!

situation: Dogbert sits on a couch with a clipboard and tells Liz, Dilbert's girlfriend, that she must pass his test to keep dating Dilbert. His first question demands seven hundred reasons dogs are superior to cats. Liz answers by flattering Dogbert's cuteness and then scratches his belly, which makes him melt.
punchline: Liz, who is apparently a cat person, wins the test by flattering Dogbert and scratching him, and he is so overcome that he gives in despite his own demand.
summary: A pompous dog interrogating his owner's girlfriend is easily disarmed when she compliments him and gives him a good scratch.

file: 1994/1994-01-01_making film_pretending_kiss_girl friend_hug_dogbert_mother_send film_stop worry_family.gif
title: Faking a Girlfriend on Film

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mmm... Oh, Dilbert! Mmm...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Cut!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you really think this will make Mom stop worrying about me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Only if you raise your voice for the "mmm" part.

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a door
situation: Dilbert hugs himself and makes kissing noises while pretending to be with a girlfriend, as Dogbert films him with a camcorder from a stool. Dogbert calls cut, and Dilbert asks whether the fake footage will really stop his mother from worrying about him. Dogbert gives him acting direction instead of reassurance.
punchline: Dogbert's only concern is whether Dilbert's pathetic solo make-out performance is convincing enough, implying the ruse is sad and nothing else about it matters.
summary: Dogbert directs Dilbert as he embraces thin air for a home video meant to convince his mother that he has a love life.

file: 1994/1994-01-05_no raises_promotions_job titles_named beverly.gif
title: Flattened Org Means No Raises

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're flattening the organization to eliminate levels and put everybody in a wide salary band.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now instead of not getting a promotion you'll only not get a raise.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So, what job title do we use?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll all be named Beverly.

setting: Office, in front of an employee
situation: The Boss announces a reorganization that flattens the company by removing levels and putting everyone in one wide salary band. He cheerfully explains that employees will now merely fail to get raises instead of failing to get promotions. An employee asks what job title to use, and the Boss absurdly replies that everyone will be named Beverly.
punchline: The flattened organization is just a cover for removing any path to advancement or pay increases, and the Boss's nonsensical answer about job titles shows he hasn't thought it through at all.
summary: A manager spins a restructuring that scraps promotions as a harmless change, then gives a ridiculous answer when asked what everyone's title will be.

file: 1994/1994-09-05_opinion_charge fee_copensation_idiots_cost you.gif
title: Dogbert Charges For Opinions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: From now on, I'm going to charge anybody who gives me their opinion.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People are idiots. If I have to listen to their opinions, I deserve compensation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're forgetting that "From the mouths of babes... comes... something good."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That'll cost you a buck.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, in bed at night
situation: Dilbert is lying in bed reading a book while Dogbert sits on the blanket. Dogbert announces he will charge anyone who gives him their opinion, because listening to idiots deserves compensation. When Dilbert offers a counterpoint quoting a proverb, Dogbert immediately bills him a dollar.
punchline: Dogbert enforces his new fee on the very first opinion he hears, and Dilbert's well-meaning counterargument costs him a buck.
summary: A dog declares that anyone sharing a view with him must pay, then promptly collects from his owner's first objection.

file: 1994/1994-02-18_resources vailable_common employees_more money_project_all gone_hypocrite boss_no time.gif
title: Boss Promises Resources, Then Refuses Them

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Although I'm technically the "boss" I believe it's my job to make resources available to you, the common employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need more money for my project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sorry. All gone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll get on your calendar so we can discuss it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've got twenty minutes next summer.

situation: The Boss tells the assembled employees that it is his job to make resources available to them. When Dilbert asks for more money for his project, the Boss says the budget is all gone. Dilbert then suggests booking time to discuss it, and the Boss offers a slot months away.
punchline: The Boss's lofty claim about supporting his staff is immediately contradicted when he refuses funding and is practically unavailable to even discuss it.
summary: A manager boasts about being a provider of resources, then turns down a simple funding request and offers a meeting nearly a year away.

file: 1994/1994-03-01_reengineering_questioning employees_get fired_objective data_business process_flying monkeys_finished design.gif
title: Reengineering With Flying Monkeys

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Reengineering is simple. You start by questioning the employees who would get fired if you succeed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then you use that objective data to design a more efficient business process.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you say you use flying monkeys to deliver the finished design?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They're very fast.

situation: The Boss explains his method of business process reengineering to Dilbert and other employees, starting with interviewing the people whose jobs would be eliminated. Dilbert, who has apparently been tuning out, asks about flying monkeys delivering the design, and the Boss simply defends their speed.
punchline: The Boss's reengineering method is absurd at both ends: it relies on biased data from people who would lose their jobs, and its output is delivered by flying monkeys, which he defends only on speed.
summary: A manager outlines a flawed process-redesign method, then calmly defends an even more ridiculous delivery mechanism.

file: 1994/1994-06-25_date_dilbert nervous_date aware_hypotheisis_hold hands_one clammy_hand loses ontrol.gif
title: Dilbert's Hand Betrays His Nerves

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I can tell that you like me because you don't quite know what to do with your hands.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: To test my hypothesis I will hold this hand and observe the change.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: The "control" hand remains limp and clammy. Its twin loses control. Hypothesis confirmed.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thupa thupa thupa thupa thupa

setting: Outdoors, on a walk during a date
situation: Dilbert is walking with a woman on a date. She observes that his awkwardness with his hands shows he likes her, then takes one of his hands to test her theory. His other hand starts flapping wildly and uncontrollably, which she treats as scientific confirmation.
punchline: Dilbert's nervous attraction is so overwhelming that his free hand flaps out of control, proving the date's scientific hypothesis and exposing how smitten he is.
summary: A scientifically minded date tests whether her companion is smitten by holding his hand, and his other hand flutters wildly in response.

file: 1994/1994-08-31_unpaid overtime_mba class_working for free_rub head_good luck.gif
title: MBA Student Prices Head Rubs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd stay and work some unpaid overtime with you but I'm taking MBA classes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you took MBA classes you'd understand that working for free is a low NPV.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you don't mind, before big tests I'd like to rub your head for luck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It'll cost you a nickel.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he can't work unpaid overtime because he is taking MBA classes. The boss, sitting at his desk, replies that an MBA would teach Dilbert that working for free has a low net present value. Dilbert then asks to rub the boss's bald head for luck before tests, and the boss charges him a nickel.
punchline: The boss uses the finance concept he just invoked against Dilbert by charging for the head rub, turning his own sensitivity to unpaid work into a small fee for Dilbert's superstition.
summary: A boss who lectures about the poor value of unpaid labor promptly demands payment when his employee wants a good-luck head rub.

file: 1994/1994-09-11_copier paper_laser printer_made mockery_phil_prince of inssufficient light_punishment_tracked speatrely_borrowing paper.gif
title: Paper Thief Punished by Phil

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Copy Room (sign on the door as Dilbert peeks in)

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Stop right there!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's Phil, the Prince of Insufficient Light!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: What's in your hands?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm just borrowing some paper for the laser printer. There's no law against that!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: I think we both know that the copier paper and the printer paper are purchased and tracked separately.

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: You've made a mockery of the system! I darn you to heck!

transcript.speaker: Phil
transcript.text: Your punishment is to sit at the secretary's cubicle and endure the stale wit of your co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Co-worker
transcript.text: Hey, Wendy, there's something different about you today!

setting: Office copy room and the secretary's cubicle
situation: Dilbert sneaks into the copy room to take paper for his laser printer, but Phil, dressed as a devil-like figure with a giant spoon, catches him. Phil declares that copier paper and printer paper are tracked separately and sentences Dilbert to sit at the secretary's cubicle. There, a co-worker mistakes Dilbert for the secretary, Wendy, and makes a tired joke.
punchline: Dilbert's punishment for stealing paper is to sit in the secretary's cubicle and suffer his co-workers' weak jokes, as one greets him as 'Wendy' with a stale line.
summary: A pedantic office enforcer sentences a paper-borrowing engineer to a fate of lame jokes at the receptionist's desk.

file: 1994/1994-09-09_complicated_create chart_decision process_plan_question_talking about chart_wasting money.gif
title: Chart Explaining Wasteful Decision Process

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This chart shows the decision process we're using for my project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here we're wasting money. Then someone said "Hey, let's create a complicated chart." Now we're at this meeting, talking about the chart.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great... There goes the plan.

situation: Dilbert presents a flowchart of the decision process for his project, pointing out where money is wasted and that the chart itself led to this very meeting. The Boss then says he has a question, and Dilbert glumly realizes his plan to get through the presentation is ruined.
punchline: Dilbert's presentation honestly exposes the pointless waste of the process, but the Boss's innocent question shows the meeting will drag on, derailing Dilbert's hopes of finishing quickly.
summary: A presenter mocks his own diagram of a wasteful approval process, only to have a manager's interruption confirm the waste will continue.

file: 1994/1994-03-25_world ends_year 2000_creator_universe_counting system_round numbers_feeling anxiety_dog_rat_conversation_animals.gif
title: Doomsday Prophet Sells Round-Number Fear

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm predicting that the world will end in the year 2000.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The creator of the universe works in mysterious ways. But he uses a base ten counting system and likes round numbers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So you really want to avoid being, let's say, in mobile home number 1,000,000 in the year 2000.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm feeling anxiety.

setting: Empty space with a plain background, likely Dogbert's doomsday-prophet scene
situation: Dogbert, wearing a yellow striped hat, announces a prediction that the world will end in the year 2000. He justifies it by claiming the creator likes round numbers, then pointedly suggests Ratbert avoid being in mobile home number 1,000,000. Ratbert, listening, becomes anxious.
punchline: Dogbert uses absurd numerology to scare Ratbert into feeling personally threatened, mocking doomsday predictions and their flimsy logic.
summary: A turbaned Dogbert spins a ridiculous round-number theory of the apocalypse until his small listener is nervously convinced he is in danger.

file: 1994/1994-03-27_teller_automated_machine_menus_chinese language option.gif
title: Performance Anxiety at the ATM

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm getting performance anxiety at the automated teller machine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel the impatient glare of the stranger behind me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I try to prove I'm competent by speeding through the menus.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good Lord, I hit the Mandarin Chinese language option.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh no! I think I transferred my life's savings to the "United Way."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Great... Now his eyeballs are stuck to the back of my neck.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is exactly why I hate going to the automated teller.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think a little "Visine" would make him slide right off.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There was a time I could afford that...

setting: Outside a bank at an automated teller machine, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tries to use an ATM while a stranger waits impatiently behind him. Rushing through the menus, he accidentally picks the Mandarin Chinese option and seemingly transfers his life savings to charity. The stranger's stare feels like it is stuck to his neck, and Dogbert later jokes about eye drops to wash him off.
punchline: Dilbert's rushed ATM mishap cost him all his savings, so he can no longer even afford a bottle of Visine to get rid of the staring stranger.
summary: A flustered man hurries through a cash machine and blows his entire savings while a stranger breathes down his neck.

file: 1994/1994-05-31_sexist comments_sensitivity training_midol_period_women_chicks_shopping_hits boss_crying.gif
title: Boss's Sexist Remark Earns Whumps

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm sending you to "diversity sensitivity" training.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice doesn't have to go because chicks are born already knowing this stuff. It's as natural as shopping and crying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I get a "Midol" for either one of you?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whump whump whump

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he must attend diversity sensitivity training, then says Alice is exempt because women are naturally good at sensitivity, comparing it to shopping and crying. Alice responds by violently pummeling the Boss while Dilbert dryly asks if anyone needs Midol.
punchline: The Boss's sexist remark about why Alice doesn't need sensitivity training demonstrates exactly why he needs it himself, and Alice's violent reaction is brushed off by Dilbert as a hormonal issue, mocking the same stereotype.
summary: A boss excuses a female coworker from sensitivity training with a crude stereotype and promptly gets beaten up for it.

file: 1994/1994-06-19_new cucbicle_self suffcient_work space_life suport_various tubes_watch to body_vital signs_monitor_central location_human resources dept_emergency hiring.gif
title: The Cuborg 2000 Life-Support Cubicle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's your new cubicle: the "Cuborg 2000."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a self-sufficient work space and life-support system!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These tubes attach to various parts of your body so you never have to leave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Various parts"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's just say you don't want to get these two tubes mixed up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll monitor your vital signs from a central location.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The company nurse?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, the Human Resources department, in case we have to do some emergency hiring.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it upgradeable?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, the Cuborg 3000 is expected to have air holes.

setting: Office, next to a futuristic pod-like cubicle
situation: The Boss shows Dilbert a new cubicle called the Cuborg 2000, a sealed pod with tubes that hook up to the occupant's body so he never has to leave. Dilbert nervously asks about the details, learning that HR will monitor his vital signs so they can hire a replacement if he dies. He asks if it can be upgraded and learns the next model will finally include air holes.
punchline: The company monitors employees' vital signs not out of concern for their health but to be ready to hire a replacement the moment they die, and the current pod doesn't even have air holes.
summary: A manager proudly unveils a sealed life-support cubicle that keeps staff chained to their desks, with HR watching for the moment a worker expires.
