file: 1994/1994-02-14_desparation_fabric of spce_fear_helpless_meeting forever_time division_marketing guy.gif
title: Terrorizing Marketing With Technobabble

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: What shall we tell the guy from Marketing this time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hee hee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see if we can make him feel a sense of helpless desperation and fear.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The time-division multiplexer opened a hole in the fabric of space.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: We're trapped in this meeting forever.

situation: Dilbert and a bald, bespectacled engineer plot how to mess with the marketing guy who is about to join their meeting. They decide to scare him with invented technical jargon, claiming a piece of equipment has torn a hole in space. The marketing guy sits between them looking worried as they deliver the story.
punchline: The engineers casually invent absurd technobabble to terrify a non-technical colleague, exploiting his inability to tell real explanations from nonsense.
summary: Two engineers amuse themselves by feeding a gullible marketing colleague a sci-fi fabrication about a rift in reality.

file: 1994/1994-05-08_bob_budget analyst_delegate_dinosaur_engineers_find dumber customers_letter_marketing genius_new vp_senior mangement_wedgies.gif
title: Bob the Dinosaur Wedgies Executives

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bob the Dinosaur gives wedgies to corporate people who deserve it

transcript.speaker: Budget Analyst
transcript.text: I don't understand any of our projects. So I cut the ones with "E" in their names.

transcript.speaker: Budget Analyst
transcript.text: What was that letter?

transcript.speaker: Budget Analyst
transcript.text: Eeee!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: We doubled our costs, to add back-up systems.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: You can't be too careful.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Two at once, in case one enjoys it!

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Mmm.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Genius
transcript.text: Market segmentation is the key.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Genius
transcript.text: Don't improve the product, just find dumber customers!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: These guys know how to delegate!

transcript.speaker: Senior Management
transcript.text: You're the new VP of Wedgies.

situation: Bob the Dinosaur, a giant green dinosaur, gives wedgies to various corporate people who 'deserve it' after they say foolish things. A budget analyst cuts projects with the letter E, engineers double costs adding backups, and a marketing genius suggests finding dumber customers. Each gets a wedgie, and finally two senior managers are so impressed by Bob's delegation that they promote him to VP of Wedgies.
punchline: Bob's wedgie-giving is so well suited to the corporate culture that management rewards him with a promotion, treating punishment as admirable delegation.
summary: A wedgie-dealing dinosaur punishes foolish corporate decisions and ends up promoted by the very executives who admire his methods.

file: 1994/1994-12-28_bring strangers in_test product_strangers are stupid_good candy.gif
title: Strangers Are Stupid, Have Candy

transcript.speaker: Eye-Patch Coworker
transcript.text: Sure, we could bring some strangers in to test our product for ease of use...

transcript.speaker: Eye-Patch Coworker
transcript.text: But that could take all afternoon and cost at least a hundred dollars.

transcript.speaker: Eye-Patch Coworker
transcript.text: And all it proves is strangers are stupid.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes they have good candy.

situation: At a meeting, a coworker wearing an eye patch considers testing the product's usability with strangers brought in off the street. He dismisses the idea as too slow and costly, concluding it would only prove that strangers are stupid. The Boss responds that strangers sometimes have good candy.
punchline: The Boss ignores the usability testing question entirely and fixates on the only possible benefit he can imagine, free candy from strangers, showing how little he values real user feedback.
summary: A team weighs asking outsiders to try their product, but the boss's only takeaway is the chance of a sweet treat.

file: 1994/1994-08-18_fired_outplacement agency_own cubicle_photocopies_food stamps_dollar bills.gif
title: Fired Wally Offered Photocopy Cubicle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're fired, Wally. But since we care, we've contracted an outplacement agency to help you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll get your own cubicle. And you can make all the photocopies you want!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What would I want to photocopy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Food stamps, dollar bills, that sort of thing.

situation: The Boss fires Wally but claims the company cares, offering an outplacement agency's help. He sweetens the deal with his own cubicle and unlimited photocopies. When Wally asks what he would copy, the Boss suggests food stamps and dollar bills.
punchline: The Boss's idea of a generous severance perk is free photocopying, and his suggested uses reveal that he expects the fired employee to end up broke and on welfare.
summary: A boss pretends to be kind while dismissing an employee, then unwittingly predicts the man's poverty with his idea of a perk.

file: 1994/1994-05-15_pretending_personal lives_interested_management technique_job satisfaction_more money_boost intangible benefits_chisel away_salaries_families_wife divorced_job lowers self esteem_attract mate_said hello.gif
title: Boss Fakes Interest in Families

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hi, guys. How are your families?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you pretending to be interested in our personal lives?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a management technique to increase your job satisfaction without giving you more money.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to boost your intangible benefits while continuing to chisel away at your salaries.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But enough about me... How are those families of yours?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My wife divorced me because you make me work so many hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This job lowers my self-esteem too much to attract a mate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tell them I said "Hi."

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert and Wally about their families, and when Dilbert challenges the sudden interest, the Boss openly admits it is a management trick to boost morale without raising pay. When he asks again, the employees reveal that the job has wrecked their personal lives, and he responds by asking them to pass along a casual greeting.
punchline: The Boss shows no concern that his employees' marriages and love lives have been ruined by the job; he only wants to look friendly while paying them less.
summary: A manager cheerfully confesses that his show of caring is just a cheap substitute for raises, then brushes off his staff's personal misery with a breezy greeting.

file: 1994/1994-06-26_lab supplies_batteries_electric motor_wheels_hand truck_build go cart_lab_building liner accelrator.gif
title: Go-Cart Disguised as Linear Accelerator

transcript.speaker: Lab Coworker
transcript.text: The new lab supplies are in!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We got the batteries and the electric motor!

transcript.speaker: Lab Coworker
transcript.text: Take the wheels off the hand-truck and we can start building our go-cart.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I'll drop in on the lab.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you working on now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're building a linear accelerator.

transcript.speaker: Lab Coworker
transcript.text: Marketing insisted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good. Good. Carry on.

transcript.speaker: Lab Coworker
transcript.text: We really don't appreciate him enough.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's put a TV in this baby.

setting: A research lab at the office
situation: Dilbert and a lab coworker use newly delivered lab supplies to build a go-cart from a hand-truck's wheels, a motor and batteries. When the Boss drops in and asks what they are doing, Dilbert claims it's a linear accelerator and blames marketing. The Boss accepts this and leaves, and the pair decide to add a TV to their go-cart.
punchline: The Boss is so easily fooled by technical-sounding jargon that two engineers can openly build a toy go-cart on company time and he praises them for it.
summary: Engineers goofing off on a homemade go-cart pass it off as serious science to a boss who swallows the story whole.

file: 1994/1994-09-03_rock paper scissors_project approved_toss up_random selection.gif
title: Boss Decides Projects With Rock-Paper-Scissors

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How decisions are made

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Rock! Scissors!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your project is approved... unless scissors can't cut rock.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Assume it's sheet rock.

situation: Under the caption 'How decisions are made', the Boss sits alone at his desk playing a game of rock-paper-scissors against himself while a project proposal lies in front of him. He then tells Dilbert his project is approved unless scissors can't cut rock. Dilbert supplies a loophole by assuming the rock is sheet rock.
punchline: Dilbert's pun on sheet rock (drywall, which scissors can cut) lets him game an absurd, random decision process, implying that management decisions are arbitrary and can be manipulated by anyone clever enough.
summary: A manager settles the fate of an employee's project by playing a childish hand game with himself, and the employee wins by exploiting a wordplay technicality.
